The heart is not a chamber.  
It is a cathedral.

A massive, thundering structure of muscle and light, beating with ancient purpose. The raft enters the atrium, and the current becomes chaotic — swirling, splitting, dividing.

The Blue‑Born try to hold onto each other, but the bloodstream does not allow it.

One by one, they are swept into different chambers, different arteries, different destinies. Their hands slip. Their voices vanish. Their faces disappear into the rushing red.

There is no time for goodbye.  
There is no ceremony for separation.  
The body simply moves them on.

This is the truth of the Heartstream:

No one stays together.  
Everyone is carried away.  
Life is a river that never lets you hold what you love for long.

works.title: The Yellow Drop and The Plain Before Sound
works.blurb: a prose poem in which falling notes of sound build a world that collapses back into waking.

passages.text:
The Yellow Drop and The Plain Before Sound

In the first morning, the ear held only a pale, waiting surface — a blank stretch of nothing that felt more like potential than space.

Then a yellow drop of sound fell.

It struck the emptiness and rippled outward in warm, trembling rings, the way the first stir of wind might ripple across a still lake. The ripple brightened the plain, hinting at depth, hinting at direction, as if the world were remembering how to begin.

A second sound followed — a high, feather‑light note that fluttered across the ripples like a bird testing the air.  
Then a deeper tone arrived, slow and weighted, settling into the ground like packed earth.  
A bright, sharp chime cracked through the space, breaking open the horizon the way a wave breaks against stone.

They fell at irregular intervals, like a hesitant composer testing notes in an empty hall.  
Each one a different shade of sound — thin silver ticks, dull red thuds, pale blue hums — spreading outward, overlapping, interfering.  
Where they crossed, new patterns formed: soft oscillations, trembling grids, invisible architecture.

This was not light painting a scene.  
This was sound building one.

High notes lifted the air, giving it height.  
Low notes thickened the ground, giving it weight.  
Mid‑tones stretched themselves into long, trembling lines that became the first hints of structure — arches of resonance, pillars of vibration, corridors made of nothing but pressure and rhythm.

The soundscape grew more intricate.  
The air thickened with tone.  
The ground hummed with quiet intention.

And still, the yellow drop kept falling.

Each drip struck the forming landscape with a steady, patient rhythm.  
Each one added a new layer of motion.  
Each one deepened the sense that something was gathering itself, preparing to become.

The rhythm quickened — not frantic, but inevitable, like a tide rising toward shore.  
The whole sound‑world leaned forward, trembling at the edge of revelation.

Then the final drop fell — bright, sharp, impossibly clear.

And the body opened its eyes.

The sound‑architecture collapsed in an instant, folding back into silence.  
The ripples flattened.  
The spires dissolved.  
The trembling ground became nothing more than sensation.

The point of view slid outward, smooth as breath — from the ear’s inner creation to the dim room beyond the eyelids.

We see now through the body’s eyes.

The alarm is buzzing.  
The morning has begun.  
But for a heartbeat, the echo of that sound‑born world lingers — the memory of a universe that rose and fell in the space between dreaming and waking.

works.title: Internal Affairs: The Body Has Notes
works.blurb: twelve comic sketches where every body part gets its own petty, bickering voice.

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
Internal Affairs: The Body Has Notes

1. The City Scene — “New York Should Come With Padding”

He walks through Midtown like everyone else: head forward, earbuds in, mind on autopilot.

But his left shoulder is already fed up.

Left Shoulder:  
“Oh fantastic, another elbow. Does no one here know how to walk? I swear this city is just a pinball machine with rent.”

Right Shoulder:  
“Calm down. It’s New York. We get bumped. It’s part of the charm.”

Left Shoulder:  
“Charm? That guy just used me as a turn signal.”

His ribs chime in, rattling with indignation.

Ribs:  
“He’s right, you know. We’re basically public infrastructure at this point.”

His knees, always dramatic, groan.

Knees:  
“Can we not fight? We’re doing all the work down here.”

His feet, exhausted and cynical, mutter without lifting their voices.

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
Feet:  
“Try being stepped on. Then talk to me about suffering.”

Meanwhile, the man himself?  
He’s thinking about whether he left the stove on.

2. The Love Scene — “The Heart Has Notes, The Stomach Has Opinions”

He sees someone beautiful on the subway.

His heart immediately leaps into a full orchestral swell.

Heart:  
“Oh. Oh. Oh. This is it. This is the moment. Everyone be cool.”

His lungs inhale sharply.

Lungs:  
“Why are we breathing like we’re running a marathon? Calm down.”

His hands start sweating.

Hands:  
“We’re nervous! We’re allowed to be nervous!”

His stomach, always the realist, grumbles.

Stomach:  
“Don’t get attached. We’re still recovering from the last crush.”

His brain, trying to maintain dignity, clears its throat.

Brain:  
“Everyone shut up. We’re going to smile politely and not embarrass ourselves.”

His heart, already composing wedding vows:  
“I think we should marry them.”

His brain:  
“We don’t even know their name.”

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
His heart:  
“Names are just labels.”

His brain:  
“Please stop.”

3. The Anger Scene — “The Body Reacts Before the Man Does”

Someone cuts him off in traffic.

His jaw clenches instantly.

Jaw:  
“Say the word. I’m ready to grind.”

His hands tighten on the wheel.

Hands:  
“Let me honk. Just once. A polite honk. A civilized honk.”

His heart spikes.

Heart:  
“Fight or flight! Fight or flight! I vote fight!”

His brain, exhausted:  
“We’re not fighting anyone. We’re going to breathe.”

His lungs, reluctantly:  
“Fine. In… out… in… out…”

His teeth, muttering:  
“Cowards.”

4. The Hunger‑While‑Dieting Scene — “Civil War in the Abdomen”

He walks past a bakery.

His nose swoons.

Nose:  
“Is that… cinnamon? Fresh bread? We should go in. For research.”

His stomach roars like a mythic beast.

Stomach:  
“YES. FEED ME.”

His brain, clutching a clipboard:  
“No. We’re on a diet. We agreed.”

His stomach:  
“I didn’t agree to anything.”

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
His mouth, already watering:  
“I mean… one bite wouldn’t hurt.”

His brain:  
“It absolutely would.”

His legs, traitorous:  
“We’re turning toward the bakery.”

His brain:  
“No we’re not.”

His legs:  
“We already did.”

His willpower, tiny and trembling:  
“Please… please… don’t…”

His stomach:  
“TO GLORY.”

5. The Quiet Moment — “Everyone Has Something to Say”

He sits on a park bench at the end of the day.

His back sighs with relief.

Back:  
“Finally. A surface that isn’t moving.”

His feet collapse dramatically.

Feet:  
“We’re retiring. Effective immediately.”

His eyes, softening:  
“The light is nice right now.”

His heart, calmer:  
“We made it through another day.”

His brain, for once, quiet:  
“Yeah. We did.”

And for a moment, the whole body agrees — a rare, fleeting peace treaty.

6. The Gym Scene — “Mutiny on Treadmill Row”

He steps onto the treadmill, determined to “get back in shape.”

His legs immediately protest.

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
Legs:  
“Oh no. Absolutely not. We did stairs yesterday.”

His lungs, already wheezing:  
“Why are we doing cardio without warning? I need a memo.”

His heart, trying to be supportive:  
“Guys, it’s good for us. We’re getting stronger.”

His lower back:  
“Speak for yourself. I’m about to file a complaint.”

His brain, pretending to be a coach:  
“We’re doing ten minutes. That’s it.”

His feet:  
“Ten minutes? On this conveyor belt of suffering?”

His arms, swinging uselessly:  
“What exactly is our role here?”

His legs:  
“You’re decorative. Stay out of it.”

Meanwhile, the man himself is thinking:  
“Wow, I’m actually doing great today.”

7. The First Date — “The Body Attempts Diplomacy”

He sits across from someone he really likes.

His heart is already playing a string quartet.

Heart:  
“This is romance. This is destiny. This is—”

Brain:  
“Stop. We’re focusing. We’re listening. We’re normal.”

His hands, sweating profusely:  
“We’re not normal. We’re melting.”

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
His stomach, nervous:  
“I swear if we laugh too hard I’m going to make noises.”

His mouth, trying to flirt:  
“Say something charming. Something clever. Something—”

His tongue:  
“I panicked. I said ‘I like your… fork.’”

His brain:  
“WHY WOULD YOU SAY THAT.”

His heart:  
“I’m still proud of us.”

8. The Job Interview — “Corporate Chaos Inside the Ribcage”

He sits in a waiting room, rehearsing answers.

His brain is in full crisis mode.

Brain:  
“Okay, we practiced. We’re ready. We’re confident.”

His hands, trembling:  
“We are absolutely not confident.”

His heart:  
“I’m beating too fast. Is that allowed? Is that legal?”

His stomach:  
“I’m going to growl. I’m warning everyone right now.”

His mouth:  
“Please don’t. Please. I beg you.”

His armpits, sweating aggressively:  
“We’re doing our best.”

His brain:  
“No you’re not.”

9. The Horror Movie — “Every Body Part Has a Different Threshold”

He sits on the couch watching a scary movie.

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
His eyes widen.

Eyes:  
“Why are we watching this. Why. Why.”

His ears:  
“I’m closing myself. I’m done. I’m out.”

His heart:  
“RUN. RUN. RUN. I DON’T CARE IF IT’S A MOVIE.”

His hands, covering his face:  
“We’re not looking. We refuse.”

His brain:  
“It’s fictional. Relax.”

His spine, shivering:  
“Tell that to the goosebumps.”

His feet:  
“We’re ready to sprint if needed.”

His brain:  
“You’re on a couch.”

His feet:  
“We’ll sprint anyway.”

10. The Grocery Store — “Diet vs. Desire: A Civil War”

He walks past the snack aisle.

His stomach gasps dramatically.

Stomach:  
“Look. Look. Chips. Cookies. Glory.”

His brain:  
“No. We’re eating healthy.”

His mouth:  
“But… the textures…”

His nose:  
“I smell artificial cheese. I want artificial cheese.”

His hands, reaching toward a bag:  
“We’re just holding it. Not buying it.”

His brain:  
“PUT IT BACK.”

His hands:  
“We can’t. It’s chosen us.”

His wallet, muffled from the pocket:  
“I beg you. Have mercy.”

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
11. The Argument — “Anger Has a Union”

Someone says something rude.

His jaw locks.

Jaw:  
“Say the word. I’m ready to clench.”

His fists tighten.

Fists:  
“We can throw hands. We’ve trained for this.”

His heart:  
“Adrenaline deployed. You’re welcome.”

His brain:  
“No fighting. We’re adults.”

His teeth:  
“Coward.”

His lungs:  
“Deep breaths. Deep breaths. Deep—”

His eyebrows, furrowing:  
“We’re sending a message.”

His brain:  
“Not that message.”

12. The Sleep Scene — “Everyone Wants Something Different”

He lies in bed.

His eyes:  
“Close us. We’re done.”

His brain:  
“No. Let’s think about every mistake we’ve ever made.”

His legs:  
“We’re restless. We want to run a marathon right now.”

His back:  
“I’m uncomfortable. Adjust. Adjust again. Adjust more.”

His stomach:  
“I want a snack.”

His mouth:  
“I second that.”

His brain:  
“No snacks. Sleep.”

His heart:  
“I’m beating weird. Is that normal? Should we panic?”

His brain:  
“No. Stop. Everyone stop.”

passages.heading: Internal Affairs - The Body Has Notes
passages.text:
His body:  
“We refuse.”

works.title: Two Takes: Stage Left, Stage Right
works.blurb: five everyday moments, each told twice from two clashing points of view.

passages.heading: Two Takes - Stage Left, Stage Right
passages.text: Two Takes: Stage Left, Stage Right

passages.heading: Public Humiliation — The Dreamer / The Drunk
passages.text:
The Dreamer  
Rain falls like a film of light; I slow everything down because that’s how you make a scene matter. His white shirt goes translucent and suddenly he’s a statue in a museum I built in my head. The piercings are a punctuation mark I want to read; the crowd is an audience I imagine applauding. I’m composing the memory—angle, light, soundtrack—when the city decides to remix my film with a hydrant solo. The blast is rude, but it’s also cinematic. I smile anyway, because if life gives you a wet punchline, you might as well laugh.

The Drunk  
Hydrant explodes and the city baptizes me in public humiliation. My dollar-store tuxedo turns into a sad flag. I taste regret and cheap beer and the kind of shame that sticks to your skin. People stare like I’m a street performer who forgot his trick. A kid watches like it’s entertainment; no one helps. I stand up, water dripping from my eyelashes, and realize the joke’s on me—except I didn’t get the memo that I was supposed to laugh.

passages.heading: Public Humiliation — The Dreamer / The Drunk
passages.text:
Hospital Waiting Room — The Daughter / The Nurse

The Daughter  
I count beeps like they’re currency and I’m broke. Every magazine headline is a sermon I don’t want to hear. I rehearse the right face for the doctor—calm, competent, not a puddle—and fail spectacularly. A woman across from me offers a stale donut like it’s a peace treaty. I accept it because what else do you do with small kindnesses when the world is loud and clinical?

The Nurse  
I hand out coffee like it’s a miracle drug. My smile is a tool; my clipboard is armor. I’ve learned to translate panic into tasks: check vitals, fetch blankets, tell a joke that lands badly but does the job. The daughter’s eyes are a map I’ve seen before; I give her the donut and the joke and the exact phrase that makes people breathe again. Later, in the supply closet, I eat my own stale donut and pretend it’s not the same one I handed out. That’s the secret: we recycle hope.

passages.heading: Subway Encounter — The Teen / The Commuter
passages.text:
The Teen  
I practice my look in the window reflection—bored, dangerous, slightly tragic. My piercings are punctuation; the pole is my prop. I imagine someone noticing and saying the exact line I’ve been waiting for. The train lurches and I hold the pose like a statue. If someone laughs, it will be the right kind of laugh.

The Commuter  
I’m late, my coffee is lukewarm, and I have a meeting where people pretend to care about synergy. The teen is performing and I have no patience for auditions on public transit. He’s trying to be a poem; I’m trying to be a person who gets to work. He leans too close and my coffee sloshes. He freezes like he’s been caught mid-verse. I glare. He thinks it’s attention. It’s not. It’s coffee.

---

passages.heading: Job Interview — The Applicant / The Interviewer
passages.text:
The Applicant  
I fold my answers like origami—neat, hopeful, ready to unfold into a job. I smile the practiced smile and tell the story where I always learn the lesson and never cry. I want this to be the hinge that opens a better life, so I polish every corner until it shines.

The Interviewer  
I’ve heard the origami story before. I’m not cruel; I’m a curator of small truths. I ask the question that makes people drop their paper cranes and show the glue underneath. When the applicant flinches, I don’t pounce—I nod, because sometimes the honest flinch is the only thing worth hiring. Also, I like watching people try to fold their way into dignity. It’s entertaining and occasionally useful.

---

passages.heading: Grocery Aisle — The Widow / The Cashier
passages.text:
The Widow  
I reach for the same cereal because it tastes like a morning that used to have two mugs. The label is a map back to a kitchen that still smells like him. I move slow because memory is heavy and the sale signs are loud. I don’t need anyone to notice; I just need the box to be there when I get home.

The Cashier  
I scan and smile and pretend I’m not cataloguing lives by barcode. She always buys the same cereal and I’ve memorized the way her hands tremble at the coupons. I fold her receipt like a small prayer and hand it back. She looks at me like she’s surprised someone saw the ritual. I don’t say anything big—just “have a good day”—and watch her walk away with a box that smells like the past. It’s a tiny victory for both of us.

works.title: Melting Away
works.blurb: a lonely freshman is lured to a party by a "friend" who is quietly hunting him.

passages.heading: Melting Away
passages.text:
Melting Away

His phone chimed as a text popped onto the screen. Daniel glanced at the message; he was the new student at a prestigious college known for its exceptional education and… wild parties. The message read: “Don’t be boring, Daniel. We hate boring. Party this weekend. Be there.” Daniel let out a sigh. Parties and their associated activities were not his cup of tea. He had always been a bookworm, dedicating himself to maintaining good grades to secure a promising career like his father. His father had always discouraged him from reckless behavior and he did whatever his father told him to, but maybe this time it could be different?

If he stayed in his room, he was the creep. If he went, he risked his father’s disappointment. Either way, he was trapped. Finally, he decided: “What harm could it do? I’ll give it a try.”

passages.heading: Melting Away
passages.text:
The following days passed swiftly, and Daniel was getting ready for the upcoming party in his private dorm room. Thanks to his father’s extra payment, he didn’t have to deal with a lousy roommate who might “influence him negatively” according to his father. As he glanced at himself in the mirror, he couldn’t help but feel self-conscious. His scrawny frame, thin shoulders and ill-fitting glasses epitomized the image of a social outcast. Contemplating a change, he removed his glasses, hoping they might enhance his appearance and make him seem cooler. Though it meant sacrificing clear vision, Daniel reassured himself: “It’ll be fine. What’s the worst that can happen?”

The music could’ve been heard from 3 blocks down. Nervousness hit Daniel as he climbed the steps of the frat house, neon lights flickering like warning signs through dingy curtained windows. The booming music echoed disrupting his heartbeat. Suddenly the door flung open, a drunk student stumbles out the door and vomits over the railing, losing his balance and tumbling into the bushes. Daniel froze, ready to bolt at the sight —until strong hands grabbed him.

passages.heading: Melting Away
passages.text:
Matty, the lively girl who had texted him, smiled too wide. Her eyes lingered on him, measuring. Ralph her boyfriend, stood towering next to her, his hulking frame sending fear through Daniel. Ralph’s grip on his shoulders was uncomfortably tight but Matty’s words were worse, “You weren’t thinking about leaving, were you?” Matty teased.  
“No,” Daniel lied.  
“Good. We hate quitters. Now come inside and let’s get this night started.” Matty said with a blissful tone.

Inside, the party was chaos. Blaring music. Students chanting “chug, chug, chug.” Lines of cocaine on tables. Smoke so thick it made Daniel choke. Dealers handed out handfuls of loose pills like candy. Daniel’s stomach turned. Report it, and he’d be a snitch. Leave, and he’d be a loser. Stay, and maybe he’d finally belong.

Matty shoved a red solo cup into his hand. “Drink.”  
He gulped, vodka, his throat burned but the warmth spread. Another cup followed—sweet, syrupy, strange. His body hummed, light as air, his mind started moving slower.

passages.heading: Melting Away
passages.text:
Walls dripped like wax. Faces melted into grotesque masks, whispering his name. He reached for his glasses, but they were gone. How could he see without them, now the blur became monstrous—colors bleeding, shadows twisting. He was just trying to keep it calm, cool, collected. Then all of a sudden, Matty appeared again, a few blotter tabs in her palm, mixed with a few red and white pills. Matty didn’t take any. 
“Open up,” she said.  
He paused.  
“I said open up!” Her tone was menacing and Daniel was too far out of it to think for himself right now. 
So, He obeyed.

The world fractured. His heartbeat thundered, then slowed to a crawl. The floor rippled beneath him. His own hands looked alien, melting into the couch. His breathe seemed to hitch, the corners of his mouth felt locked, his stomached churning.

Matty leaned close, her lips brushing his ear as her words cut sharp:  
“You’re done, Daniel. No books. No daddy’s money. Just you—foaming, choking, dying. I’m gonna watch as you suffer and I’m gonna enjoy it.” She almost giggled with this last part. Daniel was in horror, he thought Matty was his friend now he knew otherwise.

passages.heading: Melting Away
passages.text:
He collapsed, convulsing, froth spilling from his lips. The room warped into endless corridors, each echoing his father’s disappointed face.

Dawn came and police lights flickered outside the frat house. Daniel’s body was hauled onto a stretcher, barely hanging on.

“Officer, I found him like this,” Matty said, voice trembling with false concern. “Will he be alright, I would hate for anything to happen to him” she said faking a whimper of sadness. 
The officer just nodded, commending her bravery, and said “ there isn’t anything we can do, these kids aren’t going to listen, they’ll just keep doing this stuff. So trust me, he won’t be the last. Just stay safe and keep out of trouble.” The officer left and Matty stood there alone in front of the frat house stairs watching as they left on the ambulance. She smiled politely but inside, her sick satisfaction bloomed. As the ambulance doors shut, her phone buzzed again. Another name lit the screen. Another lamb.

passages.heading: Melting Away
passages.text:
She typed back:  
“Don’t be boring. We hate boring.”

works.title: Project: Man Eater
works.blurb: a CIA recruit is slowly starved and transformed at a secret base built on Windigo folklore.

passages.heading: Project - Man Eater
passages.text:
Project: Man Eater

Deep in the woods and mountains of North Dakota, the CIA constructed the "Project Man Eater." Fisk, a newly recruited member of the CIA, has been deployed and drafted as a member of "Project Man Eater." When he arrives on base, something seems amiss; the facility is heavily armored but not to keep things out, but instead to keep them in. Even though the barracks are relatively new, they appear rundown; deterioration and other issues have already occurred. Although he would like to say this is the weirdest thing here, it is not; the crew members look sick and slightly anorexic. There are giant claw marks on the walls, and for some reason, it is freezing. Sure, outside, it is winter, and snow is covering the ground, but even inside, you can still see your breath; it almost seemed colder inside than out. These things had unsettled Fisk, but he had been in worse places. His first time drafted, he had been stationed in New Mexico, where the Barracks got so hot many recruits died of heat stroke, and worst of all was the smell. When night came, everyone's socks and other articles of clothing, drenched in sweat the day before, would fry in the night and smell like a cloud of body odor suffocating the whole base. Many crew members developed lung issues; Fisk had been one of the lucky ones. A barked order brought him out of his daze.  
"Sir yes Sir," he called back. "Agent Fisk, let me show you to your quarters. I am the head of this project, and we won't go by all that formal fluff. You can just call me Sam," Sam summoned from across the room. Fisk quickly followed him down many straight and narrow hallways, each about 4 feet wide but a whopping 15 feet high. They stop at a door just as disproportionate as the hallways. "This is where you'll be staying, so get comfortable. There are a few rules I must provide you with first, however. Rule one: You will be eating a strict diet, and that means no food outside what you get in the cafeteria. Rule two: Do not, under any circumstances, leave this room after 10:00 precisely. Finally, rule three, you are not to leave the base under any circumstance, no matter the reason." Sam stressed the last part and left it to hang like a doomsday cloud, covering the barracks in a smoke screen of fear. "Sir yes Sir," Fisk replied flatly. Sam left without another word, and down the hallway, he went.  
Later that night, Fisk was in bed curled up in 3 sleeping bags, still shivering, when he heard a noise like a call. Low melodic groaning, almost flute-like, caught his ear. He felt a mix of emotions run over him. He felt scared but also slightly comforted. It was an odd assortment of feelings. He looked at the clock, and it was precisely 10:00. He wondered what it could be when his bunkmate got up and opened the door. Fisk noticed that his bunkmate might have been the skinniest man he had ever witnessed. In fact, he thought almost for a second he could see his bones. Fisk watched as his bunkmate left the room and closed the door behind him. Suddenly, the sound of groaning stopped, and he was alone. Fisk didn't even try to stop his bunkmate. It was as if the sound had called him, and they had both excepted. He suddenly felt drained, and he fell to his pillow.  
He woke to the sun shining in through the window. It was still cold, and his bunkmate hadn't returned, but he couldn't quite make himself feel sad about it for some reason. It reminded him of the feeling he felt last night when he had just accepted him leaving. Fisk put on his uniform and went to the cafeteria, where he was served a disturbing meal. It looked like lab-grown meat but not the usual garbage served in most CIA facilities. This was different, almost too disturbing to eat, but he did, and it was like nothing he had ever eaten before. He didn't enjoy the taste, but he wanted more. It was like he had become more hungry by eating it, and soon, he had eaten his entire daily ration when he was told he couldn't have anymore. They gave him a loaf of bread, which made him feel full, and he continued his day. 
He felt lighter for some reason, almost like he had grown thinner since lunch. He felt around his waist; he had become slightly leaner. He could now feel his rib cage prominently push against his skin. His knuckles began to grow whiter and lighter, too. It was odd but not uncommon; he had heard stories of agents drafted from one extreme climate to another and that their bodies had reacted in very different ways. So he paid it no mind and continued down the hall towards his bunk. He walked through the insanely disproportionate door to his bunk and saw Sam waiting inside. "Good afternoon, agent; I just wanted to inform you that your former bunkmate has been transferred, and he will no longer be stationed here. We had the conversation last night around 10:00, so about when you would have been asleep, and he said he didn't feel like this was the right project for him. We deployed him somewhere else and have decided to provide you with a new bunkmate who will be here sometime this evening." Sam provided all this information while, in the back of Fisk's mind, he knew something was off.  
Fisk lay in bed. He looked at the clock. The hands touched 10 again, and he heard the same groaning as before. This time, he felt like it was calling him. He got out of bed and slunk to the door. His new bunkmate, Jax, got up with him. A silent agreement was voiced between them; they both wanted to know what it was and why they had been lied to. Fisk had clued Jax in on what had been happening: how Sam had lied to him about his last bunkmate and that something horrible must have happened for him to completely go missing; how he had felt something off about the shape of this place and everything else that had been going through his head. Jax was just as eager to uncover the secrets as Fisk was, and they were both about to come to the point of no return. They had followed the groaning down the hallway and could feel themselves getting closer. They could now tell it was indeed a flute they heard, and the air felt frozen. Fisk's blood began to get cold, and his fingers showed the first sign of frostbite. Fisk could feel his mind leaving him as the cold stabbed at his brain. Still, he pushed through. They rounded the corner, and what they saw shattered their puny minds, scattering what was left of their sanity.  
There stood a man pale as snow, bones bare, and skin stretched thin; he stood at an enormous height, almost touching the ceiling, with his anorexic limbs seemingly stout. He played the flute slowly through heaved breaths. The thing looked upon the two trespassers who dared to linger and uttered, "Beware the Windigo, for I am he. Follow in my footsteps, and you will become me." With a gust of cold mist, the Windigo vanished into thin air. Fisk could feel his skin tightening around his bones, like his body was eating itself from the inside out. He felt sick, but simultaneously, a growing strength in him. Two dazed by what they had just witnessed, neither Jax nor Fisk heard the footsteps that slowly and silently approached behind them. Suddenly, cloths wrapped around their mouths, and a gas leaked into their lungs, causing them to lose consciousness. They were dragged down many halls, stairs, and long dark corridors until finally they stopped. Fisk's eyes shot open; the drugs had worn off, and he knew what had happened. Sam slipped out of the shadows, a smirk painted across his face, his eyes twisted in an attempt to mask his dissatisfaction. Fisk struggled, but he had been tied to a nearby stalagmite that jutted up from the cave floor.  
"Where am I, and what are you really up to here?" Fisk roared with all the strength he could muster. The drugs he had been given seemed to do much more than just put him to sleep. " Do you not realize what this place is? Long ago, back in a far less hospitable time, Native Americans would suffer through long and harsh winters where, in the most devastating of times, they had to resort to cannibalism; this brought about the birth of the Windigo. A curse was placed upon those who had partaken of the flesh of another human? My superiors wish to harvest this curse and use it for scientific advancements, but first, we must have a surplus of test subjects." Sam continued, but Fisk interrupted. "You still haven't answered me; what is this place? Why do you want us? We are not Windigos, nor will a single man in his right mind eat another human." Sam's face twisted and quickly began again. "You must be kidding me. I didn't expect you to be so stupid. This place is the first recorded birthplace of a Windigo. Here, we have begun our project by feeding you all flesh and other chemicals to cause the same effect but at a quickened rate. Look at you; you're skin is tightening around your bones, and you are slowly becoming one yourself. Soon, you will be our next test subject, but we won't make the same mistakes as we have with the rest." Fisk's eyes were tearing up, and a lump formed in his throat. He couldn't speak he couldn't think. He felt another cloth go around his mouth, and once again, he was filled with the toxic fumes. The room went black.  
When he woke up, what he saw horrified him. He had now been entirely transformed. A tube ran through his arm. Parts of his body, which had been amputated, were being examined on a nearby table. He was now a test subject and would never see the light of day again, but that wasn't all he knew. Deep down, this would only spread. As his mind went blank and his thoughts became those of an animal, he knew he would always hate these people but would never get revenge. He was like an animal in a zoo... The end.

works.title: Following The Sheep
works.blurb: a job interview at a towering, numerologically-cursed office turns into a demonic blood contract.

passages.heading: Following The Sheep
passages.text:
Following The Sheep

Shaun, a young man in his late 20s fresh out of college, was on the lookout for his full-time career. One day, he stumbled upon an application for a job opening titled, "Young interns wanted!" As he scrolled through the requirements, he was pleasantly surprised to find that he met all of them, even the ones that seemed out of place. Without judgment, he called and scheduled an interview for the next day.

Afterward, Shaun decided to head home and prepare his résumé. The following morning, he woke up early and followed his usual routine: working out at 6:00, having breakfast at 7:00, and by 8:00, he was dressed in his finest suit, ready to leave the house. Shaun was a highly driven individual, and there was nothing he wouldn't do to succeed.

passages.heading: Following The Sheep
passages.text:
Approaching the grand building's stairs, Shaun couldn't help but notice its enormous size, towering 66 floors with 666 offices. The number worried him and sent a shiver down his spine. "It's just a crazy coincidence," he reassured himself quietly as he pushed through the doors and entered the lobby.

Inside, an emblem on the floor caught his attention—a snake devouring a lion. It was a logo unlike any he had seen before, piquing his curiosity. Suddenly, a receptionist called his name over the speakers. The speakers emitted a hissing sound before abruptly cutting off. Shaun went to the front desk, where he was handed a sheet to fill out before his interview. The questions on the sheet were unusual, delving into personal information like his birthplace and background. Though uncomfortable, he reluctantly filled it out.

Returning the sheet to the receptionist, Shaun noticed her blank expression, as if something was amiss. She took the sheet from him and swiftly pricked his finger, collecting a blood sample. Startled, Shaun recoiled and demanded answers, his voice a mix of rage and fear. The receptionist remained impassive and pointed towards a set of large double doors. Hesitant, he approached them, realizing that aside from the receptionist, he was the only person in the building. Puzzled, he wondered why a large corporation would have so few people present.

passages.heading: Following The Sheep
passages.text:
Entering the double doors, Shaun discovered an elevator waiting for him. Without him making a selection, the doors closed, and the elevator began ascending. A voice, previously absent, emerged in the back of his mind, soothing him with a sense of calm. It reassured him that he was heading in the right direction, though he couldn't quite explain its presence.

Upon reaching the 66th floor, Shaun exited the elevator and found himself in a long, dimly lit hallway. Surprisingly, there were no windows, and the only light source came from flickering overhead LEDs. The eerie atmosphere should have unsettled him, but an inexplicable feeling urged him to continue. Shaun navigated the hallways and turned with a familiarity he couldn't explain, considering he had never been there before. After an eternity, he arrived at a pair of imposing double doors resembling something from a dungeon. To his surprise, they opened independently, but Shaun's reaction was accepting rather than fearing.

passages.heading: Following The Sheep
passages.text:
Inside the room, there was a large desk made of cobblestone, elevated to Shaun's height. He sat on a small wooden chair that didn't fit him and waited... and waited... until finally, a tall man dressed in dark attire entered through the door. The dim lighting and the man's imposing height made it difficult for Shaun to discern his features. As the man approached the enormous desk, it seemed to shrink in comparison. "Let's get down to business," a deep, booming voice emanated from the figure across from Shaun. In response, Shaun nodded, feeling as if his motor skills were no longer under his control, moving slowly and surrendering to whatever his body did.

It was some time before the man spoke again. "I am a follower of the great one, the one who will return to vanquish the weak and rule in darkness. Your kind has defiled his name, and for that, you shall pay with your soul. Do you understand?" Once more, Shaun nodded mechanically. "Good. I'm pleased that we have agreed." The man slid a document in front of Shaun, but due to the poor lighting, he couldn't read its contents, even if he had tried. It felt as if his mind had been wiped clean of all previous knowledge leading up to this moment. The cacophony of voices in his head grew louder, screaming in unison. Shaun attempted to sign the document but realized he had no pen. "Sir, may I have a pen?" he asked shakily. "Of course, how could I forget?" the man replied, reaching forward and grabbing Shaun's hand.

passages.heading: Following The Sheep
passages.text: Shaun wondered what was happening, but before he could react, the man swiftly produced a knife and sliced through Shaun's right index finger. Shocked, Shaun tried to scream as blood gushed from the wound. Finally snapping back to reality, he realized this was no job interview; it was a demonic ritual. He desperately tried to resist, to run, but his body refused to obey his commands. It felt as though he had lost control of himself, becoming a mere passenger in his own body. The screams of the voices forced their way into his mind once more, and he felt himself sinking deeper within himself. In a trance-like state, he dragged his bleeding finger across the blank space of the document. As he finished, the last remnants of his will faded away, and he became a servant in the dark lord's empire. The voice sounded distant, but Shaun knew without a doubt that it was none other than the devil himself.

works.title: Low In The Water
works.blurb: a swamp-gothic opening fragment undercut by a waffle-craving stranger at the door.

passages.heading: Low In The Water
passages.text:
Low In The Water

The boat’s motor hummed low and rhythmic as it cut through the water. Shadows cast from the boughs low beams loomed like demons into the marshy bed. The mud squelched underneath as the boat shot through  The Waffle House sign flickered: bright yellow, then dark, yellow, then dark, yellow… then dark. Water dripped from the roof as the weather worsened. Lightning struck in the distance, and thunder sounded like an explosive drum. Ding ding, the door chimed as it shut fiercely behind a hooded silhouette. Then suddenly… the man pulled back his hoodie to reveal a kind, sweet-looking face of an old man. His grey mustache curled from the humid weather but with little to no hair atop his sweat-beaded head.

Goede dag, the man said in a high-pitched, squeaky German accent. "I'm here for your finest waffles," he said with a squirm of delight and plopped himself at one of the tables, kicking his legs up onto the seat across from him.

works.title: Tie by Tie
works.blurb: the founding legend of HollowMere — a surveyor, an island man with a stolen cup, a gang of tinners and a priest converge on a lake that will not be crossed, and drain it into the earth to lay the last mile.

passages.heading: Tie by Tie
passages.text:
> HOLLOWMERE — EST. BY THE RAILROAD EXPANSE
>
> *Station sign, east platform. Painted twice since. Never corrected.*

The sign tells the truth, as far as it goes. The town was laid down tie by wooden tie, spike by iron spike, and the Expanse laid it. What the sign leaves out is the water, the four roads that came to it, and what the last mile was laid on.

Before there was a mere there was a lake, and before there was a town there was a line on a map that would not bend.

passages.heading: The Survey
passages.text:
Silas Rook counted his steps out loud. He had done it since he was a chainman of fifteen, and twenty years later he still did it. The numbers came off his tongue like beads off a broken string: four hundred and twelve, four hundred and thirteen. The crew stopped hearing him after the first week. The pines never stopped hearing him. They stood on the north side of the grade like a congregation in black, so close and so tall that the light came down between them thin as milk through cloth.

On the south side were the caves. They were hollow in a way that rock should not be, and they breathed cold out of their mouths in the mornings like cattle.

Between the pines and the caves lay the lake.

It was long and grey and so still it seemed to be thinking. At dawn the fog lay on it like a sheet over furniture in a shut house. At noon it held the sky so exactly that a man could lose his footing just by looking down. Rook walked its shore three times with his level and his chain, looking for a way round, and three times the ground told him what the map had told him. There was no way round. The pines would not be cleared by first frost. The caves would not take a grade. The only line that could be laid ran straight across the water.

passages.heading: The Survey
passages.text:
Cornelius Thorne's charter said first frost. Rook had never met Thorne. He had met the charter, which was the same thing, folded.

So he did what the Company paid him for. He waded out to his thighs and then to his chest and drove painted poles into the bottom where there was bottom. Past the poles he took sightings to the far shore, and he wrote in the field book, in his neat clerk's hand, *grade sound*. The Company wanted those two words, and he had learned long ago to give a company what it wanted in the shortest form.

In twenty years of survey Rook had never once seen the end of a line he had staked. Other men laid the track and drove the last spike, and other men stood on the platforms when the first trains came in. He was always three valleys on by then, counting.

passages.heading: The Survey
passages.text: That night he sat on the shore and watched the poles stand in the water in a row. The last mile was staked across the lake. The poles went out into the dark like the spine of something that had lain down to drink and never got up.

passages.heading: The Island Man
passages.text:
Tamsin Crumb came inland with the cup held against her body.

That was how she thought of it afterwards: not *with Aldous Vane* but *with the cup*, as if he were a road she had taken. He had come off the island with tin money sewn into the lining of his coat and a stoneware cup with a waxed-cloth lid, and the cup held a measure of the Mother of Mothers. She did not ask how he came to have it. He did not say. On Port-au-Levain the Mother lived in her glass vat under the Great Hearth, fed by the mountain's own breath, and nobody carried her anywhere. That was all Tamsin let herself think about it. Whatever the island thought, it thought behind the fog.

The cup was Vane's. He kept it in a strapped box that rode on his own mule, and he kept the key on his own watch-chain.

passages.heading: The Island Man
passages.text:
Every night at the same hour Tamsin fed the bread on the island's clock, not the mainland's: the hour the Hall of Platters had kept for four hundred years. Each night Vane unlocked the box, and each night she took one spoon from the cup. She did not take it for herself. She fed it into a crock of her own, flour and water and the spoon, until the crock had a life in it that was the cup's life and not the cup. Her daughter culture. It rose in her crock the way a tide comes up a beach, slowly, and then all at once it was there.

The cup went where Vane went. The daughter went where she went.

Afterwards people would ask whether she came inland out of loyalty to him or to stay near the cup. She never answered, because she did not know which. She knew the hour, the spoon and the crock. Some faiths are no bigger than that, and hold.

passages.heading: The Island Man
passages.text:
They came by sea and then by mule through the black pines, and at the end of the pines was the lake, grey and thinking. Vane looked at it for a long time. Then he looked at the caves on its south shore. Tamsin watched him do arithmetic with his face, the way island bakers do it over a proving loaf, judging by the rise and not by the clock.

He bought the caves outright from a land office three days' ride east, with tin money, in a single afternoon. The deed gave the caves and everything beneath them to their furthest extent. The clerk did not ask how far the caves ran. Nobody yet knew they ran under the water. Vane owned what lay under the lake, and only he had thought to buy it.

passages.heading: The Tinners
passages.text:
Jory Kitto did not like the dark. He would have told you so if you asked, and laughed at himself for it, a tinner afraid of the dark like a fisherman afraid of being wet. He kept his fear in the same place he kept his wages, a tobacco tin in the breast pocket of his shirt, where he could feel its corners against his ribs when he breathed.

The tin was for Wenna. She was eleven years younger than he was and still back east, in a room over a laundry. She ironed other people's collars and wrote to him in pencil, because ink cost money. When the train comes, she wrote. When the train comes, he wrote back, and they both knew it meant the fare, and the fare meant the tin.

The gang came up from diggings that had failed back east, eight men who had signed on together because none of them could read a contract alone. Vane's man read it to them at a trestle table under the pines. The words went over Jory like weather. He signed where the others signed.

passages.heading: The Tinners
passages.text:
They opened the Tin Gallery mouth that autumn. The seam was good. It ran into the hill like a vein in a wrist, bright when the lamp caught it, and they followed it down and then sideways and then down again. The deeper they went, the colder and wetter the air grew, and the gallery began to smell of something Jory had not smelled underground before. Rain. Not real rain. The ghost of it: the smell of stone that has had water on the far side of it for a very long time.

In the evenings he whittled spoons from the offcuts of the props, small ones, with a notch in the handle for a thumb. He had made a dozen and given most away. He kept the best one unfinished in his pocket beside the tin, because a finished thing is a thing you can lose.

In the fourth week the roof began to weep. It was not a leak, only a sweat on the stone, slow and patient and cold, and it beaded and ran like the inside of a window in winter. The gang foreman held his lamp to it and said nothing. Then he took out a pencil stub and the plan, and drew a line on the plan. Jory, who could not read, could read a line. It went under the blue part. The blue part was the lake. The gallery roof ran under the lake.

passages.heading: The Priest
passages.text:
Father Bray came on foot, which was the only way a man of his means came anywhere. He arrived at the lake in rain so fine it did not fall so much as hang in the air.

There were eleven fisher families on the water. They lived in plank houses on stilts at the north shore, where the pines came down to the reeds. They took perch and something they called lake-cod, which was not cod, and they had been there longer than anyone could say. They had no church. They had the lake-light.

The light hung from a great oak at the waterline on the edge of the Fenwood. It was a ship's lantern in a cage of iron, at the height of a tall man's reach, and a young man called Fennick kept it. He was nineteen and solemn, his father's son and his father's lamp. When the fog came down, and it came down most nights, Fennick climbed the oak's lower limbs and trimmed the wick, and the light swung out over the water like a slow, held note. The boats came home to it. Nobody in that place had drowned in Fennick's memory, and he took this personally, the way a young man takes a thing that is his.

passages.heading: The Priest
passages.text:
Bray stayed. He raised St Brannock's on the shore with fish money and his own two hands, a chapel of rough planks no bigger than a boathouse, with a door that faced the water and a frame for a bell he did not have.

On the first Sunday he stood at that door and said what the fishers needed said. A priest makes promises on God's behalf, and Bray had never been cautious with them. He swore the lake's water to the fishers. He told them God had given it to them before any land office was built, and no deed written by a clerk three days east could take what God had given first.

The fishers believed him. That was the trouble, later.

> THORNE & EXPANSE LINE — WIRE — TO CHIEF SURVEYOR ROOK
> CHARTER TERMS STAND STOP RAILHEAD BY FIRST FROST OR GRANT LAPSES STOP NO EXTENSION STOP NO EXCEPTION STOP LAY THE MILE
> — C. THORNE

passages.heading: The Priest
passages.text: ## II. The Lake That Would Not Be Crossed

passages.heading: The Trestle
passages.text:
Since the line was staked across the lake, it had to be built across the lake, and Rook built it.

The crew felled the near edge of Black Pine for the timber, a long bite out of the forest's hem. They left a field of stumps that stood afterwards like the stubs of burnt candles on an altar. Nobody named it then. The name came later, and the stumps would earn it.

They drove piles where Rook's poles had stood and laid a trestle out from the north shore, tie by tie. The ties went down pale and new and smelling of sap, and the lake took the reflection of each one so exactly that from the shore the trestle seemed to go out over a second trestle hung upside down beneath it. Every morning Rook walked to the end of it, counting. Every morning the count was longer.

The fishers came out in their boats to watch, and stayed well back. They did not say anything. Fishermen in that place did not waste speech on water.

passages.heading: The Trestle
passages.text: At the end of the third week Rook stood at the trestle's head and took a bearing on the far shore. He found himself counting the far shore's distance and not the near's. That was how he knew the trestle reached the middle of the lake.

passages.heading: The Swallowing
passages.text:
Rook woke in the dark that night and did not know what had woken him. Then he did. Nothing had. The lake had made no sound at all.

At dawn the trestle was gone. It had not fallen, broken or burned. It was gone the way a word goes from the tongue: piles and stringers and a thousand ties, and the two horses that had been left tethered at its end to draw the next day's load. The water lay as flat and grey as it had the day Rook first saw it, holding the sky exactly. There was not a plank floating on it. Not a bubble.

He took a boat out with a lead and line. He let out sixty fathoms at the place where the piles had stood. There was no bottom. He tied on more line and let out more, and still found none.

The oldest of the fishers rowed out to him and drifted alongside. The man was white-whiskered, and the fishers called him Uncle, though he was nobody's uncle. He looked at the line going down and down into the grey, and he said the one thing he said that autumn: "It has no floor, that one. It never had." Then he rowed away.

passages.heading: The Swallowing
passages.text:
Rook sat in the boat a long while with the line in his hands. Below him, somewhere, lay a thousand ties he had counted onto the water one at a time. He thought of the field book with its two neat words, *grade sound*, and of the wire in his pocket with its *no exception*, and of the frost, which was already whitening the reeds at the margin in the mornings like salt on a rim.

He had been given a line he could not cross and a date he could not move. Sixty fathoms down, past the end of his rope, a thousand ties lay under the lake with two horses in the dark.

passages.heading: The Bargain
passages.text:
Vane sent for him.

Rook went to the tent on the south shore, below the cave mouths. Inside there was a lamp, a table, a strapped box Rook did not ask about, and a man with the island still in his voice, who listened more than he spoke and listened as if he were weighing something on a scale that only he could see.

Vane laid it out without hurry, the way he did everything. He owned what lay under the lake: the deed said so, to its furthest extent. His men's gallery roof already ran under the lake: his foreman's plan said so, in pencil. And Rook's ties lay under the lake too, a thousand of them, sixty fathoms down and further. So, Vane said, everything the two of them wanted was already down there. The only thing in the way was the water.

He would break the gallery roof. The lake would go down into the mine the way a bath goes down a drain, and in a week or a month the bed would be dry enough to bear a sleeper. The Expanse would have its mile. In return Vane wanted the freight contract on the new line, for tin and everything else, and he would leave the naming of the station to the Company. He did not care what it was called. That, he said, was the difference between him and Mr Thorne.

passages.heading: The Bargain
passages.text:
Rook said he would have to wire. Vane said of course.

The answer came back in a day. It was a single line, all capitals, and it was the shortest wire Rook ever received from the Expanse, because it did not need to be longer.

Rook stood outside the telegraph tent with it in his hand and looked at the lake. It lay grey and still in the evening, holding the last of the light the way a held breath holds the last of a word, and he understood that the lake's water was sold to the earth. He did not mean the shore or the bed. He meant the water itself, the oldest thing in the valley, sold to the stone underneath it at a price fixed between a man with a cup and a man with a charter, and the stone would take delivery.

> FREIGHT AGREEMENT, THORNE & EXPANSE LINE / VANE TIN CO.
> *Clause 4. The party of the second part undertakes to relieve the right-of-way of standing water by means within its own workings. The party of the first part accepts no liability for the means.*

passages.heading: The Vigil
passages.text:
Bray heard of it from a tinner at confession. The man was not confessing anything of his own. He only wanted someone else to know.

Bray had sworn the lake's water to the fishers before God. Now the lake's water had been sold to the earth by a clerk's agreement, and between those two sentences stood Bray himself and nothing else. He did not sleep that night. In the morning he went to the stilt houses and told the eleven families what he had heard. He did not tell them what to do. He told them where he was going, and they came.

They stood at the Tin Gallery mouth with lanterns: men, women, children too young to know what the lanterns were for. Bray stood in front of them in his one good coat with his hands open at his sides. The tinners came up the path for the morning shift and stopped.

passages.heading: The Vigil
passages.text:
There was no speech. There was a long silence like the one before a bell. Then the tinners turned back down the path, because to go into the gallery they would have had to lay hands on a priest. Most of them were men who would sooner go into a flooded shaft than do that.

The lanterns burned at the gallery mouth all that day and all that night, a ring of small lights at the black arch like coins laid on a dead man's eyes. The fishers sang a little near dawn, not hymns, which they did not know, but the songs they sang hauling nets, and the cold came out of the cave mouth and moved among them like a tide. The tinners did not come back. The gallery stood unworked.

On the second morning Bray looked at the faces around him in the grey light and saw that they had held. The fishers stood between the tinners and the gallery. For one day the lake was kept by people standing in the way.

passages.heading: The Bell
passages.text:
Vane did not come with men or guns. He sent bread.

It came up the path on the second evening in baskets, carried by Tamsin Crumb and a boy. It was round loaves with a dark crust that cracked when you broke it, and an inside that smelled of something nobody at that lake had smelled before: sour and deep and alive, like the floor of a forest after rain. The fishers ate. They had been standing two days. Bray ate too, and the bread was good, and he hated that it was good.

Then Vane came himself, alone, and stood just outside the ring of lanterns. He did not argue the water. He spoke about winter. He said the train was the only flour that would ever come over those pines. Without the line the fishers' children would winter on lake-cod and bark, as they had the winter before, when three of them had died. Bray had buried none of them, because Bray had not been there. Vane knew that. He knew the number and he knew the names.

passages.heading: The Bell
passages.text:
And he said St Brannock's had a frame for a bell and no bell.

Bray stood with the bread still in his mouth and understood that he was being bought. He understood the price, and he understood that it was fair. That was the worst part. It was not a lie. The children would starve without the train. A chapel with a bell could call the boats in through fog when Fennick's lamp was not enough. A priest is a man who makes promises on God's behalf, and here was a second promise, a better one, set next to the first: *I swore them their water; I can swear them their bread.*

He chose. If anyone had ever written the life of Bray, that is the word it would have used: he chose. He went into the gallery mouth with a lantern, raised his hand, and blessed the stone, the seam and the roof that ran under the water. Bray blessed the breach in the same words he would have used to bless a boat. The fishers watched him do it, and one by one they put out their lanterns and went home.

passages.heading: The Bell
passages.text: The bell came on a wagon a fortnight later, cast back east with the Company's mark stamped into its shoulder, and St Brannock's hung a Company bell.

passages.heading: The Last Plug
passages.text:
The tinners had waited for the blessing. They would not have gone down without it. Now that Bray had blessed the breach, they went down.

The work was slow and close. They cut up into the roof under the lake in a long rising drift, bracing as they went, and they left a plug of stone at the top. It was a door they would not open until the end, a cork in a bottle the size of a valley. The plug sweated. In the last days it more than sweated: it ticked, a sound like a clock in another room, as the water found the hairline seams. Then the foreman called the gang together in the lamplight and said someone would have to stay below and strike it.

It paid double wage.

Jory did the sum before he meant to. Double wage was the rest of Wenna's fare and a little over: enough for a coat for the train, because it would be cold on the platform, and she had written that her coat had gone thin at the elbows. He felt the tin against his ribs. He said he would.

passages.heading: The Last Plug
passages.text:
Nobody argued. Nobody argues with a man who volunteers for a thing nobody else will do.

On the last night he went up the drift alone with a lamp, a hammer and a bar. The others went up and out into the air, and the gallery closed behind them like a mouth. He sat on a timber under the plug and listened to it tick. He took out the unfinished spoon and turned it in the lamplight. The handle was done and the notch was done. The bowl was still rough, waiting for a knife he had left at the bunkhouse. He thought he would finish it on the platform while he waited for her train. He thought he would give it to her.

He could smell rain. Not the ghost of it now. Rain itself, near and heavy, as if the whole sky had come down and lay on the other side of the stone, waiting to be let in.

passages.heading: The Last Plug
passages.text: Jory Kitto stood alone under the lake at the last plug. Two fathoms of rock and a valley of water lay over his head, and he sat beneath it with a hammer, a spoon and a tin, and he was so afraid of the dark that he left the lamp turned all the way up, though it would cost him oil.

passages.heading: The Going-Down
passages.text:
He had no watch. Afterwards it was said to have been 11:47. That was said by a great many people who had not been there, which is how most things in HollowMere come to be said.

He struck once, and the plug held. He struck again, and the plug held, and the ticking stopped. He understood what the silence meant and was turning away, toward the drift and the long way down and out, when the stone opened.

That is all of it that belongs to him, and all of it that will be told. The lamp, the turn, and the opening. Whatever was under the lake came down to whatever was under that, and he was between them.

---

Silas Rook stood on the north shore at dawn with his level and did not need it.

The lake had gone into the earth in the night without a cry, the way it had taken the trestle. Where it had lain there was a bed of bare grey mud as far as the far shore, steaming faintly in the cold like the flank of a horse that has been ridden hard. Down at the Tin Gallery mouth the water stood level with the arch, black and still. The gallery was flooded to its lips, and the great pump beam the tinners had rigged at the mouth hung over it uselessly, like a heron over a pond with no fish in it. No pump in the Territory could have drawn a lake back up out of the stone.

passages.heading: The Going-Down
passages.text:
Out on the mud lay the ties.

The thousand ties the lake had swallowed under his trestle lay everywhere across the bed. Some were scattered, some still pinned in their stringers, and all of them were pale and whole, as if the water had only been keeping them for him. They lay in long ribbed rows across the grey like the bones of something enormous that had died lying down, and Rook stood and looked at them and laughed once, a sound he did not recognise as his own. The lake had taken the first attempt to cross it. Now it gave the first attempt back as the means. The ties that had failed to bridge the water would lay the line across the place where the water had been.

Jory Kitto did not come up. He was lost below.

passages.heading: The First Body
passages.text:
They laid the last mile in eleven days, on the swallowed ties.

Rook walked it as it went down, counting. He had never walked a line as it was laid, and he found he did not know how. His numbers kept getting ahead of the rails. The mud took the ties' weight like a held breath, and held, and the iron came down on them in lengths. The spike mauls rang out across the empty bed with nothing to stop the sound, so that every blow came back off the far pines a half-beat late, like a congregation answering.

On the eleventh day they reached the south shore, below the caves, where the station would stand. The foreman set the last spike and handed Rook the maul, because it was the custom, and because for once in twenty years the surveyor was there.

Rook did not drive it. One of the gang, crouching to set the last tie square, had stopped with his hands on it and gone still. Rook came and looked.

passages.heading: The First Body
passages.text:
Jory Kitto lay face-up in the mud at the end of the line.

He lay as a man lies who has been put down carefully. His eyes were closed. The mud had not taken him; it held him, the way the lake had held the ties. His right hand was closed on something against his chest, and when the foreman knelt, he did not open the fingers. Everyone could see what it was by its corners: a tobacco tin. A small wooden spoon with a rough bowl lay on the mud by his shoulder, as if it had slipped from a pocket a moment before.

He was a mile from the gallery mouth. The water had gone down into the stone, and he had come up out of it, at the very place where the rails stopped.

Nobody could say how. Some of the gang said the channels under the lake ran further than anyone knew. The fishers said nothing, and their silence said it was the lake: that it had kept what it held, all of it, and given it back where it chose. Rook did not say anything. He stood with the maul in his hand at the end of a line, the first end of a line he had ever seen, and the first thing at the end of it was the man who had opened the way.

passages.heading: The First Body
passages.text:
That night the gang foreman wrote up the week in the Company's book.

> VANE TIN CO. — GALLERY LEDGER — WEEK ENDING
> *Kitto, J. — tinner — lost in the workings. Double wage forfeit (shift not completed). No next of kin on file.*

It is set down here as it was written. Jory had not been lost in the workings. He had been found at the end of the line, by eleven men who knew it. The ledger said otherwise, and the ledger was the Company's, and the Company was the law.

passages.heading: The Wake
passages.text:
Tamsin Crumb had never baked for a death off the island. She found she knew how.

On Port-au-Levain the dead were mourned in bread. Every soul had a platter in the Hall, and when a soul went out, the bakers made the wake: one loaf for each mourner and three for the dead. Each loaf held a crumb token sealed in wax, so that every mouth that ate carried away a small hard piece of the one who was gone. She had watched it done a hundred times. She had never done it herself, because there it was done by the guild.

This was the first body. There was no guild here. There was her.

She baked through the night in the clay oven Vane's men had built her behind the tents, the oven that would later stand at the back of Crumb's Ovens. She baked from her daughter culture, not from the cup. The cup stayed in its strapped box on Vane's side of the camp, and she did not ask for it. What went into the dough for Jory Kitto was the crock she had fed one spoon at a time every night since the island, on the island's hour. It was the cup's life but not the cup. It was hers to give.

passages.heading: The Wake
passages.text:
Eleven tinners, and the foreman, and Rook, who came though no one asked him. Eleven fisher families. The loaves came out of the oven dark and cracked, and the smell went out over the bare lakebed like a lantern going out over water. She pressed a crumb into each one and sealed it with candle wax, and the seal set white on the dark crust like frost on a stone.

Three loaves for the dead she set on a plank by the grave.

Bray buried him at St Brannock's, in the first plot on the slope behind the chapel, under the new bell. He said the words. If his voice shook, nobody there knew him well enough to say whether it usually did. The tinners stood bareheaded and ate their loaves one by one, and each of them closed his teeth on the hard crumb in the wax and kept it.

passages.heading: The Wake
passages.text:
Not one of them went back into the gallery. There was no gallery to go back into. It was full of a lake. But they would not have gone in any case, and everyone at that grave knew it.

The island had buried its dead in bread for four hundred years. Now, by one woman and one crock, the island's wake loaf was HollowMere's mourning.

passages.heading: The Mere
passages.text:
The bed never dried.

The Company had promised a dry bed. Vane had promised it, Rook had written it down, and the rails ran across it on the drowned ties. But the bare mud they had laid the last mile on stayed mud. The rains came and did not drain. Reeds came up through it like hair through a scalp. The grey went green and black, and the green and black went soft, and by midwinter what had been a lake was not a lake and not land. It was a fen that lay under the rails like a held grudge.

Fennick watched it happen from the oak.

The cough came first. It came up off the fen in the fog, and the fog came every night now, thicker than the lake had ever made. It got into the stilt houses, then the bunkhouse, then the chapel. Everyone in the valley carried it, a wet rattle deep in the chest like a stone turning over in a stream. The fishers called the thing in the fog *mere-rot*. The Company's doctor, when one came, wrote *miasma*. They meant the same thing, and neither word helped.

passages.heading: The Mere
passages.text:
Then came the footsteps: on the trestle boards over the channels, on the duckboards to the stilt houses, on the planking of St Brannock's porch. They were steps with nobody walking them, steady as a man counting.

Then the wolves. They had always been in Black Pine, and they had always kept to it. Now they came down to the fen's edge and stood there at dusk, a dozen grey shapes in the reeds, and did not leave when shouted at. They watched the lights. They stayed out of the light, every one of them, as if it were a fence. They pressed right up against the edge of it.

On the worst night of that first winter the lake-light fell.

The oak had stood at the waterline for longer than anyone remembered. Now the water was gone from its roots, and the mud under it shifted, and a limb let go. The old ship's lantern in its iron cage went down into the fen, and Fennick, coming out at the sound, watched it sink. He saw it go under and stood waiting for it to go dark.

passages.heading: The Mere
passages.text:
It did not go dark. It burned on under the black water, green-gold and steady, deep in the fen beneath the oak, like an eye that had closed and was still seeing. It burned the next night, and the next. Fennick never trimmed it again, and it never needed trimming. Nobody in HollowMere has ever said who keeps it lit. Nobody has ever said that anyone does.

Fennick did not ask. He did what a keeper of a light does. He took a new lantern up a new pole at the new edge of the marsh, at the lip of the town that was beginning, and hung it, and lit it, and he climbed up to it every fog-bound night afterwards for the rest of his life. He was young then. In time they would call him Old Fennick.

Vane, for his part, paid a man to keep the wood. The wolves were bold and the pines were Company timber now, and a man with a rifle and a wage was cheaper than wolves. That was how the town came to have a gamekeeper before it had a constable.

passages.heading: The Mere
passages.text:
The stumps of the near edge of Black Pine, where Rook's crew had cut the timber for the trestle, got their first gallows that winter. It was built of drowned ties: the ones that had come up out of the mud too warped to bear the line. The town had not hanged anyone on it yet. It would. A gallows built is a promise made. After that the stumps had a name, and the name was Gallows Wood.

And the mere had tides.

That was the last strange thing, and the one the Company liked least. It was a fen with no sea for three hundred miles, yet twice a day the water in the channels rose and fell, a hand's breadth, as regular as breathing. Vane had brought a tide chart out from the island, an old chart for the harbour at Port-au-Levain. Someone pinned it to the wall of the tavern that was not yet a tavern, and someone else circled the next low tide on it, and the mere kept to it. Or seemed to. Whether it was the drained lake's channels running under the stone toward some water nobody had mapped, or something else, nobody could say. People in HollowMere still say a great many things about it. None of them has ever been proved.

passages.heading: The Mere
passages.text: The lake was a mere now, and the mere-rot was in every chest.

passages.heading: The First Train
passages.text:
The station was a platform of drowned ties at the end of the line, on a spur along the east edge of the new town. It had one lantern on an iron post and a sign, fresh-painted, that said what the Company wanted said. Bray stood at the end of the platform where Jory Kitto had been found, and waited with everyone else for the first train.

It came out of the pines at midmorning like a black thought arriving, steam going up white into the grey, and the whole town came out to see it. The town was not much yet: tents and plank houses, a chapel with a bell, an oven, a fen. The train docked at the platform where the rails stopped and stood breathing.

It brought flour, and the town wept a little at the flour. It brought whiskey, and mailbags. Out of the second car, last of all, after the crates were down, came a young woman in a thin travelling coat. The coat was gone at the elbows. She stood on the platform with a carpetbag and looked around at the fen and the pines and the strangers, and asked in a voice too careful to be steady where she might find Jory Kitto. He had written that he would meet the train.

passages.heading: The First Train
passages.text:
Bray went to her. Whatever he said, he said it in a low voice at the end of the platform, at the end of the line, and nobody heard it, and it is not recorded here. Afterwards Tamsin Crumb brought her a loaf from the oven with a crumb sealed in wax at its heart, and the foreman, who had written *no next of kin on file*, did not look at her. Someone gave her a small wooden spoon with a rough bowl. The story does not say who.

Up on the rise, where the south shore had been, Vane's men were raising the frame of a manor. In time it would have a hall, and in the hall a clock. It is said that clock stopped at 11:47 and never ran past it again. It is said a great many ways, by people who were not there. Nobody has ever said who stopped it, and the hands still stand where they stand.

passages.heading: The First Train
passages.text:
Bray went back up to St Brannock's and rang the Company bell for the train. The rope was new hemp and rough. He rang it as long as the train stood at the platform, and it burned his palms through his gloves. He did not stop.

The bell rang out over the mere, the drowned lantern and the end of the line, and came back off the black pines a half-beat late, like an answer. HollowMere had been founded: on water sold to the earth, a promise broken for bread, and a man who opened the way and was given back at the end of it. Whatever it owed, it owed from that day. In time the debt would pass to people who never knew they had inherited it.

The sign does not say any of this. The sign says the Expanse built the town, tie by tie. It is not wrong.

passages.heading: The First Train
passages.text: *The tie under your boot at dawn is who you are.*

works.title: Eleven Forty-Seven
works.blurb: the night after the will is read, Horace the Butler walks Vane Manor's last round with thirty-one keys and his day-book, and each wrong thing (the clock, the safe, the bootprints, the crepe, three study keys) undoes his excuse for the last, until at 11:47 the day-book is already written in his hand.

passages.heading: Eleven Forty-Seven
passages.text: In the hall of Vane Manor it was eleven forty-seven, and it always had been.

passages.heading: Front door, barred. Hall, dark. Clock, as ever.
passages.text:
Horace wrote the line before he walked it. He had kept the day-book that way for twenty-two years: write the round down, then go and make it true. He saw no reason for a will to change that.

The last mourner had gone at half past nine, with her wake loaf wrapped in her shawl. Horace held the door for her and bowed, and she did not look at him. Then he barred it. He left the day-book open on the hall table, as he always did, so the ink could dry while he walked.

He carried the lamp in his left hand and the keyring in his right. He counted the keys the way he did in the dark, by their teeth against his thumb. Cellar. Pantry. Linen. Wine. Safe. Study. Thirty-one keys, and he knew each one by its bite.

The hall looked the way a hall looks after a crowd. Chairs out of line. Crumbs on the runner. A cold smell of wet wool.

passages.heading: Front door, barred. Hall, dark. Clock, as ever.
passages.text:
The clock stood at the foot of the stair. Eleven forty-seven. It had said so on the day he came to be interviewed, when he was a young man with his hair still black, and nobody had ever told him why. On Sundays he drew the weight up its chain, always stopping two links short of the top so the chain would not strain. The clock never ran. Nobody had ever told him to stop.

He had let himself think about the will once, at the reading. *Whoever remains when the last lantern goes out.* He had looked down at his own lamp, and then he was ashamed, and he put the thought away like a spoon in a drawer.

Then the clock ticked once.

One tick, from a clock that had none left.

passages.heading: Clock. Cold in the brass.
passages.text:
"Cold in the brass," he said aloud, because a thing said aloud in an empty house is half true already.

Nobody had lit a fire since the reading. Brass shrinks in the cold, and old wood complains. And he was tired, and a tired ear will hear what it is waiting for.

He found the clock key by its teeth and opened the case to prove it to himself. He put his palm flat on the pendulum. It hung still and cold, and it had been still for as long as he had served here.

Good.

Then his knuckles brushed the chain.

The weight had been drawn all the way to the top, not two links short. Someone had drawn it tonight, and not the way he did it.

The chain was wet. He brought his fingers to the lamp and smelled them: reed, rot and standing water. The mere.

passages.heading: Clock. Cold in the brass.
passages.text:
Cold does not wind a clock.

Somebody had wound it tonight with mere-wet hands. Somebody with the fen on them.

passages.heading: Safe, locked.
passages.text:
So it was a mourner, then. He knew how it happened. They had come in from the fen for the reading: fishers whom the fog kept off the boats, tinners whose mine was shut and whose hands were not. Each of them hoped to hear their own name read out and did not. One of them had stayed behind when the rest went out.

He did not blame them. He only wanted to know where they were.

There was a stranger in the house, then. And a stranger would go to the safe.

He crossed the hall with the lamp held low. The safe stood in its alcove beside the clock, and it was locked. He tried the handle twice. Only one key opened it, and Vane had put it on his ring the year the house was finished. It had never come off.

He opened the safe anyway, to be sure.

passages.heading: Safe, locked.
passages.text:
The will lay inside, just where it had lain before the reading. It was folded in thirds, the way he folded letters for the post, with the crease pressed down hard under a thumbnail. At four o'clock that afternoon he had watched the Company clerk slide that will into a satchel and walk it down to the Bank.

No draught. No mourner. No key but his.

Only his key opens it.

passages.heading: Boots, blacked.
passages.text:
Grief, then, and habit.

Every night since the wire came, he had laid out the master's slippers by the bed: left, then right, toes to the wall. A man who could do that could walk to a safe in his sleep. He could fetch back a paper he had seen leave, fold it his own way, and put it to bed, all without waking.

His own hands, then. Nobody else's.

He looked down at his boots to prove it. He had blacked them at six. They were dry, black and clean.

Then he lowered the lamp.

There were bootprints on the carpet, in fen mud still wet enough to shine. They came from the barred front door and went to the clock, then to the safe, right past where he stood, and on to the stair.
