He set his own foot beside one of them. It did not fit. He went through the mourners: the Widow's small boot, the clerk's town shoes, the tinners in their hobnails. It was none of theirs.

passages.heading: Boots, blacked.
passages.text:
The size matched no one in the house.

They went up the stair.

passages.heading: Stair. Study door, locked.
passages.text:
He followed them up, lamp in one hand and ring in the other. He had stopped asking whose they were. He had run out of people.

The prints climbed the stair steadily and without hurry, the way a man walks up his own stairs. On the landing they turned left and stopped at the study.

He had locked the study door himself, at three o'clock before the reading, and tried it twice. It was locked now. He put his hand on the knob and it did not give.

Black crepe hung on the door.

He knew that crepe. It had hung on the front door for three nights, and he had taken it down at noon because the Widow said a will is business, and business does not come in through crepe. He had folded it and laid it in the linen press. Now it was tied across the study door in his own knot: a reef with the tail tucked under, the knot his mother taught him.

passages.heading: Stair. Study door, locked.
passages.text:
Crepe goes on the front door of a house with a death in it, where the street can see it.

This door was inside.

The house was mourning someone behind the study door. Not Vane.

passages.heading: Study.
passages.text:
He did not knock.

Opening doors was what he was for. He knew every door in Hollowmere: which ones stuck in wet weather, which ones a woman could lean against in the dark and weep, and which ones he must never open without being asked.

The ring was in his hand. He counted for the study key by its teeth, as he had counted all his life.

Study.

Study.

Study.

There were three. One was his. The second had barn straw caught in its bow and a pale twist of goat hair. The third was so cold it ached, and when he raised it to the lamp it smelled of the Undercroft's gas.

He had never hung either of them. He had never cut a copy of a key in his life.

The ring was no longer his count.

He stopped counting.

He fitted a key without choosing which one, and it turned.

The study was as it had always been. The desk. The master's chair, with its back to the window. The curtains drawn, as he had drawn them.

He put his hand on the chair. It was warm.

The day-book lay open on the desk.

He had left it downstairs, on the hall table, to dry. He knew that as surely as he knew the teeth of the keys. Now it lay open on the desk with tonight's page written all the way down. The ink was still wet, and every word was in his hand.

*Front door, barred. Hall, dark. Clock, as ever.*
*Clock. Cold in the brass.*
*Safe, locked.*
*Boots, blacked.*
*Stair. Study door, locked.*
*Study.*

Then the lines he had not walked yet.

*Crepe, front door.*
*Key, Hale Barn.*
*Key, Undercroft.*
*Clock, wound.*
*Hall. One clock, standing.*
*11:47.*

He read it twice. It was a good round. He would have written it the same way himself. He had.

The night was already written, and it ended at 11:47.

So he walked it.

He untied the crepe from the study door and carried it down, and he tied it across the front door in a reef with the tail tucked under.

He drew back the bar and went out across the wet ground to Hale Barn, where the wolf pelt hung on the door. The goat watched him, as goats watch everyone, and he hung the key with the straw in its bow where it would be found.

He crossed the square. Every window was dark. He went down the Well Ladder rung by rung, into the cold and the smell of gas, and laid the third key in the Undercroft where it would be found.

He came back in by the front door. He had barred it. He did not wonder about that.

His boots were not dry any more.

In the hall he opened the case and took the chain in his wet hands and drew the weight all the way to the top.

The hands did not move.

He did not put out the lamp. He did not ask himself why.

In the hall of Vane Manor it was eleven forty-seven, and it always had been.

works.title: What the Well Remembers
works.blurb: a girl who counts things hides on the Well Ladder at curfew, is driven down by a stranger washing at the well-head, and crosses the Undercroft into St Brannock's, where a sleeper's pallet, a post-dated Gazette and a red-darned glove in the bell rope take Father Bray's train east away from her.

passages.heading: What the Well Remembers
passages.text:
Father Bray went back east on the train.

My mother said it at supper, the week he went, the way you say the pump is frozen. She said it to the bread. Nobody at the table asked her anything else.

I remember him in three things.

He set the hymn numbers on the board every Sunday, and while he set them he made me read them back to him, and that is how I learned numbers. After Mass he read the Gazette on the chapel step and let me sound out the big letters at the top. That is how I learned letters.

He let me stand inside his arms when he rang the Company bell. The rope went up past my face and came down past it again, and the floor hummed.

His gloves were worn through at the palm from that rope. He darned them himself in red wool, badly. The darn sat right in front of my eyes when I stood inside his arms. I used to count the stitches. Nine on the left hand. I never saw the right one close enough.

passages.heading: What the Well Remembers
passages.text:
I count things. Planks on the platform: forty-two. Lanterns on the square: four. Plates on Crumb's wake table: ten, every time, whether there are ten mourners or two. Counting is how I keep things. If you have counted it, it happened.

So I believed it. Trains go east. Priests go with them.

Saloon was over. The Curfew bell rang. The wolves came down to the fence the way they do, and the Watchman walked the lanes knocking on shutters and sending children in.

I did not go in.

There is a ladder in the well on the square. Iron rungs, set into the shaft wall, going down to the shortcut under the town. Grown men use it sometimes in the day, sideways, cursing, because the rungs sit too close to the stone for a man's shoulders. They don't fit me badly at all. I have hidden on it on curfew nights since I was seven. You go down three rungs, where the light from the square still reaches, and you sit with your knees against the wall, and when the Station Rush starts you climb out and walk home like you've been to the pump.

Three rungs down. Knees on the stone. Four lanterns on the square. I counted them lit, one, two, three, and I was still waiting on the fourth when I stopped watching for it.
Up was always the way home. Up was the only way home I knew.

Boots on the well-head.

Not the Watchman's. The Watchman drags his left heel. These didn't drag.

The bucket came down past my face on its chain and went into the water below me and came up again full, close enough that it brushed my hair. Then washing. Hands, by the sound. Rubbing. Rinsing. Rubbing. A long time. Longer than flour takes. Longer than mud.

Water spilled over the lip and came down the shaft onto me. It was colder than well water. In the little light it was darker than well water, too. I did not look at my sleeve after. I am telling you that so you know I didn't.

Then the washing stopped, and he did not leave.

He stood at the top of the well with his hands held out, maybe, waiting for something to dry. I could not see a face. I could only see that something was standing between me and the lantern, because the light on the rungs above me had gone.

You cannot climb past someone at the top of the only ladder. You can't even breathe loudly. The ladder up was held by whoever had washed there, and I was small, and quiet, and I stayed still the way you stay still.

He did not go.

So I went down.

Below the rungs I knew there were more rungs, and below those there was a passage, low and wet, and at the end of the passage there was the Undercroft.

I had never gone that far. I knew where it came out, the way you know what is behind a door you've been told not to open. The Undercroft lies under St Brannock's. There is a stair from the Undercroft up into the chapel. The chapel door is never barred, because Father Bray said God's house has no bar, and nobody since has thought to fit one.

That was my plan. Down. Across. Up the stair. Out the chapel door. Home by the back lanes before anyone at the well thought to look down it.

And nobody would be in the Undercroft. I was sure of that. Nobody comes down there at night. It is a cellar. Cellars are for the dead and the potatoes.
Dark. Cold. A smell of gas.

The Undercroft has two alcoves for the gas, one north and one south. The north one was dark.

The south one was lit.

The lamp was turned down to a bead, a blue drop on the end of the pipe, but it was burning. Under it was a pallet made of sacking, pressed flat in the shape of a body that had lain there more than once. A tin cup. A candle stub, burned to a puddle. On the shelf over the pallet, a key with a brass tag. I could read the tag. STUDY, and under it, smaller, VANE.

Someone sleeps here.

I knew it the way you know a bed has been slept in. You don't need to touch it.

So I made it into something. A stowaway off the train. The Gazette says they come in the freight crates, under the flour, and they have to sleep somewhere when they get out. Somewhere dry. Somewhere nobody comes down to at night. A stowaway had found the Undercroft before I did, and that was all.

I took the key. I don't know why. Children keep things. It went into my pocket and it stayed there.

A stowaway. That was all.

There was chalk on the wall by the pallet. Low down, where a man lying on his side would write if he had a piece of chalk and nothing to do with the night.

Four numbers.

23. 140. 8. 271.

I knew them. I knew them the way you know your own name said in another room. They were the hymn numbers from Father Bray's last Sunday. I read them back to him that morning while he slid the cards into the board, and he said *good*, and he said *again*, and I said them again. They are still on the board upstairs. Nobody has changed them since he went. Nobody has set any numbers at all.

A stowaway off the train would not know those numbers. Nobody off the train would.

So that wasn't it.

So it was him. It was Father Bray who slept here, and it was before his train. A night, maybe two, before he went east. He came down under his own chapel to say goodbye to it from underneath, and he wrote his last hymns on the wall so he'd have them. That is a thing a priest might do. It is.
Before his train. Before.

If Father Bray slept here before his train, then something of his might still be here. I wanted something of his. I had kept his hymn numbers in my head all that time and nobody had told me I could keep anything else.

I lifted the head of the pallet to look underneath it.

A Gazette, folded flat. Folded the way he folded it on the chapel step, in half and in half again, so it would fit in a coat.

Mine now, I thought. His or not.

I unfolded it to see what he had been reading.

You read the date first. He taught me that. *Before you believe a paper, find out what day it thinks it is.*

I read it the way he taught me. Letter by letter, under the blue bead of the lamp. The day. The month. The number.

The number was after his last Sunday. Not much after. Enough.

The Gazette comes in on the Daily Train. That is the only way it comes. So this one came in on a train after the train that took him east.

Someone else brought it down, then. That's what I said. Anyone could have. Anyone could fold a paper in half and in half again. I said it in my head twice, the way he made me say the hymns twice, and the second time it was thinner than the first, and I did not believe it either time.

And the lamp.

The lamp in the south alcove was turned low. Not out. Turned down to a bead, the way you leave a lamp you are coming back to. You turn a lamp out when you go away. You turn it down when you are going up to do something and you will want it again before morning.

Whoever slept here was out, and the alcove's sleeper was coming back tonight.

The lamp was turned down, not out.

Up the well was the washer. Down here was a bed someone was coming back to. The chapel was the only other way out I knew.

I took the stair.

St Brannock's at night. Plank walls. Pews. The smell of cold wax. The hymn board, white cards in black slots, *23 140 8 271*, still. The windows grey. The door at the far end. And between me and the door, the place under the bell, where the rope comes down.

The chapel was empty. I told myself that. It was empty, and the door was ten steps away, and the way to it ran under the bell and past the rope, the way it always had.

Ten steps. I counted them.

The Company bell hangs over that spot with the Company's mark stamped on its shoulder. I have looked up at it every Sunday of my life.

The rope was moving.

Only a little. A slow sway, side to side, getting smaller. The way a rope does after. After someone has let go of it. After something has come off it. So the chapel was not empty. Or it had not been, a moment before I came up the stair.

There was something caught in the rope. Twisted into the lay of it, about where a grown man's hands would be if he reached up to ring.

A glove.

Not a whole one. The cuff, and half the palm, the rest torn away. The palm worn through from rope. Darned over the worn place in red wool. Badly.

I knew it.

I have stood inside those arms with that darn in front of my eyes. I have counted those stitches.

I started to tell myself something. Other men darn their gloves. Other men ring bells. Red wool is cheap. Everybody has red wool. I got that far. I could not get any further. I could not get to the end of it, and I have never got to the end of it since.

I did not count the stitches. I did not want to know if there were nine.

What the glove did not tell me: whether he rang that bell until the rope tore his hand out of it. Whether he climbed. Whether the rope was for something else. Whether someone took it off him. Whether he pulled his hand out himself and left the glove behind and walked down to the platform and got on the train like they said.

The bell did not ring. Nothing rang.

I did not take the glove. I had the key.

I knew whose it was.
I could not unknow it. I have tried. It does not go back.

I went out by the chapel door, which has no bar, and home by the back lanes, and I was in my bed with my wet sleeve under the blanket before the Station Rush.

The whistle out of the pines. The platform lantern going pale. The well-head stones, when I went out for water, dark and wet, and nobody standing at them.

The train had brought a Vicar. He came up the square in a coat too good for the mud, with his bag in one hand, looking at everything the way you look at a house you have been told is yours. He stopped at the pump, where I was. He bent down, because grown men do that to children, and smiled, and asked me.

Where did Father Bray go?

The key was in my pocket. My mother was at our door. Mrs Grieves was sweeping the tavern step, and she had stopped sweeping.

"Father Bray went back east on the train," I said.

The Vicar nodded. My mother nodded. Mrs Grieves nodded, and went back to her sweeping.

Three.

I counted them.

works.title: Behind the Peephole
works.blurb: A hotel-set thriller told only through guests' returns from unseen missions.

passages.heading: Behind the Peephole
passages.text:
Book Scripts

Behind the Peephole: A Thriller Told in the Quiet Aftermath

Most thrillers show you the danger.  
Behind the Peephole shows you what happens after.

This upcoming novel takes place inside a single hotel — a crossroads for people who live on the edge. Mercenaries. Whistleblowers. Art thieves. Undercover journalists. Hackers. Activists. People whose lives burn fast and bright, but whose secrets only surface when they think no one is watching.

The twist is simple and devastating:

You never see their missions.  
You only see their return.

Each chapter opens with a guest slipping back into their room late at night. The story unfolds through the smallest details:

• A smear of dirt on a collar  
• A phone call cut short  
• A trembling hand holding a keycard  
• A suitcase that wasn’t there yesterday  
• A stranger knocking at 2:14 AM  
• A TV channel chosen for comfort or for cover  
• A ritual repeated with obsessive precision

passages.heading: Behind the Peephole
passages.text:
The reader becomes the detective, piecing together the invisible lives of people who risk everything outside the hotel walls.

And the peephole — that tiny circle of glass — becomes the book’s central metaphor.  
A threshold.  
A surveillance device.  
A confession booth.  
A trap.

Because the more you watch these guests, the more you realize something is wrong. Their stories overlap. Their secrets rhyme. Their patterns converge.

They’re not here by accident.  
They’re not alone.  
And someone is watching them all.

Behind the Peephole is a slow-burn, atmospheric mystery built from negative space — a story that invites readers to lean in, observe, and assemble the truth from the fragments left behind.

If you love thrillers that reward attention, tension built from silence, and mysteries that unfold like a mosaic, this is a book that will stay with you long after you close the door.

works.title: Missing Campsites
works.blurb: A campground quietly erases itself around a group nobody else notices is missing.

passages.heading: Missing Campsites
passages.text:
Missing Campsites: A Slow-Burn Horror Mystery About Vanishing Reality

Imagine arriving at a remote campground only to discover something is… off.

Not dangerous.  
Not dramatic.  
Just wrong.

In Missing Campsites, a group of campers pulls into a national forest expecting a quiet weekend. But the first few campsites — the ones that should be right there at the entrance — simply aren’t. Not destroyed. Not taped off. Not overgrown.

They just don’t exist.

The map shows them.  
The signs point to them.  
But the land is empty.

The campers are unsettled, but everyone else — rangers, families, hikers — acts like nothing is missing.

The next morning, more campsites have vanished.

No one notices.  
No one cares.  
No one even remembers they were there.

Except the campers.

By the end of the second day, the entire campground has been erased from reality — all except the last five sites, the ones where the campers are staying. They’re now the only fixed points in a landscape that’s quietly unraveling.

passages.heading: Missing Campsites
passages.text:
And then comes the final morning.

They wake up to find the forest transformed.  
The sky is wrong.  
The air feels heavier.  
The trees are arranged in patterns that shouldn’t exist.  
Their phones show no signal, no time, no date.

They haven’t just lost the campsites.

They’ve slipped into a different dimension — one that has been pulling them in, piece by piece, since the moment they arrived.

Missing Campsites is a creeping, atmospheric horror story about unnoticed disappearances, the fragility of shared reality, and the terrifying moment when you realize the world has been quietly rewriting itself around you.

works.title: Beetles for Brains
works.blurb: Boot-camp recruits' mandatory sleep cycles may be letting something crawl into their minds.

passages.heading: Beetles for Brains
passages.text:
Beetles for Brains: A Psychological Horror About Sleep, Control, and the Things That Crawl in the Dark

In this world, sleep isn’t rest — it’s exposure.

Beetles for Brains follows a group of recruits entering an elite, secretive boot camp known for producing the toughest soldiers on the planet. What no one tells them is the real reason for the camp’s brutal schedule: mandatory, unnaturally long sleep cycles.

At first, it seems like a strange training method.  
Then the symptoms begin.

Recruits wake up disoriented.  
Their thoughts feel foggy.  
Memories slip.  
Reflexes dull.  
Personalities shift in subtle, unsettling ways.

Rumors spread about “the bugs” — tiny organisms that supposedly enter the body during sleep and slowly interfere with neural pathways. No one knows if they’re real, a myth, or a psychological tactic used by the instructors.

passages.heading: Beetles for Brains
passages.text:
But the longer the recruits sleep, the worse the effects become.

Some start hearing faint clicking sounds when they close their eyes.  
Some feel phantom sensations under their skin.  
Some swear they can sense something moving in the quiet spaces of their minds.

The camp insists everything is normal.  
The recruits know something is wrong.  
And the truth is far more disturbing than any of them imagined.

Beetles for Brains is a slow-burn psychological horror about control, paranoia, and the terrifying idea that the most vulnerable moment in your life — sleep — might be the moment something else takes hold.

works.title: The Bloody Alarm Clock
works.blurb: An inherited clock that consumes its owner's time through inescapable nightmares, then moves on.

passages.heading: The Bloody Alarm Clock
passages.text:
The Bloody Alarm Clock: A Horror Story About a Timepiece That Won’t Let You Wake

Some cursed objects announce themselves.  
This one just… ticks.

The Bloody Alarm Clock follows an ordinary person who inherits an old bedside clock with a strange quirk: it never rings out loud, yet every night it plays inside their head. The sound isn’t a tone or a melody — it’s a pressure, a pulse, a presence that drags them into vivid, terrifying dreams.

At first, the dreams are just unsettling.  
Then they become unbearable.

Each night brings a new nightmare: running out of time, suffering mysterious internal pain, drowning, collapsing, or meeting some unseen fate. And every morning, the victim wakes with real‑world echoes of what they dreamed:

• Waking soaked after dreaming of drowning  
• Feeling faint after dreaming of losing blood  
• Hearing phantom ticking long after opening their eyes

passages.heading: The Bloody Alarm Clock
passages.text:
Worst of all, their ears begin to bleed when they wake — a quiet, chilling sign that the clock is doing something far more dangerous than disturbing their sleep.

The victim tries everything to get rid of it.  
Throwing it away.  
Smashing it.  
Leaving it behind.

But the clock always returns — sometimes on the nightstand, sometimes in a dream, sometimes in a place they don’t remember putting it. It’s as if the clock is choosing them, not the other way around.

As sleep becomes a threat, the victim starts avoiding it entirely. Exhaustion leads to waking hallucinations — daydreams that feel just as real and terrifying as the nightmares. The line between dream and reality dissolves, and the ticking becomes constant, inescapable.

Eventually, the victim realizes the truth:

The clock doesn’t measure time.  
It consumes it.

And when it finally takes the last of theirs, the clock quietly moves on — appearing in the home of its next unsuspecting owner, ready to begin the cycle again.

passages.heading: The Bloody Alarm Clock
passages.text: The Bloody Alarm Clock is a psychological horror story about dread, inevitability, and the terrifying idea that something as harmless as a bedside clock could be counting down to your end.

works.title: Chasing Cold Clues
works.blurb: Pulp cryptozoologist Dr. Sterling Vanguard chases a cryptic clue into jungle danger.

passages.heading: Chasing Cold Clues
passages.text:
Chasing Cold Clues

Character design:

Main character:

passages.heading: Dr. Sterling Vanguard
passages.text:
Bio:

Dr. Sterling Vanguard is a renowned cryptozoologist and esteemed explorer with a deep passion for unraveling the mysteries of the natural world. With a PHd in zoology and a wealth of knowledge in the field, Dr. Vanguard has dedicated his life to studying and documenting elusive and undiscovered creatures. His expertise in cryptozoology, combined with his extensive experience as a versed adventurer, has led him to remote and unexplored corners of the globe in search of rare and mythical creatures.

First story plot line:

Opening Scene:  
The scene opens with a high-energy chase through the bustling marketplace. Dr. Vanguard, a seasoned adventurer and scholar, is in pursuit of a mysterious boy weaving through the crowded streets. The chase intensifies as Dr. Vanguard tries to catch up, his determination fueled by the sense that something important is at stake.

Rising Action:  
During the chase, Dr. Vanguard manages to catch the boy, who reveals a cryptic clue that leads him on an unexpected and thrilling journey. Intrigued by the enigma before him, Dr. Vanguard delves deeper into the mystery, uncovering fragments of a forgotten history that could change the course of knowledge forever. He realizes that he is up against powerful adversaries who will stop at nothing to obtain the secrets he's stumbled upon.

passages.heading: Dr. Sterling Vanguard
passages.text:
First Climax:  
Dr. Vanguard finds himself deep in a dense jungle, relentlessly pursued by a group of hunters desperate to obtain the valuable clue he possesses. With nowhere left to run, he faces an ultimatum: surrender the clue or face dire consequences. As tension reaches its peak, Dr. Vanguard makes a split-second decision, choosing to trust his instincts and take a leap of faith.  
To be continued...

works.title: A 9-5 Could Kill You
works.blurb: An isolated man personifies his own reflection into a lover, then a rival, on the road to recovery.

passages.heading: A 9-5 Could Kill You
passages.text:
Part One— A 9-5 Could Kill You

A man in his early twenties finds it hard to make friends. He is isolated, lonely, and he hates himself for it. He works a 9-5 and the position is drab: no excitement, he spent years in college for it but in the end he is not fulfilled. He’s never let himself get hurt ever since his first break up. It was what he would’ve considered true love. Mostly it was just him sacrificing himself but that isn’t brought up till much later. After that break up he has become an incel. He was out of shape and unattractive his whole high school history. It wasn’t till he got to college where he made friends and got fit but his toxic personality towards women after his breakup furthers his position as an incel. After college his friends stopped talking to him because he never went anywhere. He’s struggled with mental problems since he was little but for the most part he doesn’t know. He takes medication that he was prescribed at a very young age never told what they did. One day after another he had enough — after meeting up with a few of his ex-friends and trying out a few to many toxic dates, he decides to quit taking it because he doesn’t care anymore. He calls his job and he quits. His life goes downhill, he bed rots, doomscrolling till his fingers get stiff and blistered. He’s depressed and desperate but this doesn’t stay the case. The first half of the book ends with what seems like the start of another social failure.

passages.heading: A 9-5 Could Kill You
passages.text:
Part Two — Romance is in the Air… or in This Case the Mirror

The second opens with the break of the depression episode. He gets out of bed, takes care of himself, and begins to move from it all. This is where the book takes its turn. Strange things happen to him. Stories start to mesh together. This is when the book starts to combine tropes and the main character realizes it. He gets into his car dressed for church — maybe he’ll try religion… as he gets off the train to go into work he wonders how he got here. Didn’t he start in his car? And didn’t he lose his job? With the storyline further branching and seemingly impossible to understand, it all comes backtrack to reality. He wakes up in his bed. He fell asleep and slept for 48 hours after stopping his medication. Again the scene of him escaping the depressive episode plays out. Except this time he starts to talk to himself in the mirror. While he resumes his life (which he only hallucinates leaving the house), he creates the idea he’s a great man, friend, and employee. He got his position back at his job and it turns out he’s really important — everyone loves him. This is the point where no bad things happen except small occasions where it feels so dramatic. Slowly he begins to talk to himself more and more. He arranges dates to listen to himself. Over time it almost seems like he isn’t the only one answering the conversation. His reflection and himself essentially start dating, leaving a good portion of this book to an almost perfect romance story of two men who happen to live together and over time started dating but can’t remember why. Once this part of the story happens the mirror is no longer his means of talking to his lover. He has now fully personified a version of himself and talks to it as if it was another person. Eventually the relationship turns sinister marking the third part of the book.

passages.heading: Part Three — Hate Rears Its Ugly Head
passages.text: In this part his self-hatred begins to come out. His memories seem to ebb and flow like strange episodes that bring him more and more hatred. Eventually he cannot stand his partner (himself personified separately) leading to him offing his imaginary partner. This is the lowest point since he was on the medication. He remembers. He has multiple existential crises. He is confused and doesn’t understand what could be happening. At the loss of his partner he has weird episodes where he rampages through the house breaking things, screaming, crying, and cursing his partner. Eventually the neighbors complain and one fateful evening while he is in the middle of an episode, he hears a knock on the door and it is loud. The sound echoes through him almost as if his soul had left himself and he was hollow. In a turn of events he believes it is his partner come back for him. He knew he wouldn’t leave him. But the mess — he’ll see the mess. So he leaves a candle on the kitchen counter and turns the gas on the stove to clean up the mess (later incinerating his house). He then proceeds to walk out the door where he is met by the law. His illness next to leaves him. This is the first time since he could remember seeing another face other than his own. He breaks down crying, begging that they help him. Marking the beginning of the fourth part of the book.

passages.heading: Part Four — Time with His Therapist
passages.text: He sits in a softly lit office. The air smells faintly of coffee and antiseptic. The therapist doesn’t start with the fire. She starts with the mirror. At first, he tells her about his “partner” as if it were real. She doesn’t correct him. She asks questions that feel like scalpels, peeling back the layers. The sessions are slow, repetitive, and exhausting. Sometimes he swears he hears the partner’s voice in the room. Sometimes he sees a flicker of movement in the therapist’s glasses. She teaches him to name the shadows without becoming them. One day she asks him to imagine the partner sitting in the empty chair across from him. Instead of rage, he feels grief. He admits — for the first time — that he loved that version of himself, even if it was toxic. This is the first crack in the armor.

passages.heading: Part Five — Living After It All
passages.text: Months later. A small apartment. No mirrors. The light is warm but the silence is heavy. He works part-time stocking shelves at night. He likes the anonymity. He walks in the mornings. He cooks simple meals. He reads. Sometimes he talks under his breath, but it’s not to the partner — it’s to himself, as himself. Recovery is not a triumphant montage. It’s a negotiation with boredom, loneliness, and the temptation to relapse into fantasy. One evening, he passes a shop window and catches his reflection. For a moment, he thinks he sees the partner smiling back. But instead of fear or longing, he just nods — a silent acknowledgment — and keeps walking.

works.title: Narrative Voice
works.blurb: A god-consciousness edits its own past lives in a repeating cycle that turns into reincarnation.

passages.heading: Narrative Voice
passages.text:
Narrative Voice

A god overlooks himself in the past as he makes changes to produce his favored outcome but in the end nothing changes. Throughout the book a person goes through life with the narrative of his conscious voice remaining stationery, watching himself from an outward view. Over each moment in his life he becomes slightly more conscious as his realization of be a god comes into view which also correspond to characters years of life which he created each with just minor tweaks in his behavior that lead to a all of a sudden change where he is completely different followed by many days depressed thinking about life and ultimately leading to bad times in his life before he finally manages to get a hold of it then the cycle repeats. Later on towards the end of life the book repeats starting back with the god but this time the concept of reincarnation (give multiple views, and ideology on this).

works.title: The Show Must Go On
works.blurb: A head injury makes a kid's life start playing out like a sitcom only he can hear.

passages.heading: The Show Must Go On
passages.text:
The Show must go on

Starts off with a completely normal kid who one day hits his head. He wakes in the hospital surrounded by his loved ones but something is different he just can’t place it. Soon he gets home and that’s when weird stuff starts happening he notices at first but before long it just becomes normal for him. The problem he contracted is that his life takes on the appearance of a sitcom. He pops in and out from reality. He believes his friends are cross over characters constantly referring to them by their last names when he meets them as if it’s a tv show. He bursts out in laughter over jokes that a talk show host tells him while nobody else knows what’s funny. Work in progress…

works.title: People of the Bark
works.blurb: a whimsical scale-inversion parable about a civilization living on a single tree's bark.

passages.heading: People of the Bark
passages.text:
People of the Bark

A mythic micro‑civilization clinging to the skin of a giant world they can’t comprehend

They live on the outer rind of a towering tree — a world so vast that even a single inch of bark is an entire country to them. Their cities cling to ridges and grooves. Their roads run along cracks. Their temples are carved into knots. Their watchtowers rise from splinters.

To them, the tree is everything:  
the sky, the ground, the history, the future.

They call it The Endless Trunk.

But to the real world?  
It’s just a tree in someone’s backyard.

That’s the quiet moral humming beneath the story — their wars, their politics, their fears, their triumphs… all unfolding on a surface we barely notice.

passages.heading: People of the Bark
passages.text:
🎬 Opening Scene — “The Tremor”

At dawn, the bark people wake to a strange vibration.

Not an earthquake.  
Not a storm.  
Not an enemy.

Just a squirrel landing on the trunk.

But to them, it’s a cataclysm.

Dust rains from the ridges.  
Homes carved into the bark shudder.  
The elders declare omens.  
The young warriors rush to the battlements.  
The scholars scramble to record the tremor’s pattern, believing it to be a message from the gods.

Meanwhile, the squirrel is just scratching an itch.

This is the tone:  
Epic stakes inside a world that is cosmically tiny.

🌿 The Culture of the Bark People

They are small, agile, and deeply spiritual. Their entire worldview is shaped by the tree’s rhythms:

• Windstorms are divine trials  
• Rain is a seasonal blessing  
• Birdsong is prophecy  
• Falling leaves are omens of death  
• Sap is sacred water  
• Insects are monsters or gods depending on their size

passages.heading: People of the Bark
passages.text:
They believe the tree is alive and conscious — a slow, ancient being whose moods shape their fate.

They’re not wrong.  
But they’re not right either.

The tree is alive, yes.  
But it’s just… a tree.

⚔️ The Conflict — “The Coming of the Shadow”

One day, a shadow falls across the bark.

It is enormous, stretching across their entire world.  
The people panic.  
The priests chant.  
The warriors prepare for war.

But the shadow is just a human hand reaching toward the trunk.

To them, it is the arrival of a god.  
To us, it’s someone checking for termites.

This is where the tension comes from — the collision between their mythic worldview and the mundane reality outside it.

🌱 The Moral (woven, not stated)

Their fears are enormous.  
Their hopes are enormous.  
Their conflicts feel world‑ending.

But in the grand scheme?  
They are tiny.

And yet — their lives still matter.  
Their stories still matter.  
Their courage still matters.

passages.heading: People of the Bark
passages.text:
The moral isn’t “your worries don’t matter.”  
It’s:

Even the smallest world is a universe to the ones who live in it.

works.title: The Redacted Testament of Lira Calyx
works.blurb: a four-book world bible of the post-nuclear Convergence Era, told as a found and redacted testament.

passages.heading: The Redacted Testament of Lira Calyx
passages.text: The Redacted Testament of Lira Calyx

passages.heading: THE WORLD: The Convergence Era
passages.text:
After the nuclear cataclysm, the tectonic plates didn’t just shift — they collided with such force that the crust folded upward into sky‑piercing megapeaks. These mountains are so tall they create their own weather, their own gravity anomalies, and their own ecosystems. The fallout fused with deep‑earth minerals, creating Aetheric Compounds, which became the foundation of the new civilization.

The world is divided into three vertical ecological realms:

1. The Lowlands — The Scorched Biome

• Harsh radiation pockets  
• Mutated desert flora with crystalline bark  
• Fungal mats that detoxify soil  
• Scavenger fauna adapted to heat and chemical storms

2. The Mid‑Slopes — The Verdant Reclamation Zone

• Dense forests grown from radiation‑resistant seeds  
• Hybrid species formed from old DNA and new Aetheric influence  
• Rivers that glow faintly at night  
• Human settlements built into cliffside terraces

3. The High Peaks — The Aetheric Frontier

• Thin atmosphere  
• Floating spores and bioluminescent moss  
• Creatures adapted to low gravity  
• The source of the Aetheric Compounds  
• Forbidden zones where storms form inside the rock

passages.heading: THE WORLD: The Convergence Era
passages.text:
This vertical world is the spine of the story.

Core throughline: Dr. Lira Calyx’s field journals begin as careful catalogues of a world remade by the Convergence and end as a forensic record of a conspiracy that engineered that remaking. Across four books the story moves from observation to hypothesis, from political fracture to moral action, and finally to a scientific reckoning that is incomplete and costly. Lira’s voice—precise, curious, and increasingly urgent—carries lab‑grade analysis alongside lyrical field notes. An unknown follower, later revealed as the archivist, leaves faint marks through the earlier volumes and ultimately steals the testament from the Continuum. The result is a narrative that refuses tidy closure: knowledge survives, but its author does not, and the world remains dangerously unstable.

passages.heading: Book I Biology of the Modern World
passages.text:
Lira arrives at the Mid‑Slope research terrace with instruments, notebooks, and a patience born of long field seasons. She reestablishes baselines—light spectra from crystalline bark, spore densities in Spore‑Weaver webs, migration counts for Ridgeback Striders—and writes with the calm of someone who trusts method.

Fieldwork and the first anomaly.  
On the third night she records the Spore‑Weavers pulsing in a valley like a single organism. Her photodiode array returns a waveform she cannot explain: phase offsets that propagate across kilometers with a coherence no circadian driver accounts for. She labels the interference Pattern α and sketches the waveform in the margin.

A subtle hand.  
On page 47, beneath Lira’s sketch of a Ridgeback Strider gait, a tiny marginal note appears in a different hand: “Phase offset miscalculated. Re‑sample at 0.5 s resolution.” Lira circles it and writes, “Who wrote this?” The question is left unanswered. The note is the first fingerprint of the person who will later call themselves the archivist.

passages.heading: Book I Biology of the Modern World
passages.text:
Anomalies accumulate.  
Juvenile Ember Wolves are found at altitudes their physiology should not permit. Aether‑Vines curve toward a narrow azimuth on the Peaks. A small outpost is struck by a localized aetheric storm; instruments record transient gravity fluctuations and a spike in Aetheric particle counts. Lira salvages a fragment of crystalline material threaded with micro‑filaments and begins the assays that will change everything.

Hypothesis and departure.  
She formalizes Hypothesis 1: Aetheric gradients act as directional cues, biasing evolutionary trajectories upward. She publishes a cautious note and receives a thinly veiled threat from a corporate patron. A redaction appears in the official field logs. An anonymous packet references Operation ReGenesis. Lira leaves the Mid‑Slopes with the fragment and a single line in her journal: “Life is not choosing upward. It is being chosen.”

passages.heading: Book II The Aetheric Systems
passages.text:
Lira follows the fragment into archives and labs. The work becomes technical, forensic, and political.

Traces in the archive.  
Cross‑referencing microstructure with pre‑Convergence patents, she finds a buried signature: a lab consortium that ceased public operations months before the Convergence. Isotope fractionation shows non‑natural ratios—evidence of deep‑earth seeding. In a corporate lab she finds a scrap of paper tucked behind a console: “She’s close. Move the logs.” The scrap is unsigned. Someone is already trying to hide the tracks.

Politics and weaponization.  
Aetheric Compounds become currency. The Council of Peaks forms and fractures. A public hearing on harvesting turns violent when a prototype harvester destabilizes a ridge. Lira infiltrates a corporate facility and watches Aetheric pulses alter gene expression in fungal cultures. The science she loves becomes a lever for power.

The Continuum’s shadow.  
She deciphers a sealed archive that names Dr. Solace Veylor and references Operation ReGenesis—a program to seed catalysts that accelerate adaptive evolution. Lira publishes a technical brief exposing engineered catalysts; unknown actors surgically redact it and brand her a saboteur. A misfiled footnote in one of the Continuum manifests bears handwriting that matches the marginal note from Book I. The follower is closer than she knows.

passages.heading: Book II The Aetheric Systems
passages.text:
Ending.  
A clandestine note arrives: “You are looking at the wrong end of the needle. Look below.” Lira begins to suspect a subterranean organization and prepares to go deeper.

passages.heading: Book III The Human Threshold
passages.text:
Lira moves from data to people. She travels among Peakborn, Midlanders, and Lowland Remnants, recording rituals and oral histories that echo a single motif: a second transformation.

Myth as encoded observation.  
She correlates storm‑songs with aetheric flux cycles and finds statistical alignment—myth functioning as distributed sensing. The Peakborn sing phase offsets that match AFU spikes; Midlander storytellers encode nodal maps in harvest chants. Lira’s science reads myth as data.

Infiltration and betrayal.  
With a Peakborn ally she gains access to Continuum outposts and discovers a subterranean city powered by Aetheric cores. There she confronts an archivist who speaks in half‑truths and riddles. A Midlander engineer she trusted betrays her for promises of restoration. One of the Continuum logs she steals is later found corrupted—overwritten with false timestamps and fabricated sensor readings. Someone is actively sabotaging the data streams that feed her models.

Flight and redaction.  
Lira escapes with stolen logs proving Veylor’s intent: The Second Genesis—a plan to destabilize the Peaks to force a selective reset. The Continuum begins targeted destabilizations; her journals are tampered with and redacted. She broadcasts a raw data dump to settlements; the signal is jammed, but fragments leak and spark uprisings. Her handwriting grows erratic. A page she thought she wrote later appears in the archive with a second set of annotations in a different hand—the archivist’s hand—trying to nudge her away from a fatal assumption.

passages.heading: Book III The Human Threshold
passages.text:
Climax.  
She goes into hiding. The world begins to show new, worrying patterns: aether storms cluster in sequences her models did not predict; Spore‑Weaver pulses shift into warning rhythms she cannot decode. The follower’s marginal notes continue to appear—small corrections, misnumbered pages, a misfiled coordinate—breadcrumbs left by someone who is following, not yet revealed.

passages.heading: Book IV The Redacted Testament — Final Reckoning
passages.text: This book is the testament and the trap. It is the volume where Lira tries to act, and where the cost of action becomes absolute.

passages.heading: Act I — The Peaks Awaken
passages.text:
Synchronized aether storms threaten to collapse Mid‑Slope terraces. Lira assembles a coalition: Mara, a Peakborn storm‑singer; Joren, the repentant Midlander engineer; and Kade, a Lowland scout. She models Aetheric flow as a coupled oscillator network and proposes a non‑destructive rebalancing: introduce phase‑offset pulses to damp runaway resonance.

The model she trusts.  
She formalizes the system as a network of coupled oscillators:

\ddot{x}_i + \gamma \dot{x}_i + \omega_i^2 x_i = \sum_{j} K_{ij} (x_j - x_i)

and the stability criterion:

\lambda_{\text{max}}(L) < \frac{\gamma}{2}

where \(L\) is the Laplacian of the coupling network. Her plan: deploy fungal‑integrated emitters to introduce staggered phase offsets and force destructive interference across runaway nodes.

A hidden variable.  
Unknown to Lira, the Continuum has seeded a deep core beneath Peak 12 that alters local coupling constants \(K_{ij}\) and injects false phase data into Spore‑Weaver networks. Her inputs—those phase correlations she trusts—are partially corrupted. The model is brilliant; the data are compromised.

passages.heading: Act II — The Descent
passages.text:
The coalition descends into the Continuum’s core. Instruments must be tuned to the Peaks’ natural frequencies; timing is everything.

Confrontation without closure.  
In the core Lira confronts Veylor. He is not a caricature but a man who believes in necessary cruelty. He reveals that he anticipated her model and seeded false data into the networks years ago. He calls his work directed resilience and offers a cold, persuasive logic: the old world was weak; a hard reset is a mercy.

Sabotage revealed.  
Lira realizes the inputs that informed her coupling matrix were altered. A key term in her coupling matrix—an apparent constant of environmental damping—was a Continuum artifact. Her phase‑offset schedule, calculated to stagger by \(2\pi/N\), is based on corrupted nodal coordinates. The emitters she deploys are tuned to the wrong modes in several critical nodes.

passages.heading: Act III — The Choice and Aftermath
passages.text:
Lira triggers the phase‑offset pulses. The result is not the elegant reconfiguration she modeled.

Partial effect, partial catastrophe.  
The pulses produce a temporary, unstable equilibrium—a pause in the worst oscillations but not a solution. Some nodes damp; others amplify. A Continuum core fractures partially and collapses, but other cores shift and re‑synchronize in new, unpredictable ways. Veylor escapes deeper into the mountain. The Continuum splinters but does not fall.

Lira’s capture and the cost.  
During the partial collapse, tunnels shear and exits seal. Lira is cornered. Witnesses later report a sound like a thousand small fractures and the mountain swallowing a voice. She is taken. Her final journal is left behind—torn, redacted, and incomplete.

The world after Lira.  
The Peaks do not settle into safety. They enter a new, more dangerous phase:

• Aether storms increase in frequency and cluster into sequences that defy prior models.  
• Mid‑Slope terraces show hairline fractures and emergency evacuations.  
• Peakborn storm‑songs become dirges; elders sing of a mountain that no longer answers.  
• Spore‑Weavers pulse in panic rhythms; their phase coherence drops in places and spikes in others.  
• Lowland caravans report new mutations in the Scorched Biome—organisms that respond to AFU spikes with sudden, aggressive behaviors.

passages.heading: Act III — The Choice and Aftermath
passages.text: Lira’s equations survive, but they are incomplete. Her appendices contain methods and ethical protocols, but they are not a cure. Her sacrifice delays catastrophe in places and accelerates it in others. The Continuum is wounded, not destroyed. Veylor is alive.

passages.heading: Final Chapter — The Redacted Testament
passages.text: The final volume is a found document: Lira’s handwriting, fevered and precise; pages blacked out; diagrams overwritten; and, finally, an unknown hand that becomes the voice of the present.

passages.heading: I. Lira’s Descent
passages.text:
Entry — Lira Calyx, hand cramped, ink smeared  
I have not slept in three nights. Every time I close my eyes I hear the Peaks breathing. Or maybe it’s him. Or maybe it’s me.

She lists near‑misses, encoded fungal messages, rumors of Continuum couriers, and a redacted ledger stamped PROPERTY OF CONTINUUM. She writes the line that will haunt the rest of the book: “I know paranoia when it blooms. This is not paranoia. This is presence.”

passages.heading: II. The Redactions
passages.text: Pages arrive with black bars—some clumsy, some surgical. Methods vanish. Coordinates are excised in a cipher. Names are replaced with bureaucratic stamps. The redactions are not only censorship; they are a map of control.

passages.heading: III. The Coded Passages
passages.text:
Lira hides meaning in form: spiraled Aether‑Vine vectors that rotate into maps; Spore‑Weaver pulses transcribed as notation; storm‑songs annotated with phase offsets. She writes in metaphor because metaphor survives ink.

The mountain’s shadow has a shadow.  
And it follows me.

passages.heading: IV. Hallucination and Data
passages.text: Her dreams and observations merge. She records a photodiode registering a 0.003 lux fluctuation at 12 Hz and, on the next line, a dream of Veylor’s face fracturing in crystalline bark. The hallucinations are precise; they reference measurable phenomena. The line between waking and dreaming becomes another sensor.

passages.heading: V. The Continuum’s Hand
passages.text: The handwriting changes—forced confessions, misspelled names, bureaucratic flatness. The Continuum tries to overwrite her voice. Pages are torn. Some are replaced with blank sheets stamped with the Continuum seal. This is an attempt to manufacture doubt.

passages.heading: VI. The Plan She Could Not Publish
passages.text:
Her final methodological appendix is a terse, numbered operation:

1. Map nodal points — Spore‑Weaver arrays to identify coherent oscillators.  
2. Deploy phase‑offset emitters — fungal‑integrated devices to introduce destructive interference.  
3. Use fungal networks as sensors — distributed phase coherence monitoring.  
4. Trigger controlled reconfiguration — force a new topology without collapse.

She writes the math she trusts and annotates it with field values and a single warning: timing is everything.

\ddot{x}_i + \gamma \dot{x}_i + \omega_i^2 x_i = \sum_{j} K_{ij} (x_j - x_i)

\lambda_{\text{max}}(L) < \frac{\gamma}{2}

Her assays show the fragment is a seeding lattice with catalytic activity at AFU \(> 0.7\). Her plea is clear: phase offsets, not fire.

The final sentence breaks mid‑line: “If I don’t make it out, if this book is all that remains, then let it be known that the Peaks are—” The rest is torn away.

passages.heading: VII. The Archivist Revealed
passages.text:
A new voice enters—exhausted, guilty, urgent. Not a neutral historian but a follower who trailed Lira into the tunnels and watched her taken. They confess they are the one who left marginal notes earlier in the volumes: the tiny correction on page 47, the misfiled footnote, the misnumbered page. They were not the person Lira trusted. They were the one who arrived too late.

They stole the books from the Continuum not out of heroism but out of obligation and guilt. They admit the truth Lira could not finish writing:

• Her plan was incomplete. A hidden Continuum core corrupted the inputs.  
• Her pulses did not save the world. They produced a fragile pause and a partial fracture.  
• She paid with her life. The Continuum took her into the mountain.

passages.heading: VIII. The World After Lira
passages.text:
The archivist describes the aftermath with clinical detail and a broken voice:

• Aether storms cluster in new sequences.  
• Terraces crack and communities evacuate.  
• Spore‑Weaver coherence becomes unreliable.  
• Mutations appear in the Lowlands that respond to AFU spikes with sudden aggression.

Lira’s work becomes a contested scripture: taught in some academies, banned in others, sung in Peakborn circles as a warning. Her ethical protocols are debated; her equations are used and misused.

passages.heading: IX. The Final Warning
passages.text:
The archivist turns to the reader and breaks the fourth wall not as flourish but as survival protocol. The handwriting sharpens. The tone becomes a command.

“If you understand even a fraction of what she wrote, you are infected with the truth. The Continuum hunts truth like a disease.”

“If you are reading this, you are a target.”

“You are not safe.”

“You are one of us now.”

“There is no running. There is no hiding. There is only fighting.”

“Do not let Lira’s sacrifice end in vain.”

“Close the book if you want. Or keep going. Either way — they will come.”

works.title: World Codex of Wyrmreach
works.blurb: cosmology, elf tribes, and twin-soul dragons of the Wyrmreach setting, companion bible to the novel WrymWretch.

passages.heading: World Codex of Wyrmreach
passages.text:
World Codex of Wyrmreach  
Cosmic Origin  
The cosmos began as the First Light, a singular radiant being that shattered into two primal forces: the Sun’s Roaring Anger and the Moon’s Silent Tear. From these celestial events emerged dragons, born of the Sun’s fury, and elves, born of the Moon’s sorrow. Bound by the Threefold Bond—Symbiotic Royal Bond, Ancestral Hybridization, and Twin-Soul Incarnation—dragons and elves share intertwined destinies, resonant magic, and shared origins.  
Central Plot  
Shallock Izladar, a Celestial Elf scholar, ascended into an astral entity after delving into forbidden cosmic texts. His transformation threatened reality, prompting the Luminary Priory and the six elven tribes to imprison him in a realm outside existence, sealed by memory itself. The Remnants of Izladar now seek to erase all memory of him, believing his resurrection will elevate reality. As memories fade, the world decays—forests forget how to grow, stars lose constellations, oceans forget their ecosystems, and dragons and elves weaken. Dragons awaken from dormancy, their elven twins feeling the call, and all paths lead to #Wrymreach, the birthplace of their kind.  
Elven Races  
Wood Elves — Cedarheart Enclave  
Wood Elves live in harmony with nature, skilled in archery and survival. They worship forest spirits and dwell in ancient treehouses. Their olive-toned skin, green or brown hair, and amber or green eyes reflect their woodland origins. Their twin dragon is Sylvan.  
Sky Elves — Galewing Assembly  
Sky Elves are nomadic explorers of the skies, skilled in aerial navigation, music, and astronomy. They venerate sky gods and live on floating platforms and mountaintops. Pale skin, silver or white hair, and blue or gray eyes define them. Their twin dragon is Aetherius.  
Earth Elves — Mosswhisper Tribe  
Earth Elves are craftsmen, miners, and farmers with deep ties to the land. They honor earth deities and ancestral spirits, living in underground cities adorned with gemstones. Their earth-toned skin and soil-colored hair reflect their connection to the land. Their twin dragon is Gaia.  
Water Elves — Tidecaller Circle  
Water Elves are sailors, healers, and navigators of the sea. They worship water spirits and live in coastal or underwater settlements. Their aqua-toned skin, blue or silver hair, and ocean-colored eyes mirror the tides. Their twin dragon is Aquatica.  
Dark Elves — Duskbane Syndicate  
Dark Elves are shadow mages, spies, and assassins dwelling in subterranean labyrinths. They honor night deities and possess obsidian skin, silver or black hair, and violet or crimson eyes. Their twin dragon is Umbra.  
Celestial Elves — Luminary Priory  
Celestial Elves are spiritual beings devoted to enlightenment and cosmic harmony. They meditate upon celestial forces and live in floating crystalline forests. Their luminous skin, silver or gold hair, and starlit eyes reflect their celestial nature. Their twin dragon is Astraia.  
Draconian Races  
Sylvan — Dragon of the Wood Elves  
Sylvan commands nature, shaping plants, healing forests, and communicating with woodland life.  
Aetherius — Dragon of the Sky Elves  
Aetherius wields air magic, shaping winds, calming storms, and sharing telepathic knowledge.  
Gaia — Dragon of the Earth Elves  
Gaia commands geomancy, shaping stone, resonating with crystals, and recalling fossil memories.  
Aquatica — Dragon of the Water Elves  
Aquatica controls water, shaping tides, purifying seas, and communicating with aquatic life.  
Umbra — Dragon of the Dark Elves  
Umbra manipulates shadows, creating illusions, concealing itself, and hunting in darkness.  
Astraia — Dragon of the Celestial Elves  
Astraia channels astral energy, creating shields, projecting celestial beams, and glimpsing cosmic futures.  
Geography  
#Wrymreach  
A cosmic wound where the Sun’s anger and Moon’s tear collided. Reality thins, time folds, and memory bleeds. Wyrm bones hum with ancient resonance. It is the birthplace of dragons and elves.  
The Six Realms  
West: Cedarheart Forest North: Galewing Peaks South: Mosswhisper Depths East: Tidecaller Shores Below: Duskbane Underworld Above: High Realm  
The Astral Expanse  
A realm outside existence, the prison of Shallock Izladar.  
Creature Bestiary  
Forest: Grove Stags, Whisperfoxes, Rootbound Golems Sky: Stormriders, Cloud Serpents, Star Moths Earth: Crystal Crawlers, Fossil Wurms, Stoneback Behemoths Water: Tide Serpents, Moonfish, Kelprunners Dark: Shadehounds, Nightmares, Obsidian Spiders Celestial: Starborn Owls, Luminae, Astral Wyrmlings  
Magic System  
Memory-based reality shapes existence; when memory fades, reality decays. Twin-soul magic amplifies spells, senses, and dreams between elves and dragons. Celestial magic draws from Sun and Moon, while elemental magic reflects each tribe’s dragon.  
Factions and Orders  
Luminary Priory: Celestial scholars Duskbane Syndicate: Shadow operatives Remnants of Izladar: Memory-erasing fanatics Wyrmguard: Dragon-bonded warriors Circle of Seasons: Wood Elf druids Tidecallers: Water Elf healers Stonekeepers: Earth Elf crystal-smiths Galechanters: Sky Elf wind-singers  
Timeline  
1. First Light shatters  
2. Birth of dragons and elves  
3. Rise of the Six Tribes  
4. Discovery of the Twin-Soul Bond  
5. Shallock Izladar’s ascension  
6. Astral Cataclysm  
7. Great Imprisonment  
8. Remnants form  
9. Memory-Plague begins  
10. Awakening of the Dragons  
11. March to #Wrymreach

works.title: The Canon and Trope Ledger of Who Did It
works.blurb: a Thorne & Expanse clerk's ledger setting the game's record against the Bible's canon, entry by entry, with a 127-row account book of every trope the project owes.

passages.text:
*Kept at HollowMere, Coldwater Territory, for the Thorne & Expanse Line. Anno 1893.*

---

passages.heading: The Clerk's Oath
passages.text:
I swear to the Line that I will enter what is written. I swear I will enter what is said. I swear I will enter what is ruled.

I will enter nothing I have not seen written or heard said by more than one mouth. Where the paint says one thing and the town says another, I will set the two side by side and rule between them, as a clerk rules between two columns that ought to agree. I will not strike out a Company name. I will draw a line through it, so the next man can still read what it was.

My name is not needed for the ledger. The Line knows it, and that is enough.

*Margin: An oath to a railroad is an oath to a timetable. I have sworn it anyway.*

Entered.

---

## Entry I. The Year, the Territory, the Line, the Baron

passages.heading: The Clerk's Oath
passages.text:
**Record.** The sign at the platform reads "HOLLOWMERE — EST. BY THE RAILROAD EXPANSE". It hangs above the rail spur on the east edge, beside the platform lantern. The paint is newer than the post.

**Canon.** The town says it was not built by pioneers and not blessed by saints. It was laid down by the Railroad Barons, tie by wooden tie and spike by iron spike. The Barons own the mill. They own the bank. They own the dirt under a man's boots.

**Ruling.** The year is 1893, the year of the Panic. Banks are failing back east, railroads are failing back east, and strikes are spreading. Everywhere that is not here is "back east".

The country is Coldwater Territory. It is not yet a state, and the law is thin, so the Company is the law.

The line is the Thorne & Expanse. Its Baron is Cornelius Thorne. He is alive. He does not live here. He comes by train when the town riots, and he brings Pinkertons. "The Railroad Barons" is the town's word for Thorne and his partners, and the clerk enters it as a plural because the town says it as a plural.

passages.heading: The Clerk's Oath
passages.text:
*Margin: Scrip is still honoured at the Company window. For now.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry II. The Mere
passages.text:
**Record.** The town is named HollowMere. A mere is a lake.

**Canon.** There is no lake. There was one. It drained into the flooded tin mine and left a fen behind it: black water, reed, mud that freezes and thaws and freezes again. The town calls it a drowned marsh.

**Ruling.** The name is kept, and the lake is entered as lost.

The marsh gives off a sickness. The townsfolk call it mere-rot. The Company calls it miasma. The clerk enters them as one thing under two names, and lists what it does:

- It makes the wolves bold.
- It makes footsteps where nobody is walking.
- It makes the town cough.

*Margin: I have written "miasma" in the Company's books and "mere-rot" in my own. I cough in both.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry III. Aldous Vane, of Port-au-Levain
Entry III. Aldous Vane, of Port-au-Levain
passages.text:
His widow, Widow Vane, keeps the parlour in HollowMere. His portrait hangs there turned to the wall. The clerk enters the portrait as hung and as turned, and does not enter why.

*Margin: Wire or rumour. The telegraph room has no slip for it. "Three nights" dead has been three nights dead for as long as I have kept this book.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry IV. The Drowned Lantern
passages.text:
**Record.** The Company's books list the "Rusty Lantern Saloon". The licence is in that name, and so is the whiskey order.

**Canon.** A barman drowned in the mere carrying the saloon's sign lantern. The town has called the place the Drowned Lantern ever since, and the Company name has not been spoken there since.

**Ruling.** The house is the Drowned Lantern. The Company name is struck through, not erased. Mrs Grieves keeps it.

It holds the dartboard, the shutters, the flour bin, and the photographs of drowned sailors behind the bar. In the back room there is an oil barrel.

The barman's name is not in the record. The clerk does not supply one. The town remembers one thing about him: at dusk, when he trimmed the wick of the sign lantern, he would hum the same hymn every time, never all the way through. The clerk enters the habit because it is what the town kept.

passages.heading: Entry IV. The Drowned Lantern
passages.text:
*Margin: There are photographs of drowned sailors in a town with no sea. I do not know which of them were sailors.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

## Entry V. Black Pine, Gallows Wood, the Fenwood

**Record.** The maps give three names: Black Pine, Gallows Wood, the Fenwood.

**Canon.** It is all one forest.

**Ruling.** Black Pine is the whole forest. It has two parts:

- **Gallows Wood** is the near edge, where the planks are laid and where the town hangs people.
- **The Fenwood** is the drowned heart. In it are the hanging oak, the charcoal clamp, the drowned lantern still glowing in the marsh fog, and the den.

Mother Moll keeps her charcoal hut in the Fenwood. Her terms are "Four sprigs of herb, dear. The fog is in everyone's chest." The clerk enters the terms as fair.

*Margin: The drowned lantern is still lit. Some say it is the old lake-light, fallen from the oak. Some say the barman went under with it. I do not know who lights it now.*

passages.heading: Entry IV. The Drowned Lantern
passages.text:
Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

## Entry VI. Father Bray, and the New Vicar

**Record.** The chapel is St Brannock's. There is a rope in it, with a torn glove caught in the rope.

**Canon.** Father Bray, the old priest, is gone. The town says he died. The town also says he fled. A new Vicar came on the train.

**Ruling.** Bray's going is why the Vicar came. The clerk rules on that much. Whether Bray is dead or fled, the clerk does not rule.

The Vicar's own words are entered: "Everyone in Hollowmere confesses to you sooner or later." He brings the town to his faith. A Zealot, if one rises, would kill him and walk in his robes for as long as the body goes unreported. The clerk enters that as a thing that can happen in this town, not a thing that has happened.

His last words, should he come to them, are already known to the town and are entered here as the town has them:

passages.heading: Entry IV. The Drowned Lantern
passages.text:
> "In the end I sought nothing else but to serve God. And serve him I did. With this death's last breath I pray this prayer: may the Almighty grant me the strength of ten in the next life. And in return, tenfold my own."

His memorial is a lavender field, a lone orange tree, and a blue sky.

passages.heading: Margin: Whose glove?
passages.text:
Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry VII. Tamsin Crumb, of the Island
passages.text:
**Record.** Crumb's Ovens. In the shop are the wake table, ten plates and the dead loaves. Behind it are the cold room, the mixing room, the oven room and the proofing room.

**Canon.** Tamsin Crumb came from Port-au-Levain. She crossed with Vane. She brought the wake-loaf custom with her: one loaf for each mourner and three for the dead, each loaf carrying a crumb token sealed in wax.

**Ruling.** HollowMere's mourning is an island custom. Through it the island has a part in every funeral here. Crumb crossed with Vane, and the clerk enters that and nothing more. A shared crossing is not a shared purpose.

*Margin: Ten plates were laid. I counted the town afterwards. I will not write the number here.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

## Entry VIII. BlackPine, from Vane to Harrow; from Tin to Coal

**Record.** At BlackPine:

- the mill is called Vane Sawmill;
- the Deep Level holds a tin crate and a refuge table;
- the motto over the camp reads "PRODUCTION IS OBLIGATION.";
- the tally board in the Blackpine Workings has one name chalked out.

passages.heading: Entry VII. Tamsin Crumb, of the Island
passages.text:
**Canon.** BlackPine was Vane's timber-and-tin camp. The tin ran out. The Harrow Timber & Coal Syndicate bought it and found coal under the old workings.

The men there are told when they sign at the intake office that they are either feeding the furnace or they are fuel. Their tally log stands between them and a shallow grave.

**Ruling.** The deed is Harrow's, and the name on the mill is Vane's. Both stay. The tin is entered as spent and the coal as found. The clerk enters the Tally Rack as BlackPine enters it: ten numbered pine billets and ten Identity Logs, branded with the man's job, his debts and his sins. In BlackPine, the log on a man's rack at dawn is who he is.

*Margin: One name is chalked out on the board in the Workings. The board does not say whose, and nobody at the Company Office would read it to me.*

passages.heading: Entry VII. Tamsin Crumb, of the Island
passages.text:
Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

## Entry IX. The Roles and the Five Trades

**Record.** The town's cards name these places a person may hold:

- Killer, Accomplice, Heir;
- Detective, Vicar, Watchman;
- Herbalist, Gamekeeper, Butler;
- Child, Drifter, Lamplighter;
- Baker, Fisher, Tinner.

Later arrivals are the Ranger, with a crossbow and the right to arrest; the Thief, who takes heirlooms and leaves by sea; and the Medium, with seance chalk.

**Canon.** The town counts five public trades: Baker, Postmaster, Undertaker, Bartender and Company Clerk.

**Ruling.** They all stand side by side. The clerk enters them as a census of the town, not of its people.

- **The Baker** is up before anyone, flour to the elbows. She bakes Wake Loaves and Rumor Loaves, and may become a Fence or a Ration Tyrant.
- **The Postmaster** steams envelopes over a kettle, and may become a Handler, a Postmaster Assassin, or an Extortionist.
- **The Undertaker** pushes a hearse cart, and may become a Grave Robber, who seals the Vicar in a lead coffin, or a Chief Coroner.
- **The Bartender** keeps a sawed-off behind the bar and serves Rotgut, Liquid Courage and Loose Lips Lager. He may become a Union Boss or a Vigilante.
- **The Company Clerk** collects rent and works the telegraph, and may become an Embezzler or the Baron's Heir.
- **The Watchman** walks the lanes after dark and stands by one door each night.
- **The Herbalist** holds two bottles. One saves, one ends.
- **The Gamekeeper** was paid by Vane to keep the wood. If they come for him, he will not go alone.
- **The Butler** knows every door in Hollowmere.
- **The Child** is small and quiet, and hides, watches, remembers.
- **The Drifter** wants to hang.
- **The Lamplighter** lights the lanterns that keep the wolves off the square.
- **The Fisher** does not take the boats out, because the fog keeps them in. He fishes the mere channels instead.
- **The Tinner**'s mine is shut. His hands are not.
- **The Doctor** is entered without remark.
- **The Killer** walks in a borrowed character, strikes after dark when the room is empty, cleans one clue, washes at the well, and is then the loudest voice asking who did it.
- **The Accomplice** never holds the knife, only the alibi.
- **The Heir** is the Accomplice who inherits the Knife.
- **The Detective** collects, inspects and cross-references.

passages.heading: Entry VII. Tamsin Crumb, of the Island
passages.text:
Beside these the clerk enters positions a person may come to hold. They are not people:

- **The Zealot.** Under him stand the Dark Positions: Minion, Mob Boss, Cultist, High Priest.
- **The Activist.** She works the soapbox at the bell. If she survives the Redemption vote, she is plain Townsfolk again.
- **The Bandit.** Bandana, six-shooter, four scores.
- **The Hitman.** Nobody starts as one. He becomes one when the black-wax envelope comes.
- **The Law.** Detective, then Police Officer, then Judge.
- **The changed.** The Apostate, prayed for by both sides until he snapped. The Stowaway, in a freight crate with the Baron's manifest. The Starving.

*Margin: My own trade is on the list. I do not say which of its two evolutions I am closer to.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry X. The Telephone at BlackPine
passages.text:
**Record.** The Company Office at BlackPine holds a ledger desk, a safe, a map table, and a telephone. The telephone is dead.

**Canon.** The town tells no story about it. A telephone at the edge of Coldwater Territory in 1893 is a thing out of its time.

**Ruling.** It is Harrow's new line. It was strung lately, it rarely works, and it is entered as a rumour of modern times reaching a camp that has not yet had the old ones. A line that does not carry a voice is still a line on the Syndicate's books.

*Margin: It was heard to ring once. It was dead when it rang.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry XI. The Tide Chart
passages.text:
**Record.** A tide chart, with the next low tide circled in ink.

**Canon.** HollowMere has no sea and the mere is not one. A tide chart has no business here.

**Ruling.** Both readings are entered, and neither is struck:

- The chart is an old one that Vane brought from the island, and it charts the island's tides.
- The mere still rises and falls through the channel where the lake drained, and the chart is used for that.

*Margin: The circled low tide came. The mere went down at that hour. I have not ruled which of the two readings explains it.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Record.** "Old Fennick at the light.
passages.text:
**Canon.** There is no lighthouse at HollowMere. There was a lake-light at the edge of the water, put up when there was a lake, and young Fennick kept it. He is old Fennick now, and he keeps it still.

**Ruling.** It was a lake-light and is now a marsh light. It burns at the marsh edge and guides nobody anywhere in particular. Fennick keeps it lit all the same. The island's lighthouse is entered separately, as the island's.

*Margin: Bog-wisps show lights too, and they lure. I have stood at the marsh edge and could not tell Fennick's light from theirs.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry XIII. Harbourmaster Pell's Harbour
passages.text:
**Record.** The title is "Harbourmaster".

**Canon.** HollowMere has no harbour. It has a marsh dock, a leaking skiff, and a ferry that Tuck, the ferry boy, poles across the channels.

**Ruling.** "Harbour" means the marsh dock. The title is kept out of courtesy, or out of habit; the clerk cannot say which. Pell's terms of trade are entered as he states them: "The skiff leaks. Bring me resin and a plank of timber and I will lend you a lantern."

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry XIV. The Mirroring
passages.text:
**Record.** Three towns keep three sets of books, and they come to the same column totals.

**Canon.** Nobody can say why.

**Ruling.** The parallels are entered in short. No cause is given.

- **Clocks.** HollowMere, the Daily Train. Port-au-Levain, the Morning Ferry. BlackPine, the Payroll Train and the Shift-Whistle.
- **Money and tax.** Scrip paid as the Clerk's rent; Copper paid as the platter tariff; Syndicate scrip held against the Tallyman's quota.
- **Identity.** The role card; the Wake Loaf platter in the Great Hearth; the branded tally log on the Rack.
- **First vendetta.** Zealot against Vicar; Leaven-Rot against the Abbot of the Crust; Timber-Wolf against the Forest Chaplain.
- **Second.** Activist against Baron; Pyre-Master against the Grand Inspector-General; Slate-Breaker against the Syndicate Inspector.
- **Third.** Bandit; Smuggler-Blackguard; Company Enforcer.
- **Fourth.** Hitman; Black-Crust Contract; Pit-Poisoner.
- **Law.** Detective, Police Officer, Judge; Inquisitor, Guild Bailiff, High Chancellor; Camp Investigator, Mine Warden, Circuit Judge.
- **Verdicts.** Acquittal, a Heavy Fine, or Death by the gallows trapdoor; Acquittal, a Guild Fine, or Trial by Fire in the Great Hearth; Acquittal, Scrip Forfeiture, or The Great Sawmill Blade.
- **Predators.** Wolves; Tide-Ghouls; Timber-Wolves and Tunnel Crawlers.
- **Enforcers.** Pinkertons; Iron-Wardens; OEAs.

passages.heading: Entry XIV. The Mirroring
passages.text:
On the island they say the loaf sitting on your silver plate at dawn is who you are. At BlackPine they say the log on your rack at dawn is who you are. The clerk has heard HollowMere say something like it about the card. He has not seen it written, so he does not enter the words.

*Margin: Accounts that balance this well were cooked by someone.*

*Margin, later, same hand: It has since been written down. "The card in your hand at dawn is who you are." I enter it now. I did not write it.*

Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---

passages.heading: Entry XV. The Rumours
passages.text:
**Record.** None. Nothing about this is painted, chalked or stamped.

**Canon.** Something runs between HollowMere, BlackPine and Port-au-Levain. It travels faster than the train and faster than the ferry. Each town's crimes echo the others'.

**Ruling.** The clerk has ruled three columns and filled none of them.

*True?* The echoes are real. Entry XIV has them. A widow's portrait is turned to the wall inland, and a death opens every telling on the island. A name is chalked out at BlackPine.

*Alive?* At BlackPine they say something out there in the black pines isn't cutting trees. In HollowMere they say the pines were not empty. The marsh makes footsteps where nobody walks.

*Carried?* The train brings a black-wax envelope in the mailbag. News of a death on the island reached the telegraph room before any boat could have. The ferry casts off in fog. The Stowaway reads the manifest. Tamsin Crumb came across the water. Vane came across the water before her, and went back.

passages.heading: Entry XV. The Rumours
passages.text:
Against all three columns, the clerk enters three objects and does not rule on any of them:

- a gravestone with tomorrow's date;
- chalk hopscotch under a lantern, with no child seen playing it;
- the drowned lantern in the Fenwood, still glowing.

*Margin: I have tried to rule on this three times. Each time the page came out the same.*

Entered. Not settled.

---

passages.heading: Entry XVI. The First Body
passages.text:
*Entered out of order. The book was closed when I found him.*

**Record.** A grave in the yard of St Brannock's, under the Company bell. The Company's entry for the man in it reads "lost in the workings".

**Canon.** His name was Jory Kitto, and he was a tinner. When the lake was drained into Vane's gallery to lay the Line's last mile, he struck the last plug. He was found afterwards at the end of the line. He was the first body it had.

**Ruling.** The Company's entry stands, struck through, so the next man can read what it was. Beneath it the clerk enters his name and his trade. On him was a tobacco tin, and in it were his wages, saved toward his sister's fare. The clerk enters the tin. He does not enter whether she came.

*Margin: The town says the plug went at 11:47. The town says it.*

passages.heading: Entry XVI. The First Body
passages.text:
Entered. Ruled. Not believed.

---
