passages.heading: The Testament of the Mother of Mothers
passages.text:
*Being the Archive of the Sovereign Sourdough Council, as kept in the Counting-House of Port-au-Levain, its last entry dated in the year 1893.*

[PROPERTY OF THE COUNTING-HOUSE]

> "Out here beyond the reef, bread isn't just food. It's law, it's lineage, and it's life."
> — from the proclamation-board of the Council, painted over three times and never changed

---

passages.heading: Of the Rock
passages.text:
**The Reef.** It is the one way in. Black stone lies under green water, and the channel through it is known to pilots and to the drowned. The Morning Ferry is the island's clock. It casts off at dawn, and what misses it stays until the next dawn, or for good. The distance to the mainland is a distance the Council has never published.

**The Great Hearth & Hall of Platters.** The Hearth is the oldest fire on the rock and has never been let go out. The Hall around it holds a silver platter for every soul on the island. On each platter sits a Wake Loaf stamped with its owner's guild seal. A soul without a platter has no name in law. A platter without a loaf is a death, or a sentence, or both.

**The Windmill Cliffs.** Here the Council's flour is ground. In fog the fishermen read the turning sails the way other people read a clock face. When the sails stop, the wind has stopped, and when the wind stops the island waits.

passages.heading: Of the Rock
passages.text:
**The Subterranean Yeast Vault.** The Mother of Mothers lives here, in a vat of pressurized glass, fed by steam that rises out of the mountain's throat. The Vault has two keys and one feeding hand. Below the vat there is only heat.

**The Salt-Flats & Smuggler's Wharf.** This is where things come ashore that the Counting-House did not count. The Salt-Flat Drowners walk here at low tide, and the Tide-Ghouls when the tide is wrong. Neither is entered in the census. Both are entered in the burial rolls.

**The Alchemist-Herbalist's Apothecary.** It sells tinctures and sour-salts, and keeps a register of poisons that the Inquisitor reads every quarter.

**Gallows Square.** It is the second-oldest structure on the rock, after the Hearth. The rope is replaced each spring whether it has been used or not.

**The Lighthouse.** It lights the reef and not the town. When the fog comes in off the water it takes the harbour lamps one by one, like a hand pinching wicks.

passages.heading: Of the Rock
passages.text:
**The Counting-House.** It holds the archive, the tariffs, the Guild Copper and the yeast tokens. It is this book's home and, some will say, this book's author.

**The Port Tavern.** Here rumour is weighed before the Council weighs it. Its weights are kinder.

**The Sacred Kitchen.** Ten rooms, entered here as the liturgy enters them:
- The **cellar**, for the cool rest.
- The **cold pantry**, for what is kept.
- The **command desk**, where the day's bake is ordered.
- The **dish pit**, for penance.
- The **expediter**, where nothing passes unseen.
- **Front of house**, where the people receive.
- **Hygiene**, where purity is inspected.
- **Lamination**, for patience in folds.
- The **shaping bench**, where a loaf becomes a person's.
- The **sub-basement**, the door above the Vault, whose key is one of the two.

**The Council & the Guilds.** The Sovereign Sourdough Council sits in the gallery above the Hall. Below it sit the guild offices: Master Proof-Reader, Spice-Master, Tide-Watcher, Hearth-Warden, Ledger-Clerk. The Iron-Wardens enforce what the Council decides, and do not ask why.

passages.heading: Of the Rock
passages.text:
**Copper & Yeast-Tax.** Every platter owes a tariff, paid in Guild Copper and in yeast tokens. *An unpaid tariff makes a loaf Unregistered. An Unregistered loaf is a soul the Council no longer feeds.*

**The Law.** The Inquisitor asks. The Guild Bailiff takes. The High Chancellor decides. There are three verdicts:
- Acquittal.
- A Guild Fine.
- Trial by Fire in the Great Hearth. *The Hearth receives the loaf, and then the one the loaf named.*

> the loaf sitting on your silver plate at dawn is who you are.

---

passages.heading: Book One: Of the Mother
passages.text:
**The Bringing.** Four hundred years before this entry, the Master Bakers came over the reef with a crock wrapped in wool. They carried it the way one carries a sleeping child, as though it might wake and cry. The Mother of Mothers was older than their names. They set her down where the mountain breathed, and the mountain fed her.

**The Hymn.** The founding hymn is sung at every first loaf. It has four verses and a refrain, and children learn it before they can count. They are counting when they sing it, though they do not know it. The first verse is the feeding hour. The second is the steam, given in the old measure. The third is the flour-to-water, and the fourth is the rest. Whoever forgets the song forgets the Mother. The Council has never written the song down, because a song cannot be confiscated.

*[— in another hand: the second verse is wrong in every copy after the plague year. Sing it a breath slower.]*

passages.heading: Book One: Of the Mother
passages.text:
**The Vat.** The first vat was clay and the second was copper. The third, which stands now, is glass, so that the Mother can be watched. Glass also means that anyone who comes down the stair can see her: a pale tide inside a lamp, breathing.

**The Platters.** The first census on the rock was baked, not written. Each family shaped one loaf from the Mother's leaven and set it on a plate. The Council counted plates. Where there was a plate, there was a person. Ink came later, to keep the count honest. It has not.

---

passages.heading: Book Two: Of Bread Made Law
passages.text:
**Lineage.** A child's first loaf is shaped from a parent's leaven. So the line of a house is not written but fermented: what fed the mother feeds the daughter, and what soured in the father sours in the son. A disinherited child is given flour and no leaven. On the rock, that is the whole of the punishment, and it is enough.

**The Tariff.** The yeast-tax was first levied in the eleventh year of the Council. The names of the first loaves left Unregistered are kept in this ledger:

████████, a net-mender.
████, who kept goats on the cliff path.
████████████, and her two.
███, no trade given.

*[— in another hand: the goatkeeper's name was Ysolde. She sang to the goats. She was not behind in her tariff; she was behind in her prayers.]*

**The Four Sour-Practices.** The Council records four heresies against the Mother. Each is given here as it was charged and judged, and no further.

passages.heading: Book Two: Of Bread Made Law
passages.text:
*Leaven-Rot, against the Abbot of the Crust.* This was the belief that the Mother could be soured on purpose, and that a sour Mother could be prayed through. Its heretics were named by office, not by name: the Spore-Caller, the Groat-Master, the Cellar-Ghoul and the Arch-Fermenter. Verdict: Trial by Fire, all four. The Arch-Fermenter asked to keep his apron, which his wife had mended twice at the same corner. It was not permitted.

*The Pyre-Master, against the Grand Inspector-General.* This was the belief that the Hearth belonged to the island and not to the Council. Verdict: Trial by Fire. *[STRUCK BY ORDER OF THE HIGH CHANCELLOR]*

*The Smuggler-Blackguard.* This was a pocket-mortar at the Wharf, and loaves swapped on the platters, so that one man's name sat on another's bread. Verdict: a Guild Fine, then Gallows Square when the fine went unpaid.

*The Black-Crust Contract.* This was a message rolled into a pigeon's cylinder and a glaze the Apothecary's register could not account for. The bird was never found. Verdict: ████████.

passages.heading: Book Two: Of Bread Made Law
passages.text:
*[— in another hand: the Black-Crust woman kept a child's loaf back from her own platter every week for a year. The Council called it hoarding. It was for the boy she lost in the plague year.]*

**Trial by Fire.** The Hearth has received ████ souls since the Council first sat.

passages.heading: Book Three: Of the Offices
passages.text:
**The Old Brigade.** Before the Council had titles it had a kitchen, and the kitchen had ranks. They survive as the island's oldest offices, older than the gallery and the seal. Each is entered with its duty and its disgrace.

- **Le Boulanger.** The bake. Disgrace: a loaf that does not rise on the day of a wedding.
- **Le Levain.** The feeding hand, the only hand that touches the Mother. Hereditary. Disgrace: there is no recorded disgrace of this office, which is itself the record.
- **Le Commis.** The carrying hands. They carry flour, water and ash. They carry everything to the Mother and nothing from her. A Commis may carry, but may never feed the Mother.
- **L'Apprenti.** The one who watches. Disgrace: speaking.
- **Le Rat de Cave.** Keeper of the cellar door. Disgrace: the door.
- **Le Champignon.** The office of the first heresy, abolished. Its seal was ground into the floor of the dish pit, where the Plongeur kneels on it.
- **Le Chef de Cuisine** and **Le Sous-Chef.** Command and its shadow. These became the Council and its clerks.
- **L'Aboyeur.** The caller at the expediter, who calls each loaf by its owner's name as it passes. The island's first herald.
- **Le Tourrier.** The pastry, the folds, lamination. Disgrace: haste.
- **Le Plongeur.** The dish pit. Penance, by sentence or by birth.
- **Le Garde Manger.** The cold pantry and what is kept there.
- **L'Inspecteur Sanitaire.** The hygiene room, and the forerunner of the Grand Inspector-General.
- **Le Critique Gastronomique.** The outsider whose verdict the Council could not overrule. The office has been vacant for two hundred years. The Council keeps a chair for it, so that no one may sit in it.
- **Le Croissant Rassis.** "The stale one." This is not an office but a title, given to a disgraced holder of any other.

passages.heading: Book Three: Of the Offices
passages.text:
**The House of Vane.** The Vanes are a Council family. Their platters sit nearest the Hearth, where the silver goes faintly gold from four centuries of heat. For as long as the archive runs, the office of Le Levain has passed down their eldest line. Theirs is the feeding hand. The Mother has known the touch of no other house.

[SEALED: SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL]

---

passages.heading: Book Four: Of the Second Son
passages.text:
**The Stamping.** In the year ████, a younger son of the house of Vane came to his shaping. His name was Aldous. The Council looked at his loaf, at his line and at his elder brother. It stamped his platter **Commis**, not Levain. The feeding hand went to the elder line, as it always had. Aldous bowed to the gallery, as the custom is. From that day his platter said what he was: a Vane who may carry, but may never feed the Mother. He carried flour down the Vault stair every morning for six years. Every morning he set it at the foot of the vat and climbed back up without touching the glass.

*[— in another hand: he counted the steps. Ninety-one. He told me once that the Mother breathed slower when his brother fed her, and faster when no one did.]*

**The Cup.** He was a Vane who would never feed the Mother, and on a night in the seventh year he went down to her anyway. The archive is plain about what happened and silent about how. The sub-basement door was opened with its key. The Vault was opened. By whose hand the record does not say; it names only a keyholder the record bars.

passages.heading: Book Four: Of the Second Son
passages.text:
The keyholder on the night in question was ████████████.

He took a cup. It was a single cup, the kind a Commis uses to carry water down. For the first time in four hundred years, part of the Mother of Mothers was outside the vat. The steam went on rising into glass that held a cup less of her than it ever had. The keyholder locked the door behind him, and the record locked the keyholder behind a bar.

passages.heading: [— in another hand: ]
passages.text:
**The Short Count.** At the dawn feeding the elder brother found the Mother lower in her glass than the hymn allowed. The Hearth-Warden was called, and the Inquisitor after him. A thing outside the vat is a thing outside the law, and the Inquisitor opened a file on it before the fog had lifted from the Hall.

By then the Morning Ferry had cast off. On it, according to the ferryman's tally, was a young man with a carrying-cup wrapped in wool, held the way one holds a sleeping child. Aldous Vane was gone inland with the cup. The Inquisitor's file was open, and nothing on the rock could close it except the one who had left.

**Verdict in Absence.** The Inquisitor's file was open and the accused was across the water, so the Council did what the law allows. It tried an empty chair. The charge was theft of the Mother. The verdict was Trial by Fire in the Great Hearth.

passages.heading: [— in another hand: ]
passages.text:
The accused could not be given to the fire, so his loaf was given in his stead. His Wake Loaf was lifted from the Vane platter and carried down the Hall by the Aboyeur, who called his name as it passed. Then it was set in the Hearth. The platter was left where it stood, empty, nearest the fire, and stamped:

[UNREGISTERED]

*[— in another hand: I watched it burn. It took a long time for so small a loaf.]*

---

passages.heading: Book Five: Of Tin
passages.text:
**The Years.** The record of the next years is short.
- Year one: the platter stands empty and Unregistered in the Hall. The house of Vane pays its tariff on the other platters and not on that one.
- Year three: the same.
- Year six: the house of Vane falls behind. Two Vane cousins are moved to the dish pit.
- Year nine: ████████.

**Copper from Inland.** In the eleventh year copper came ashore at Smuggler's Wharf. It did not come through the Counting-House. It came in crates stamped **VANE TIN CO**, set on the salt at low tide by men who did not stay for supper. The copper was good, mainland coin melted down and recast in the Guild's weight. It paid the house of Vane's arrears, every year of them, to the token.

The empty platter was meant to be the end of him. A son the Council had unwritten was meant to stay unwritten. Instead he fed his house from across the water. The island learned what everyone inland already knew: there was tin in the ground back there, before the Barons came for it, and a man named Vane had found it. The Vane house was fed by copper from the stolen bread. Every loaf on its platters, the elder brother's among them, was risen on it.

passages.heading: Book Five: Of Tin
passages.text:
*[— in another hand: the elder brother fed the Mother every dawn with hands his brother paid for. He never once said so.]*

**The Sealing.** The house was fed by copper, and soon the Counting-House was too. The tariffs of the Vane house had become the largest single sum in the ledger. In a lean year the Council does not burn its largest sum. So the Vane seat in the gallery was let stand. The chair was empty, but it was not struck. And wherever the name of Aldous Vane appeared in the archive, in the Inquisitor's file, in the verdict, in the ferryman's tally, a clerk set the Council's seal over it.

[SEALED: SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL]
[SEALED: SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL]
[SEALED: SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL]

This was the first seal ever set over a person rather than a heresy. His name lay under a Council seal and his tin lay in its treasury, and the two were never entered on the same page.

passages.heading: Book Five: Of Tin
passages.text:
**Rumours Cross.** *The following is entered as an aside and is not part of the record of the house of Vane.*

In these years rumours began to reach the island from a place inland called HollowMere. One was of a town at the end of a railroad, where the Barons own the dirt under your boots. One was of a baker there who set a wake table with one loaf for each mourner and three for the dead, each sealed with a crumb in wax. That is the island's custom, said in another accent. One was of a sickness in a drowned marsh that made the wolves bold.

Rumours of the island seemed to reach HollowMere too. A clerk of the Counting-House noted that the crossings fell on days when the vat ran sour. He was not asked to note it again.

[STRUCK]

passages.heading: Book Six: Of the Return
passages.text:
**The Ferry Home.** In the year 1893, when the banks were failing inland and the railroads after them, the Morning Ferry brought back a man who was coughing.

His name was under a Council seal, and the seal had been the bargain: the copper came, the name stayed buried, and the man stayed away. He broke it by stepping onto the wharf. He was the younger son, and he looked older than his brother. He coughed with the wet, low cough of the inland fens, which the island had no name for. In his coat, wrapped in wool, he carried a cup.

He went up through the town in the fog and asked for the Ledger-Clerk by office. He asked one thing: that his platter be registered before he died.

*"It is empty,"* the Clerk said.
*"I know,"* he said. *"I paid for the others."*

The archive records that the cup came back lighter than it left. It records nothing further on the point.

passages.heading: Book Six: Of the Return
passages.text:
So the cup was back on the rock, and Aldous Vane, who had been out of reach for thirty years, was in the Council's reach.

**The Verdict Called Due.** The Inquisitor had him in reach, and so the file was reopened. It had never been closed, only sealed. The case went up to the High Chancellor. The High Chancellor ruled from the gallery, and the Council's stenographer took it down:

*A verdict passed in absence is not discharged by a loaf. The loaf was the accused's proxy, not his sentence. The accused being present, the verdict stands, and is due.*

The Hearth was set for him. The Iron-Wardens took him to the cold pantry to wait. It was the coolest room in the Sacred Kitchen, and the only one with a lock on the outside. The old verdict was called due for the third dawn.

*[— in another hand: he asked for flour. They did not give him any. He shaped nothing with his hands for two nights and I think that was worse to him than the fire.]*

passages.heading: Book Six: Of the Return
passages.text:
**The Night Before the Hearth.** The verdict was called due, and the Hearth was banked high, and the Hall was swept. On the night before, the Rat de Cave brought the prisoner's water, and the entry for that night reads in full:

*The prisoner was found at the second bell.*
*He was not breathing.*
████████████████████████████████████████

Aldous Vane died with his sentence unserved. The archive does not say whether it was the cough he brought from the fens, the fog that came under the pantry door, or a hand. On the rock people ask what the island has always asked, in the Tavern and in the Hall and under their breath at the platters: *who did it.* The Council has not answered.

In his coat they found the cup, washed and empty, and a folded tide chart of the mainland coast with the next low tide circled in pencil. The tide had come and gone two days before. He had never used it.

passages.heading: Book Six: Of the Return
passages.text:
The news reached the mainland before any ferry could have carried it, by wire or by rumour. The archive cannot say which. Inland, in HollowMere, he was Lord Aldous Vane. There his widow keeps the parlour, his manor stands with its clock stopped, and his will was read. There he is three nights dead, and has been for as long as anyone on the rock can reckon.

*[— in another hand: three nights. It is always three nights, there. I have stopped asking how.]*

**The Ordinance of Dusk.** A sentence unserved is a wound in the law, and the Council does not leave wounds open. It cannot burn a dead man, and it cannot leave a verdict standing over nothing. So the Council ordained a third thing.

From that night on, every night on Port-au-Levain begins with his death. At dusk, when the Morning Ferry is long gone and the fog has taken the harbour lamps, the Aboyeur carries a Wake Loaf down the Hall. He calls no name. He sets it on the empty Vane platter nearest the Hearth, and the night is reckoned from that loaf. The night watches are counted from it. The Iron-Wardens begin their rounds from it. Whatever happens on the rock after dark, and things do, happens in the hours after Aldous Vane is dead.

passages.heading: Book Six: Of the Return
passages.text:
The loaf is taken away at dawn and never eaten.

[SEALED: SOVEREIGN SOURDOUGH COUNCIL]

---

passages.heading: I. The Record Reconsidered
passages.text:
From this point the archive is kept in one hand only, and it is not the Counting-House's.

*[— in another hand: I have corrected this book for thirty years. I have restored the goatkeeper's name and the Black-Crust woman's boy. I have sung the second verse a breath slower. I have unsealed every name in it but one.]*

The entries in the official hand thin. They become dates without events, then events without dates. By the end of this chapter the corrections outnumber the entries.

passages.heading: II. Blank Pages
passages.text:
[PROPERTY OF THE COUNTING-HOUSE]

[PROPERTY OF THE COUNTING-HOUSE]

[PROPERTY OF THE COUNTING-HOUSE]

*[— in another hand: these three pages were never written. They were stamped so that it would look as if they had been taken. Count the stitches in the binding: nothing was cut. The Council forges its absences, too.]*

passages.heading: III. The Cup
passages.text:
The cup was taken from the dead man's coat and carried down the ninety-one steps by the elder brother, who held the Levain office. What it held was poured back into the vat. The Mother rose in her glass, a little, and has fed the island since.

The cup came back lighter than it left.

*[— in another hand: I will not write why, because I do not know. I will write what I do know. The rumours from inland have not stopped. They have not slowed. On the nights the vat runs sour, something in HollowMere goes wrong, or something here does. I cannot tell you whether that is the Mother. I cannot tell you that it is not.]*

passages.heading: IV. The Second Hand
passages.text: *[— in another hand: The archive says the keyholder on the night in question was ████████████. I will lift the bar now.]*

passages.heading: [Honorine Vane. Ledger-Clerk. Keeper of the second key.]
passages.text:
*[I was his sister. I opened the sub-basement door, and the Vault after it, and I held the lamp while he filled the cup. I locked the door behind him, and in the morning I wrote the record of the short count with my own hand, and I put a bar over my own name. Thirty years I have kept this archive. Thirty years I have corrected every lie in it but mine.]*

*[It was I he asked for, by office, when he came off the ferry. I told him the platter was empty. I did not tell him why I could not fill it: to register him I would have had to unseal the night he left, and the night he left has my name in it.]*

Here, in the margin, beside the bar she has lifted, the record's keeper stands confessed as the one who let the cup out.

passages.heading: V.
passages.text:
*[— in another hand: I have stood confessed before no one but this page, and that is not enough, and it is all the Council will allow. So I am giving it away.]*

*[Whoever holds this when the last lamp in the Hall goes out: the Vane platter is yours. It is empty and nearest the fire. Every dusk they set a loaf on it for a man who did not live to burn, and every night here begins with that loaf. You know now who opened the door. You know the cup came back lighter. You do not know where the rest of it went, and neither do I, but it went inland, and the rumours come back on the sour nights, and the fog is coming in now under the Counting-House door. I can hear the Aboyeur in the Hall. He is carrying the loaf. He is not calling a name. He is walking toward the platter, and when he sets it down the night will begin, and the first thing that happens in it is always a death, and tonight I think it will be]*

works.title: A Lamplighter's Round of HollowMere
works.blurb: the gazetteer of HollowMere walked as the Lamplighter's dusk round, in three rings: every scene, the four back rooms of Crumb's Ovens and every Bible building, each given its light, what stands there and what the town says, ending as she raises the pole to the last lantern.

passages.heading: Kept at dusk, Coldwater Territory, 1893.
passages.text:
> "You light the lanterns that keep the wolves off the square."
> — the Lamplighter's card

> "Only the Lamplighter's lanterns may be lit."
> — Articles of the Line, Schedule B: Curfew Hours

The Saloon bell went at dusk the way it always went, flat and quick, a bell that wanted to be done. The train stood at the platform with steam up and its doors still open. She took the can from its hook, the wick-pole from behind the door and the short ladder from the wall, and went out by the back way, because the round began where the oil was.

Curfew in HollowMere does not fall at an hour. It falls when the train leaves. After that, by the Company's own paper, the only lawful light in the town is hers.

She had kept the round long enough to know it was a list, and every list in HollowMere is a list of what the Company owns. She kept this one anyway, lantern by lantern, in her head and under her breath. A number, said low. A hand on the post to light it. A hand on the post again to leave it. Two touches, every post, every night. She could not have said where she learned that. She had never once skipped it.

passages.heading: Kept at dusk, Coldwater Territory, 1893.
passages.text:
The Company paid her in scrip, by the lantern lit. A lantern left dark was docked. That was the whole of her contract, and she understood it better than most people in the town understood theirs.

---

passages.heading: The Drowned Lantern, back room — tavern_back
passages.text: She filled the can to the seam and no further. A full can slopped on the ladder, and slopped oil was docked like any other. Through the wall the saloon was getting louder. She did not hum. She had never hummed at this barrel, and she had never asked herself why not.

passages.heading: The Drowned Lantern — tavern_bar
passages.text: She read the circle on the chart the way she read it every dusk, with her thumb under it. Low water early tonight. The Fenwood path held at low water and did not hold otherwise, and that one circle of ink decided how far her round went. A man at the bar said the wolves were bad this week. She said they were at the fence already, which was true, and went out the front to see the train go.

passages.heading: The platform — overworld.platform
passages.text: The train went at dusk and did not wait; it had never waited for anyone. She stood with the pole up and watched the back car pass, the car the coffins ride out in, the conductor's lamp swinging at its rail. Then there was only the sound of it going into the pines toward the Gallows Wood siding, and then not that. *One.* Touch. Light. Touch. Behind the train the town closed, without anyone closing it.

passages.heading: The platform — overworld.platform
passages.text:
**The railyard and its workbench — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** None. A Company padlock on the gate, and a second Company padlock on the first one's chain.

**What stands:** A workbench under a tin roof, a vise, a rack of files. Lead and gunpowder off the morning train, stacked by weight. Freight crates stencilled for return to Thorne Junction.

**What the town says:** That some crates come in heavier than they go out. That some go out with a person in them. That a person in a crate can read the Baron's manifest through the slats, if the platform lantern is lit.

She had heard that one. It was not why she lit the platform first. She lit it first because it was first. But she had heard it.

Four lanterns stand on the square, one at each corner of what the town calls a square and what is really the place where four roads give up. She lit them in her own order, counting on from the platform. *Two.* *Three.* *Four.* The fourth lantern of the square, the one over the chalk by the well, she left. She always left it. She always came back to it last.

passages.heading: Hollowmere, the square — overworld
passages.text:
The wolves were at the fence. She did not look at them, and they did not come closer than the light, which was the arrangement. Across the square, under the bell, the Tribunal's bench stood out in the open with a tarpaulin over it against the fog.

**The Tribunal and the gallows at the Bell — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** None. Nothing here is lit at night.

**What stands:** The Tribunal's bench under the bell. Three verdicts painted on a board for those who cannot read: Acquittal. A Heavy Fine. Death. Behind the bench, the gallows, its trapdoor bolted, its rope taken in at dusk. Crows along the beam.

**What the town says:** That the last man through the trap went unnamed in the Gazette, because his name could not be verified. That some evenings a stranger off the train comes and stands under the beam as if waiting to be chosen. That the crows know a day before anyone.

passages.heading: Hollowmere, the square — overworld
passages.text:
She had known the last man only by his whistle. He had whistled at her ladder most evenings that autumn, two notes, up and down, the way you whistle at a dog you are fond of. He had the hands of a man who mended boots, or who once had. He had never said his name and she had never asked it, and now nobody would print it. She went past the beam without looking up. The crows walked along it to keep her in sight.

**The Well Ladder — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** The square's fourth lantern stands over it, unlit.

**What stands:** The well: a stone lip, a windlass, a bucket. Below where the bucket stops, iron rungs set into the shaft, going down to the Undercroft under St Brannock's.

**What the town says:** That whoever does it washes at the well afterwards. That the rungs were the Company's idea, or Father Bray's, or older than both.

passages.heading: Hollowmere, the square — overworld
passages.text:
She did not look down the well. That was another habit. Across the lane the Post Office window was lit.

**The Post Office & Telegraph Room — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** A window, past curfew. Not hers. Against Schedule B.

**What stands:** Mailbags, emptied and hung on pegs. The sorting frame. The telegraph key on a table of its own, behind a rail. A kettle on the stove. The Gazette is opened here every morning, and read here first.

**What the town says:** That envelopes are steamed over that kettle before they are sorted. That some mornings there is black wax in a bag, and that the man it is meant for has a choice between burning it and keeping his life the size it was. That word of Vane's death came over that key before any ferry could have carried it; or that it came by rumour, which keeps its own timetable.

passages.heading: Hollowmere, the square — overworld
passages.text:
She did not report the window. She did not report lights. Nobody had ever asked her to in so many words, and she had decided long ago not to hear it asked in fewer.

**The Constable's Office & Morgue — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** None.

**What stands:** A desk. Iron cuffs and a riot whistle on nails. Through the back, a slab, empty and scrubbed, and a trestle beside it waiting for whatever rides out next in the back car.

**What the town says:** That an empty slab in HollowMere is a forecast and not a mercy. That the one who opens the dead here can tell the hour a man died, and that it is the hour, more than the knife, that hangs people.

The lane narrowed toward the apothecary. Doc Mallory's shutters were across. Above them, the loft window was green.

passages.heading: The apothecary loft — apoth_loft
passages.text: She noted the green the way she noted all of them, and walked on to the Widow's house, where the crepe on the knocker had gone grey with three nights of fog.

passages.heading: Widow Vane's bedroom — widow_bedroom
passages.text: She stood under the window a moment. She had passed it every round since the will was read, and the town said that was three nights, and she had passed it more often than three times. The candle did not move. She did not report it.

passages.heading: Crumb's Ovens — bakery
passages.text: Down the bakery yard the four back rooms each had a window on her side, and the round had never found a reason to skip a window.

passages.heading: Crumb's Ovens — bakery
passages.text:
**The cold room — no id frozen (round 7 room)**

**Light:** None.

**What stands:** A door to the bakery. The station: butter and lard on blocks of ice cut from the mere, under sacking. A hiding spot behind the sacking, deep enough for a child or a thin man. A clue spot at the sill, where flour lies thin enough to take a handprint.

**What the town says:** That the mere's ice keeps too long. That things put down on it come up looking exactly as they went down.

**The mixing room — no id frozen (round 7 room)**

**Light:** None.

**What stands:** A door to the bakery. The station: the dough trough, scraped clean. A hiding spot under the trough board. A clue spot at the flour sacks, where the dust takes a print of whatever leans on them.

**What the town says:** That Rumour Loaves are mixed here, with a slip inside, and that a slip baked into bread is harder to call a lie than one pinned to a board. That whatever is written on it hardens in a day.

passages.heading: Crumb's Ovens — bakery
passages.text:
**The oven room — no id frozen (round 7 room)**

**Light:** The oven mouth, banked.

**What stands:** A door to the bakery. The station: the clay oven Vane's men built behind the tents before there was a town, which the bakery was raised around afterwards. A hiding spot in the wood bay. A clue spot at the ash pit, raked each dawn.

**What the town says:** That a gold coin was once left on the peel as a tip, and nothing taken but bread. That the oven is older than the town and will be warm after it.

**The proofing room — no id frozen (round 7 room)**

**Light:** None.

**What stands:** A door to the bakery. The station: slatted shelves under linen, and on the top shelf Tamsin's crock, fed one spoon at a time on the island's hour. A hiding spot behind the linen racks. A clue spot at the crock's lid, where a seal of wax would show who had lifted it.

passages.heading: Crumb's Ovens — bakery
passages.text: Past the bakery the lane gave out into planks, and the planks gave out into pines. She lit the post at the wood's edge. *Five.* Touch. Light. Touch.

passages.heading: Gallows Wood — forest
passages.text: From the end of the planks she could see the marsh. Fennick's light stood at the marsh edge, low and steady. Further out were other lights, which were not steady. Harbourmaster Pell's skiff was pulled up at the dock with a stone in it, and Tuck's ferry pole lay along the boards. Some nights she had stood here and not known which light was Fennick's. Tonight she knew, because one of the others was coming nearer.

passages.heading: The Tin Gallery mouth — cave_entry
passages.text:
She did not light the dark places. That was not a habit; that was the contract. But she stood at the mouth for the space of a breath, because Jory Kitto had paid for his own oil, and someone should.

On the way back up the lane she met the Watchman at the Constable's corner.

passages.heading: The Tin Gallery mouth — cave_entry
passages.text: "Quiet," he said.

passages.heading: So far.
passages.text:
He had chosen his door for the night. She could see it in how he stood, already leaning toward it. She did not ask which. He did not say. It was not a thing people said in HollowMere after the train had gone.

---

## Ring Two: Mill & Bank, and Manor Rise

*On nights when there are fewer of us, these doors are boarded. Tonight they are open.*

The Rise went up from the square past the bank, and the channel ran down from it past the mill. The town did not know why the boards went up some nights and not others. It knew only that when there were fewer people at the wake table, there were more boards, and it had stopped asking which came first.

**The Company Bank & Vault — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** None. A Company padlock. A guard's stool at the door, empty, with a cushion on it.

passages.heading: So far.
passages.text:
**The Baron's study — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** None. Kept dark for a man who comes only by train.

**What stands:** Above the bank, up a stair with its own lock. A desk nobody sits at. A chair turned to the window that faces the line.

**What the town says:** That Cornelius Thorne comes when the town riots, with Pinkertons and their dogs. That the room is aired the day before he comes, so that somebody always knows first; and that whoever airs it is not saying.

passages.heading: So far.
passages.text:
**The Waterwheel Lumber Mill & loft — no id (not a scene)**

**Light:** None.

**What stands:** The waterwheel on the drained-lake channel. The saw floor. The plank stack. Above, the loft, with straw pallets in rows.

**What the town says:** That debt walks to the mill. That the Indebted sleep in the loft and are counted in the morning. That the wheel turns a little when the mere's tide runs, with no hand on it. That a fire has been promised here, by someone, for a long time.

She heard the wheel go over once as she passed, a slow wet turn, and stop. The circle on the chart had said low water. She went faster up the Rise.

passages.heading: Hale Barn — barn
passages.text: Behind the barn the Rise fell away to the marsh, and the marsh path went into the Fenwood on the mud the low water had left. She took it as far as the circle allowed and not a step further. She had no post to light there. She went because the round was the round, and because a list kept is a list complete.

passages.heading: The Fenwood — forest_deep
passages.text: She stood at the end of the dry mud and looked at it the way she looked at the others, as a light she had not lit. She thought, as she thought here every night, that a lantern that wanted no oil and no hand would never be docked. She did not envy it. Then the water began to come back over her boot soles, and she turned.

passages.heading: Tonight these doors are boarded.
passages.text: She came home by St Brannock's, because St Brannock's was on the way home. Company men had nailed the boards up in the afternoon; the nail heads were still bright. There was nothing for her to light here. She came anyway, for the list.

passages.heading: St Brannock's — chapel
passages.text: She lifted the pole until its flame was level with the stone. Then she looked at the bell instead, and lowered it. There are two kinds of knowing in HollowMere, and only one of them can be put off by not looking. She did not know which kind this was. She did not find out.

passages.heading: The Undercroft — cellar
passages.text: She crossed back to the square. At the well she heard feet on the rungs below: one, and then another, slow, the way someone climbs who does not want to be heard climbing. Mere-rot makes false footsteps. Everyone knows that. She did not go to the lip, and she did not call down. The steps stopped. They did not start again.

passages.heading: The Fourth Lantern
passages.text: The wolves were at the fence. Three lanterns burned on the square, and the platform behind her, and the post at the wood's edge, and the gatepost on the Rise. Six. She shook the can and heard the last of the oil move in it. If this post stayed dark, the scrip for it would be docked. The will was in her head, as it was in everyone's. The chalk was under her boots. She put her hand on the post: the first touch.

passages.heading: Light:
passages.text: She raised the pole.

works.title: The HollowMere Gazette, Morning Edition
works.blurb: the front-page proof of Thursday 7 December 1893, on which the compositor's pencil traces the gravestone's name, Ada Brook, through the lost-and-found, the rent arrears, the wake order and the Bandit's wanted notice, and strikes and restores her.

passages.heading: The HollowMere Gazette, Morning Edition
passages.text:
*Proof, front page, forme one. The pencil is the compositor's.*

---

passages.heading: THE HOLLOWMERE GAZETTE
passages.text:
**MORNING EDITION.** Thursday, 7 December 1893.

Printed at the Eastern Office for the Thorne & Expanse Line. Carried by the Daily Train. Delivered sealed. The property of the Company until read.

**THE GAZETTE PRINTS THE SECRETS OF THE PREVIOUS DAY, AS ARE FOUND OUT. IT PRINTS NO NAME THAT HAS NOT BEEN VERIFIED. WHERE A NAME IS NOT VERIFIED, A BLANK IS LEFT, AND THE TOWN MAY SUPPLY IT.**

---

passages.heading: I. THE STONE
passages.text: The stone with tomorrow's date reads, as wired:

passages.heading: ~~ADA BROOK~~
passages.text:
The Gazette reports the stone. It does not account for it.

> *9.40. Stet, wire copy. Two words and a disclaimer. Easiest inch on the page.*

---

passages.heading: II. LOST & FOUND
passages.text:
FOUND, on the platform, at the Station Rush: a child's tin whistle, dented. Apply at the Post Office.

FOUND, by the workbench in the railyard: a ticket-punch die, star pattern. It is not the Conductor's. Apply at the Post Office.

~~LOST, between the pump and the platform, Monday, at the Station Rush: a scarf, grey wool, darned in red at one end where the moth had it. It was her mother's. The finder may have a loaf a week from her until Christmas. Ada Brook, Mill Row, third door. She will pay in bread.~~

> *10.05. Brook. Same name as col. I.*
> *A common name. There are two of everything in a mill town.*

---

passages.heading: III. COMPANY RENT RATES
passages.text:
Schedule A, as posted. The Clerk collects at the Midday Shift.

| Row | Per bed, per week |
|---|---|
| Mill Row | 1.10 scrip |
| Pump Row | 1.25 scrip |
| Railyard bunks | 0.90 scrip |

passages.heading: Entered as Indebted, as of Wednesday's Midday:
passages.text:
- BROOK, A. Mill Row, third door. Two weeks. To the Mill at Midday.
- COTTER, I. Settled. Departed by the Line.
- HADDON, B. Pump Row. One week. Warned.
- PIKE, S. (deceased). The account passes to the household.

> *10.20. Mill Row, third door. Col. II says third door.*
> *One woman.*
> *Wired the night desk at H.M.: IS ADA BROOK LIVING. Thirty cents, out of my own pocket. My own rent is Friday.*

---

passages.heading: IV. NOTICES
passages.text:
**The Company.** Curfew runs from the departure of the Daily Train at Dusk until the Station Rush. The Midday Rent is collected at the Shift, in person, and in scrip. Coin is scrip until proven otherwise.

**The Apothecary.** Doc Mallory gives notice that the fen-cough is in the Rows again. It is not catching. Keep the windows shut against the mere. The Company asks that the word be *miasma*.

**St Brannock's.** The Vicar preaches at dusk. Enquiries regarding Father Bray: none answered.

**The Lamplighter.** The light in the Fenwood was seen again on Tuesday. The Company has not lit it. Do not follow it.

**The Vane Holdings.** The Company gives notice that no claim under the will of the late Lord Aldous Vane will be heard from any person who believes himself to be among those who remain, until the question of the last lantern is settled. The lanterns within the Grant are the Company's.

passages.heading: IV. NOTICES
passages.text:
**STOP-PRESS.** *Received by wire, H.M. night desk:* ADA BROOK LIVING STOP AT MILL STOP STONE IS RUMOUR STOP GAZETTE PRINTS NOTHING UNVERIFIED

> *12.15. Living. Then the stone isn't verified, and the Rule is the Rule.*
> *Struck her from col. I. Set a blank in her place. — 7.*
> *There. Now she's only a woman who lost a scarf.*

---

passages.heading: V. THE DAILY TRAIN
passages.text:
Conductor of record: A. Pruett, No. 14.

| Station | Down | Up |
|---|---|---|
| Thorne Junction | Day | Dusk |
| Widow's Cut | Day | Dusk |
| Gallows Wood Siding | on signal | on signal |
| HollowMere | Day | Dusk |

**Inbound, Car 2.** Flour, Crumb's Ovens. Whiskey, the Drowned Lantern. Tonics, the Morgue. Lead and powder, the railyard. Mail, one bag. Gazette, one bundle, sealed.

**Outbound at Dusk, Car 3.** Coffin, one. Consigned from Mill Row. Name not entered.

> *12.40. Not entered.*
> *A blank. Not mine, though. Theirs.*
> *They book ahead in winter. A Company booking. Set as wired.*

---

passages.heading: VI. CLASSIFIED
passages.text:
**CRUMB'S OVENS.** Wake loaves for Mill Row, after the island custom: one for each mourner and three for the dead, each with its crumb token under wax. Ten ordered. Paid in full, in scrip, on Tuesday by A. Brook, who asks that the Row not be charged.

**WANTED,** at Hale Barn: a girl to mind a goat. Must not be afraid of the pelt on the door.

> *1.05. Paid Tuesday. That was before the stone.*
> *She has the cough, then. See col. IV. A woman with the cough looks at Christmas and pays ahead. People do.*
> *Box it in mourning rule, house style for a death already notified.*

---

passages.heading: THE BANDIT
passages.text:
For the score at Crumb's Ovens, Monday night. The till was emptied. One gold coin was left on the counter, as a tip.

The Company's three particulars:

- **Height:** short, by the bootprint in the spilt flour.
- **Scarf:** grey wool. Thread found caught on the till.
- **Hat:** none recovered.

**Name:** ____________. Unverified. The Town may supply it.

> *1.30. Grey wool. → col. II.*
> *Not the cough. Not settled at all. The Bell, then the trap.*

> *1.32. Pull col. II. Refund her the scrip.*
> *Kill the inch with a rule. If her scarf isn't on the page they can't lay it beside this.*

---

passages.heading: VIII. YESTERDAY'S SECRETS
passages.text:
As found out, Wednesday:

- ______ of Pump Row struck ______ at the Drowned Lantern over a hand of cards, and paid for neither the glass nor the eye.
- ______ owes the Company Store eleven scrip and has stopped buying salt.
- ______ has been seen at the fence after curfew, feeding something through it.
- A woman of Mill Row, name withheld, asked at the Post Office after a grey scarf darned in red. She was told nothing had been handed in. She asked twice. ______.

> *1.50. Verified copy. Can't pull it. It's what we're for.*
> *The town was there. They heard her ask.*

---

passages.heading: IX. FROM THE LINE
passages.text:
*Received on the up-train's wire, and printed without comment.*

BlackPine: a name chalked out on the tally board, shift unknown.

Port-au-Levain: the ferry did not cross.

---

passages.heading: X. TOWN MOODS
passages.text:
Square: Calm. The Drowned Lantern: Calm. Pump Row: Panicked. Mill Row: Entranced.

---

> *3.55. Col. I. Stet. Dots under.*
> *A blank is a blank they fill. Better mine than theirs.*
> *Col. I standing. Tomorrow's wire at nine.*
> *— 7. Forme to the train.*

Next edition: tomorrow, by the Daily Train.

**THE GAZETTE PRINTS THE SECRETS OF THE PREVIOUS DAY, AS ARE FOUND OUT. IT PRINTS NO NAME THAT HAS NOT BEEN VERIFIED. WHERE A NAME IS NOT VERIFIED, A BLANK IS LEFT, AND THE TOWN MAY SUPPLY IT.**

works.title: Mrs Grieves's Tab Book
works.blurb: the Drowned Lantern's fourth tab book, 16 October to 20 November 1893: house rules, the three pours, dated pages headed by the scrip rate, the low water and the gravestone's name, the back pages on the photographs, the oil barrel and the drowned barman's line she will not close.

passages.heading: Flyleaf
passages.text:
**THORNE & EXPANSE LINE**
**~~RUSTY~~ LANTERN SALOON**, *with* DROWNED *written over the strike in ink*
**ACCOUNTS RECEIVABLE**
*All accounts in Company Scrip, at the morning rate.*

Under the print, in her hand:

> Not all accounts.
> Fourth book. Opened Monday, 16 October 1893. Kept by me.

---

passages.heading: House Rules
passages.text:
1. I open a tab. Nobody opens one by asking.
2. No tab for anyone the Clerk has entered Indebted. That holds after noon. Before noon I have not heard.
3. A tab closes three ways: paid, the back car, or me.
4. A closed tab stays closed. It does not pass to the wife, the lodger or the Company. The Company says an account survives a man. A tab is not an account.
5. Nobody drinks on the barman's line.
6. Nobody leaves after the whistle who has far to go. There are rooms upstairs. The Company sets the price of them.
7. What is said over Loose Lips stays in this book. The Gazette can find its own.

---

passages.heading: The Pours
passages.text:
**Rotgut: ¼ a pour.**
The cheapest thing on the train and the commonest thing in the glass. Four cases a day, when the train is honest. Men drink it after the Shift and do not talk.
*What a day costs.*

**Liquid Courage: ¾ a pour.**
Drunk before something: before the Clerk, before the Bell, before the ticket window. Nobody drinks a second one. A second one is Rotgut, whatever the bottle says.
*What a door costs.*

**Loose Lips Lager: ½ a pour.**
It comes up in the same car as the whiskey and tastes of the trip. What is said over it is said to me, then to the room, and by morning it has a man's name on it and a price somebody would pay. I don't buy it. I don't sell it. I write down that it was said.
*What a name costs.*

The price of a pour does not move. The rate on the board does.

passages.heading: The Pours
passages.text:
## Brought Forward
*from the third book*

| Line | Owing | |
|---|---|---|
| *[a small lantern, drawn in ink]* | ¾ | Carried. See the back. |
| BRAY, Fr. | 2¼ | Open. |
| ARTHUR | — | Closed. Back car. Last winter. |

> Father Bray. Died or ran. They say both in here, and they say it louder after the second pour. I will not close a tab on a guess.

> Arthur. His brother puts a Rotgut on the closed line every week, in Arthur's name, and drinks it himself. I take the scrip. Some weeks he writes a letter to his Ma at the end of my bar. I don't look to see whose name he signs.

---

passages.heading: Monday, 16 October 1893
passages.text:
| Name | Pours | Owing | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *[the lantern]* | — | ¾ | Carried. |
| LEN | Rotgut ×2 | ½ | Pays Fridays. |
| RUDD, JACK | Rotgut ×3 | — | Settled in kind. |
| CLEM | Loose Lips ×2 | 1 | |
| ERNIE | Pump water | — | No charge. |
| PIKE, STAN | Liquid Courage | ¾ | For the cough. |
| COTTER, IVY | Liquid Courage | — | Against the house. |
| MAUD | Rotgut | — | Paid in darning. |
| ARTHUR | Rotgut | — | Paid. |

> Jack Rudd brought me a bottle off the whiskey and called it a tariff. The train will have a case down as short today. I know which case. Settled.

passages.heading: Monday, 16 October 1893
passages.text:
> Stan calls it a cold. It has been a cold since the thaw. Liquid Courage is not for a cough, and he knows it. He says it works on the part of him that minds.

> Ivy Cotter sat over her glass and did not touch it till near the whistle. Her fare was in a twist of paper, and she counted it out on my bar twice and would not spend a coin of it. She sews for the mill. Evenings she sits in the dark to save the wick. I put her pour against the house. Don't tell them.

> Maud darned Bar's cuff and the pocket of my apron. She will not take a pour as a gift. She takes it as a wage. Paid.

> Ernie asked Clem where the train goes after us. Clem reads everything and did not know.

> Wilf played for his pour tonight like any night, key of G. If he'd been up the hill to look, he did not say. Nobody says.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 18 October 1893
passages.text:
| Name | Pours | Owing | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *[the lantern]* | — | ¾ | Carried. |
| COTTER, IVY | — | — | Gone east. Owes nothing. |
| THE VICAR | Liquid Courage ×3, for others | — | Paid. |
| LEN | Rotgut ×3 | ~~¾~~ ½ | Dora's sum. |
| FINCH, DORA | Loose Lips | — | Paid. |
| FRANK | Rotgut ×2 | ½ | Barred. |

> The new Vicar came off yesterday's train and was in here by tonight. He drinks nothing. He bought three Liquid Courage for three men who each wanted one and could not run to it, and he sat a while with each. Everyone confesses to him sooner or later. At my bar, sooner.

> Dora Finch read my sums upside down across the bar, the way she does, through her spectacles mended with thread. She found a quarter too much on Len's line and made me strike it. Len owes less because of her.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 18 October 1893
passages.text:
> Frank said a thing about the girl Nell's fever. I will not write it in my own book. Bar had him out the door before I had my hand off the tap. A stool went, and so did one of Frank's teeth. Frank's line stays open. He owes me ½ and a stool.

---

passages.heading: Saturday, 21 October 1893
passages.text:
| Name | Pours | Owing | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *[the lantern]* | — | ¾ | Carried. |
| WILF | — | — | Closed. Back car. |
| FINCH, DORA | — | — | Closed. Back car. |
| FRANK | — | ½ | Open. Not in since. |
| CLEM | Loose Lips ×3 | 1½ | |

> Wilf. Played for his pours, key of G, and never once asked the house to sing along. The mouth-organ went in with him.

> Dora Finch. The last sum she did in this house was in Len's favour. Len stood at the window when the back car went and did not drink after.

> Percy had no line. Children don't have one. He came in on Tuesdays for Ernie, with three marbles, and he would not play for keeps.

passages.heading: Saturday, 21 October 1893
passages.text:
> Mr Thorne came in on Friday's train, with the town rioting and the dogs first off. He did not come in here. The dogs came as far as the shutters.

> Clem read us yesterday's Gazette. It has the fight at the Lantern, and it has it wrong. It does not say what Frank said. Neither do I.

---

passages.heading: Monday, 13 November 1893
passages.text:
| Name | Pours | Owing | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *[the lantern]* | — | ¾ | Carried. |
| PIKE, STAN | Rotgut ×4, Liquid Courage | — | Paid all. |
| LEN | Rotgut ×2 | ½ | |
| ERNIE | Pump water | — | Paid, by Stan. |
| RUDD, JACK | Rotgut | — | In kind. |
| MAUD | Rotgut | — | In darning. |
| ARTHUR | Rotgut | — | Paid. |
| FRANK | — | ½ | Open. |

> Stan paid all, which he never does. He paid the ¾ from the sixteenth of October as well. He stood Len a round. He paid a quarter for Ernie's water, which is no charge, and I let him.

> He coughed less tonight than at any time since the thaw, and he laughed at that. He said the cold was going. He said he'd been up the hill this morning, and then he said he hadn't. Then Len sang.

passages.heading: Monday, 13 November 1893
passages.text:
> They say a box went down the line in the back car, a Monday in October, with a thimble on a string in it. I wrote Gone east against Ivy Cotter. I leave it written.

---

passages.heading: Wednesday, 15 November 1893
passages.text:
| Name | Pours | Owing | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *[the lantern]* | — | ¾ | Carried. |
| PIKE, STAN | — | — | Closed. Back car, Tuesday, Dusk. |
| BAR | Rotgut ×9, Tuesday, "for the strike" | 2¼ | His own line. |
| BAR | Shells, two, off the train | ½ | His own line. |
| FRANK | — | ½ | Open. |

> Stan. Len sang him spike-time at the back car. Ernie held his cap. The cough had stopped Monday night. I don't know what time.

> Tuesday was not kept. Shutters up by four, square full, Bell going. Bar stood the platform crew nine Rotgut "for the strike". I asked him whose strike. He said the one we're having. He told me to put it on his own line, and I did.

passages.heading: Wednesday, 15 November 1893
passages.text:
> Tuesday night the back room was let to "the Burial Club". Twelve came. Nobody was buried.

> Wednesday, Mr Thorne again, dogs first again. Bar cleaned the sawed-off on the counter while the dogs went past the shutters. He did not look at them. They looked at him.

---

passages.heading: Saturday, 18 November 1893
passages.text:
| Name | Pours | Owing | |
|---|---|---|---|
| *[the lantern]* | — | ¾ | Carried. |
| MAUD | Rotgut | — | Paid in darning. |
| THE VICAR | — | — | Sat with Maud. |
| A DRUMMER, off the train | Loose Lips ×2 | — | Paid in coin. Scrip till proven. |
| LEN | Rotgut | ¼ | |
| FRANK | — | ½ | Open. |

> Maud came in at dusk the same as any night. She darned Bar's other cuff to match the first and asked for her Rotgut as a wage. She said we were square. We are.

> The Vicar sat with her a while. I did not hear what she told him. She did not drink to it.

> A drummer off the train, selling buttons and thread, told me the island tavern pours our three under other names. He said up at BlackPine they keep a man's worth on a log the way I keep it on a line. He said every town at the end of a line drowns its barman sooner or later. I do not believe him. I have written it down.

passages.heading: Behind the Bar
passages.text:
Six frames. My pencil goes under each one, where the glass stops.

1. A man in an island jersey with a round loaf under his arm. *Sailor. Port-au-Levain. He came over with Mr Vane's people, and drowned at sea back there before any of them came. Mrs Crumb hung him.*
2. Four men in a flat boat on the lake. *Not sailors. Lake men, from before the drain. They called themselves sailors and I let them. Two went into the mere after it was a mere.*
3. An empty frame. *Jory Kitto. Tinner. Nobody ever took his likeness. He drowned under a lake that was there and then was not.*
4. A young man in a stiff collar. *Not a sailor. Nobody. The face came in the frame from back east. People leave sprigs under it all the same.*
5. The barman, with the sign lantern on its hook beside him. *Never saw a sea. Drowned all the same.*
6. A face I don't know, water-stained at the corner. *I did not hang this one. Nobody owns to it. It was on the wall one morning, square, with no nail I had put there. It looks like nobody I know yet.*

passages.heading: Behind the Bar
passages.text: *I'm not sure of the one. I count the sixth as drowned because it is on that wall.*

passages.heading: The Back Room
passages.text:
The oil barrel. A filling is ½, at the posted rate.

| Who | Fillings | |
|---|---|---|
| The Lamplighter | One each dusk | For the square. Hers, then the wolves'. |
| Old Fennick | One on Saturdays | For his light at the marsh edge. That light. Not the other. |
| Sundry | By the book | |

> Dip, Monday 13th: 31 gallons. Sold by the book since then: six fillings, which is a gallon and a half. Dip, Wednesday 15th: 28½. A gallon short. Nobody owns to it. I have written it as spill. I will go on writing it as spill.

passages.heading: [a small lantern, drawn in ink]
passages.text:
He opened the line himself, in his own hand, the first winter the house was a house. He paid it every week. There was only ever one thing on it he did not pay: on the night he went into the mere with the sign lantern in his arms, one Liquid Courage, on the slate. It was the only Liquid Courage he ever put on his own line.

It is not closed. A tab closes three ways. He did not pay it. The back car did not take him, because there was nothing to send. And I have not closed it. I carry it to the top of every page. Nobody drinks on it.

At dusk, when he trimmed the sign wick, he hummed the same hymn, and never all the way through.

> Carried forward: one pour, and half a hymn.

> Tuck says the lantern in the Fenwood is lit again. I do not ask who.

passages.heading: Bar's Line
passages.text:
Bar keeps the sawed-off under the counter and his own line in my book, like anybody. This book has him two ways. In October he had Frank out the door. On the Tuesday he stood the crew a round for the strike and let the back room to men who bury nobody. On the Wednesday he took two shells off the train and cleaned the gun while the dogs went by. He has not told me which way he is going. I have written both down.

---

passages.heading: Monday, 20 November 1893

passages.heading: Monday, 20 November 1893
passages.text:
> The Company filed its Articles on Friday, at a quarter to twelve or near it. Clem read me the part where an account survives a man: it goes to the household, then to the lodgers, then to them. Maud had no household and lodged with nobody. She was square with me, and I have written her closed. That is the end of what anybody gets of Maud from this book.

> Bar has the sawed-off under the counter. He has not said which way. Nor have I.

> Low water at two minutes past nine. It wants a quarter to it now.

> Somebody has come in off the square after the whistle, from far enough away. New line. Name to follow.

*The line against your name at closing is who you are.*

works.title: Fourteen Things Left Lying Around
works.blurb: a deputised Detective's case file of HollowMere's fourteen standing props, each stamped NO CASE for the Baron's train, whose every entry breaks the rule he used to shelve the last, until the fourteenth thing turns out to be his own bootprints.

passages.heading: Fourteen Things Left Lying Around
passages.text:
Fourteen things. The Constable wrote them out himself.

He wrote them on Company paper in a round, slow hand, the hand of a man taught late, and he numbered them down the margin. Then he blotted the list and turned it round on the desk so I could read it.

The crepe. The clock. The tide chart. The chalk. The photographs. The shelf. The pelt. The rope. The portrait. The crate. The scarecrow. The stone. The lantern. The boots.

"Things left lying around," he said. "People talk about them. Talk's the trouble."

Beside the list he set a magnifier, a case file with nothing in it, and a rubber stamp still smelling of its box. He inked it on his own pad and pressed it once on the blotter so I could see what it said.

NO CASE.

The riot was behind us. The Baron had come up the Line once already, with his Pinkertons, looked at the square, and gone back down. Now he was coming again on Saturday's train to see whether it had held. And the town was still talking. Lord Aldous Vane was three nights dead, the way he has been three nights dead for as long as anyone here can reckon, and the will read in the manor named *whoever remains when the last lantern goes out*. That had got out of the manor and into the Drowned Lantern, and from there into every chest in HollowMere along with the cough.

passages.heading: Fourteen Things Left Lying Around
passages.text:
"He steps off," the Constable said, "and I hand him a file, and every line in it says that. Nothing happened. Nobody did anything. Saturday."

I said yes. Article IX. He swore me in over the blotter. I had kept time at the railyard for two years. I had a clean hand and a good watch, and I believed (I wrote it down that first night, so I can't pretend otherwise) that a thing left lying around was left by a hand, and a hand, if you looked, had left a receipt.

Collect. Inspect. Cross-reference. That was all the job was.

---

passages.heading: No. 1. Black crepe. Manor door.
passages.text:
Collected: one strip, cut from the lower edge with my penknife. Two inches.
Inspected: Company crepe, the cheap weave, badly dyed. The black comes off on the fingers.
Cross-referenced: Company Store ledger, the morning the wire came. *Widow Vane, crepe, 4 yds, scrip.* Her mark beside it.
Stamped.

It took an hour, most of it waiting for the storekeeper to find the right ledger. I stood in the Store with black on my fingers and watched him run his thumb down the page, and when he found the line I nearly laughed.

A widow hangs crepe. The Company sells it. Here is where it was sold.

I pressed the stamp down and held it, the way the Constable had, and lifted it clean. Under the stamp, small, as a note to myself, I wrote: every hand has a receipt. I underlined it.

It was the first thing on the list that made sense. It was also the last.

passages.heading: No. 2. The clock. Vane Manor, the hall.
passages.text:
Collected: nothing. It stands eight feet and is bolted to the wall.
Inspected: hands at 11:47. Case unlocked. Pendulum hanging still. Weights wound up.
Cross-referenced: nothing found.
Stamped.

The Butler let me in. People say he knows every door in HollowMere. He walked me to this one as if it were the only one.

"You stopped it," I said. "For the death. That's the custom."

passages.heading: It was stopped when I came into service.
passages.text:
I opened the case. The weights were up. The pendulum hung plumb and did not swing when I nudged it. I put a finger to the minute hand to set it on, gently, the way you free a railyard clock stuck in frost. It did not move. I pushed. It wasn't stiff and it wasn't rusted. It simply would not go.

The Butler watched me take my hand back.

There was no receipt. Nobody had bought the stopping of it. The Store had no line and the Butler had no memory. When I asked at the pump, the town said it stopped the hour the lake drained, and said it the way you say the weather. Said it. Nobody saw it.

So I wrote a second rule under the first: what is older than the books is history, not evidence. A clock that stopped before anyone kept ledgers is not a clue. It is furniture.

passages.heading: It was stopped when I came into service.
passages.text:
NO CASE.

I wiped that finger on my coat for a long time afterwards.

---

passages.heading: No. 3. The tide chart. The Drowned Lantern.
passages.text:
Collected: nothing. Mrs Grieves would not have it off the wall.
Inspected: an old harbour chart, island print, the paper brown as toast. The next low tide circled.
Cross-referenced: my watch. The marsh dock. The channel post.
Stamped.

It was older than any book in town, so by my second rule it was history. I had the stamp out before I had my coat off.

Then I saw the ink. The circle round the next low tide was wet. It shone. When I touched its edge it came away blue on my thumb.

"Who marks it?" I said.

"Not me," said Mrs Grieves.

passages.heading: Somebody always has.
passages.text:
Her man Bar went on wiping the same glass and did not look up.

A fen with no sea for three hundred miles. I took down the circled hour and went to the marsh dock with my watch open in my hand, and stood by the post where Tuck ties the ferry. There is a tar line on that post. I set my thumbnail on it at the water's edge.

At the circled minute the water went down a hand's breadth. Not a ripple, not the wind. Down, the way a chest goes down.

People say it's the lake's old channels, running under the stone to water nobody has mapped. People say the chart is the island's, and the island keeps its tides wherever its paper goes. I wrote down both and did not pick one.

But somebody had circled it that morning. This was not history. It was today.

passages.heading: Somebody always has.
passages.text:
So I made a third rule: the town keeps its old things current out of habit, the way a widow winds a dead man's watch. Habit is not a crime.

NO CASE. My thumb stayed blue for two days.

---

**No. 4. Chalk hopscotch. The square, under the fourth lantern.**

Collected: a pinch of chalk dust, in a paper.
Inspected: ten squares, numbered, in a careful hand. Fresh.
Cross-referenced: the night. Myself.
Stamped.

A habit has a keeper. That was the trouble with my third rule, and I knew it when I wrote it. If the town keeps its old things current, somebody in the town gets up and does it, and somebody can be seen.

So I sat the whole night under the fourth lantern, the one over the chalk and the well. I sat on the well's edge with my coat buttoned and my watch on my knee where the light fell on it. The Lamplighter came to this lantern last, as she always does, and lit it and looked at me and said nothing. Curfew rang. The wolves came to the fence, went along it, and went away. Something in the fog walked behind the pump in short steps and was not there when I looked.

passages.heading: Somebody always has.
passages.text:
I wound my watch at midnight. I remember that. I remember the click.

At dawn the hopscotch was fresh: ten squares redrawn in clean white chalk, sharp-edged, not a smudge, not a footprint through them. The old lines were gone under the new.

No chalk on the stones round it. No one.

I did not remember sleeping. I did not remember not sleeping. When the train came in at Station Rush I held my watch up to the station clock, and my watch was an hour behind.

I have kept time for two years. I have never lost an hour.

I wrote it in the margin in the Company's word, because it was the only one I had: miasma. Mere-rot in the chest and the eye. A man sits all night in the fog, and the fog takes an hour off him and does his chalk for him. That is what miasma is for.

passages.heading: Somebody always has.
passages.text:
NO CASE.

---

passages.heading: No. 5. The drowned-sailor photographs. The Drowned Lantern.
passages.text:
Collected: nothing.
Inspected: frames behind the bar, black wood and glass. Men in oilskins. Men in water.
Cross-referenced: Mrs Grieves. My note of the day before.
Stamped.

Miasma lives in the eye. If my eye was the trouble, my eye could not be the witness. So from here on I would log nothing I had not counted with someone else.

I asked Mrs Grieves to count the frames with me, aloud.

She didn't want to. She dried her hands and stood beside me behind the bar, and we went along the wall frame by frame, out loud, like children doing sums.

One. Two. Three. The third held no picture at all. "That's Jory's," she said, and went on. She has a heavy way of saying numbers, as if each one costs her.

Five. Six. Seven.

I had been in the day before, for the chart. I had counted then out of habit and put it in the file. I took out the file and showed her the page. Six.

passages.heading: No. 5. The drowned-sailor photographs. The Drowned Lantern.
passages.text:
She looked at the page, and at the wall. She did not say I was wrong.

The seventh hung at the end of the row, by the shutters, on a nail I would swear had not been there. It showed a man in a thin coat, standing in water to the waist and turned away toward more water. You could not see his face. You could see his hands, and that he had no hat.

"Who's he?" I said.

"I don't know him," she said, and went back to her end of the bar.

A picture goes up in the night between one count and the next. Somebody had a nail and a hammer and a reason, and I happened to count either side of it. I wrote down the word *coincidence* and looked at it, and it looked back at me like a word in a language I had only just learned.

passages.heading: No. 5. The drowned-sailor photographs. The Drowned Lantern.
passages.text:
NO CASE.

---

**No. 6. The NOT FOR SALE shelf. Mallory Apothecary.**

Collected: nothing. There is nothing to collect. That is the item.
Inspected: six slots, five bottles of brown glass, wax-sealed. One slot empty, and no dust in it.
Cross-referenced: Doc Mallory's stock book.
Stamped.

Mallory let me see the book because the Constable had sent me, and for no other reason. Every bottle on that shelf has a line in it, and every line has a name and a date. Five of them are filled.

The sixth line is headed in ink gone brown, and nothing is written under it. It has never been filled.

passages.heading: Reserved: Det.
passages.text:
"What goes in it?" I said.

Mallory took the book back and closed it.

A coincidence does not get a line in a book. A coincidence is what happens between people who have never met. Somebody had sat at that counter with a pen and laid a place for me.

Not me, I told myself. The office. The Company reserves things for its offices. An office is a chair, and I happen to be sitting in it.

I stamped it NO CASE. Then, because I wanted the office to be only an office, I walked to the Constable's and asked him who had held it before me.

"Nobody," he said. He did not look up from his desk. "It's new. Made under Article IX. For this list."

I thanked him. I believed him for the length of the street.

---

passages.heading: No. 7. The wolf pelt. Hale Barn door.
passages.text:
Collected: one tuft of grey hair.
Inspected: a whole pelt, nailed through the forelegs. Old nails. The pelt not old.
Cross-referenced: the Gamekeeper.
Stamped.

The Gamekeeper was in the barn with the goat, oiling a rifle. Vane paid him to keep the wood. Vane is dead, and he keeps it anyway.

"When did you nail it up?" I said.

"The week the last one went into the Fenwood."

passages.heading: The last what?
passages.text:
He looked at my case file, and at my stamp. "Detective," he said. "After the lantern. Went in at dusk with a book like that under his arm and didn't come out the side he went in."

The office is new, the Constable said. Made for this list.

The office had had a man in it before me.

I didn't go back to the Constable's. It was the first thing I did not do. Instead I wrote that the last one had been careless: a man who walked into a fen at dusk after a light everybody knows not to walk after. Careless men go into the Fenwood. I am not a careless man.

NO CASE.

---

passages.heading: No. 8. The rope. St Brannock's.
passages.text:
Collected: nothing. The glove is twisted into the rope.
Inspected: the bell rope, hemp, gone black at hand height. Caught in its lay, the cuff and half the palm of a left glove, plain brown kid. The palm worn through by rope and darned over in red wool, badly.
Cross-referenced: the new Vicar. My coat.
Stamped.

The new Vicar came up the Line after the old priest had gone. He stood under the bell with me and looked at the glove the way you look at a dog that might bite.

"They say Father Bray rang it till his palms burned through his gloves," he said. "The day the first train came. They say a lot."

passages.heading: I don't know whose it is.
passages.text:
The red wool was coarse, and the stitches went every way, as if whoever darned it did it in poor light or in a hurry or did not know how. I had no way to read that, and I did not try.

I reached into my coat for my own gloves, to put them on before I touched the rope. They are plain brown kid too, worn thin at the palm from two years of railyard levers. The right one was there. The left was not.

I turned the pocket out. Lint. A pencil end. Blue on the lining from the tide chart.

Half the men in this town wear plain brown kid. Every man who works with his hands wears it through at the palm. Mine fell in the mud somewhere between the barn and here. I wrote that down, pressing hard to keep the hand steady.

A careful man would have noticed when he lost a glove.

passages.heading: I don't know whose it is.
passages.text:
NO CASE.

---

passages.heading: No. 9. The portrait. Widow Vane's parlour.
passages.text:
Collected: nothing.
Cross-referenced: the back of the frame. Wire, nail, an inch of dust along the top edge.
Stamped.

Widow Vane had me shown into the parlour and did not stand up. The portrait hangs over the letter box, turned to the wall. What the room sees is brown backing board and a maker's label too faded to read.

"You may turn it," she said, "if it's your work."

I stood in front of it with my hands at my sides.

Everything I had turned over that week had given me something back: a wet circle, an hour, a seventh face, a line in a book with my office on it, a glove gone from my own pocket.

I logged the back of the frame, the wire, the nail and the dust. I did not lift it off the nail.

She watched me not turn it. When I was done she rang for the Butler to see me out, and said nothing at all.

passages.heading: No. 9. The portrait. Widow Vane's parlour.
passages.text:
It was the first thing I stamped without looking at it.

---

**No. 10. The VANE TIN CO crate. The Flooded Gallery.**

Collected: everything in it.
Cross-referenced: everything in it.
Stamped.

Past its mouth the Tin Gallery is dark and wet. I borrowed a lantern from the Drowned Lantern. Mrs Grieves gave it to me without asking where I was going. There was water to the ankle at the pump beam, and the ore cart lay on its side.

The crate sits on two planks above the water, with VANE TIN CO stencilled on the lid. The lid is half-pried, the nails bent up on one side and not the other, as if whoever was prying it stopped.

I finished it. It was the last thing I pushed.

Straw. Under the straw, a case file. Under the file, a magnifier and a rubber stamp. I knew the stamp before I turned it over.

passages.heading: No. 9. The portrait. Widow Vane's parlour.
passages.text:
The list at the front of the file was on Company paper, in a round, slow hand, numbered down the margin. It held the same fourteen things, but not in my order. His went the crepe, the boots, the clock, the stone, and so on, with the drowned lantern last.

Thirteen of them were stamped NO CASE. The entries under them were neat and the cross-references sound. He had found the crepe in the Store ledger, the same as I had. He had counted the photographs with somebody. He had measured the boots. He had a good hand.

The fourteenth line, the drowned lantern, was blank.

He was not careless. He had walked into the Fenwood at dusk to finish, with this file under his arm or one like it. And the file was here, dry, under straw, in a crate somebody had half-pried and left.

I held the lantern over the water a long time before I came up.

passages.heading: No. 9. The portrait. Widow Vane's parlour.
passages.text:
NO CASE.

---

**No. 11. The scarecrow in the trench coat. The square.**

Collected: one ticket.
Cross-referenced: his entry for it.
Stamped.

His entry read: *Scarecrow. Square. Coat, trench, Company cloth. Pockets not examined.*

Pockets not examined was the only lazy line in his file. I went to the square at noon, while the Clerk was taking the rent and nobody looks at anything but their scrip, and examined the pockets.

There was stamp ink on the right cuff, old, the purple-black of the Constable's pad, worked into the weave where a wrist would rest on a desk.

In the left pocket was a ticket: one-way, HollowMere to back east, all the way down the Line. Paid. Never punched. Conductor Pruett, No. 14, punches every fare with his crescent, and there was no crescent in this one. It had gone nowhere.

The way out had been in the coat, and he had not taken it.

passages.heading: No. 9. The portrait. Widow Vane's parlour.
passages.text:
I took it. I put it in my own pocket, the one with the blue lining, and kept my hand on it.

Then I made the plan he hadn't. Three things were left after this one. I would finish the list and hand the Constable the file on Saturday. The Baron would step off and read it, the train would turn round at dusk, and I would be on it with this in my hand. The list is the only thing here that ends. I'd finish it and use the ticket.

I went to the churchyard at first light for the next one.

---

**No. 12. The stone with tomorrow's date. St Brannock's churchyard.**

Collected: the name.
Stamped.

It stands alone at the end of the row: grey slate, new-cut, and the date on it tomorrow's. It is always tomorrow's. People say the name on it is new every morning, and that whoever it names is the next to die. Nobody says who cuts it. Nobody has ever seen it cut.

passages.heading: No. 9. The portrait. Widow Vane's parlour.
passages.text:
I had meant to log it, stamp it and go. It was a stone, and stones end.

But it carried a name today, and it would carry a different one tomorrow, and another the day after, for as long as there were mornings. A thing that renews itself cannot be finished. You could stamp it every day for the rest of your life. You could stamp it on the train.

The name was Edith.

No surname. The town knew which Edith.

I didn't cross-reference it. I put the file under my arm and went to find her door, because she was still alive, and I could still tell her.

---

passages.heading: Not on the list.
passages.text:
