She lives at the far end of Pump Row, in one room behind a door with the Company's number painted on it. She had the door half shut before I finished saying who I was.

"I know what it says," she said. "Half the Row's been by to tell me. Go home."

passages.heading: Then let me sit here.
passages.text:
She looked at the stamp in my hand, and shut the door.

I sat on the step with my back against it. There is no lantern on Pump Row; the Lamplighter's round does not come this way. Curfew rang.

After a while someone sat down on the other side. I heard her slide down the wood and settle there, by the bottom hinge.

"You're not here about the rent," Edith said. It was not a question.

She told me about the rent anyway. She was two weeks behind. She did washing for the manor and the mill office, and they paid her in scrip, and every noon the scrip went back to the Clerk. She had a way of saying "two weeks" as if it might, said carefully enough, come to one.

She had a sister, younger, who had gone back east on the train before the riot, to a city whose name Edith said the way you say a name you have only ever seen written. The sister had written twice. Edith was writing back.

passages.heading: Then let me sit here.
passages.text: "I haven't finished it," she said.

passages.heading: Why not?
passages.text:
"I don't know how to say the town's all right."

I didn't know either. I said she could tell her about the train. She said her sister knew about the train.

She coughed now and then and said it was the fog. She asked if they had wolves in the city. I said I didn't think so. She asked what I was writing. I said a list. She asked what number she was. I said she wasn't on it.

"Good," she said.

She told me her sister's name. She told me she had bought a postage stamp for the letter at the Post Office, a real one, two cents in money she had kept back from the scrip, and had not stuck it down yet, because once it was stuck down the letter had to go. Then she stopped talking. I heard her breathing on the other side of the wood, slow, and I sat there with my hand on the ticket in my pocket and watched the dark lane until the fog came white and the whistle went for Station Rush.

passages.heading: Why not?
passages.text:
I did not sleep. I am certain of that. I checked my watch every hour by the chapel bell, and all night it kept good time.

At first light Doc Mallory came with the Constable, because the Clerk had sent them about the rent. I stood up out of the way. The Constable knocked, and called, and put his shoulder to the door, and the bolt gave. It had been shot from the inside all night, with my back against the wood.

Edith was in her bed. The blanket was straight.

Mallory looked at her a long time and wrote something, then crossed it out and put the pen away.

On the table there was a letter, folded once and not finished, with the stamp lying loose on top.

Nobody had come in.

I went up to the churchyard. I don't know why. The stone at the end of the row already had a name on it, a new one, with tomorrow's date. I did not go near enough to read it.

passages.heading: Why not?
passages.text:
Two left.

---

passages.heading: No. 13. The drowned lantern. The Fenwood.
passages.text:
Collected: nothing.
Stamped.

His blank line. I went out to Gallows Wood and through it to where the planks stop and the fen starts and the black pines stand in water. I stopped at the last dry plank and went no nearer.

It was there in the fog, out past the hanging oak: a lantern, low to the water, glowing. Steady. Not like a wisp. Like a lamp somebody keeps.

I did not see who keeps it, and I did not look. I wrote down that it was there and that it was lit, stamped the page on my knee, and turned round.

On the planks going back, in the fog, there were footsteps behind me. Mine, and a half-beat after mine, the same weight and the same stride. When I stopped they stopped. When I went on they went on.

Mere-rot: the fen in the ear, the false footsteps everybody in HollowMere has heard. I said it out loud, mere-rot, and kept saying it the whole way back to the square.

passages.heading: No. 13. The drowned lantern. The Fenwood.
passages.text:
When I reached the pump my boots were black with Fenwood mud to the shin. I don't remember stepping off the planks.

---

**No. 14. The bootprints. Vane Manor, the hall carpet.**

Collected.
Stamped.

They have been there as long as anyone can say: a track of muddy bootprints across the hall carpet from the door to the foot of the stair, and none coming back. The Company calls them nothing. Whoever logs them never matches them.

His file had them, second on his list, measured with care: length heel to toe, breadth at the ball, the depth of the heel.

I put my own boot down beside the first print.

Heel to toe. The breadth. The heel.

A hundred men in this town wear the Company boot. I have written it. Height is a trait, and a hundred men share it.

But the mud in the prints was wet.

passages.heading: No. 13. The drowned lantern. The Fenwood.
passages.text:
I knelt and put a finger in the third print, and it came up black and cold and smelling of the fen. Fenwood mud, the same as on my boots, to the shin.

The prints go to the stair and stop. They do not come back. Mine go to the door, and I can see them now, crossing the others.

I cannot rule myself out, so I ruled nothing.

The fourteenth thing was mine.

---

I stamped it NO CASE. I held the stamp down the way the Constable had shown me, and lifted it clean.

I went down into the Flooded Gallery again with Mrs Grieves's lantern and laid my file in the crate beside his, with the ticket on top of both, unpunched. I put the straw back. I left the lid half-pried, the nails up on one side, the way I had found it.

On Saturday the Baron's train came in at Station Rush with its Pinkertons and stood at the platform all day, breathing. The Baron went up to the Constable's and came out again, and at dusk the train went back down the Line.

passages.heading: No. 13. The drowned lantern. The Fenwood.
passages.text:
I watched it go from the square. It doesn't wait. It never has.

On Monday I went past the Constable's window. He was at his desk, with Company paper in front of him and a new stamp still in its box, writing in a round, slow hand and numbering down the margin.

Fourteen things. The Constable wrote them out himself.

works.title: Cable Construction Circus
works.blurb: a narrative rap portraying a chaotic work site crew as a circus troupe.

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
Seven in the mornin’, sun barely risen,  
Locates all wrong like somebody wasn’t listenin’,  
Half the crew standin’ around like they lost in a vision,  
Boss pulled up and immediately started the bitchin’

——

Step right up, hard hat on, leave your pride at the gate,  
Best damn circus in the county, don’t you dare be late,  
Cable construction circus, everybody losin’ they mind,  
Clowns on the trencher, monkey one step behind,  
Boss breathin’ on our necks, dirt flyin’ every direction,  
Whole job site’s a shit show with a fiber optic connection,  
Roll up — big top sunk deep in the mud,  
Cable construction circus, runnin’ on coffee and blood

——  
(storytelling cadence, laid back, heavy)  
Now Rob’s in the hole complainin’ like the hole is the problem,  
Greg’s playin’ with himself, somebody really oughta stop him,  
Foreman’s on the phone screamin’ at the fuck who laid out —  
Third time this week, same lazy pout, same sorry mouth,  
Waterline got hit, boss man’s face went south,  
Veins in his neck like the cable comin’ out,  
Walker ringin’ my phone talkin’ ‘bout he needs it by four,  
Bore path ain’t marked, no locates, sun ain’t even sure,  
Paperwork from yesterday, locates by tonight —  
Sir we just got here, with respect, you ain’t right,  
Machine hit rock at nine, gas line right at noon,  
Should’ve known from the jump we’d be cryin’ pretty soon —

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
——

(beat drops out)  
JACOB.

JACOB WHAT THE FUCK ARE YOU DOING.

I SAID DRILL STRAIGHT YOU DUMB SON OF A BITCH.

WE TALKED ABOUT THIS.

WE TALKED ABOUT THIS YESTERDAY.

PUT THE DAMN PHONE DOWN AND LISTEN YOU STUPID BITCH.

EVERY SINGLE TIME.

EVERY GODDAMN TIME.

(beat rolls back in slow and heavy)  
Inspector pulled up, surveyed the scene, turned around and fled,  
Came back at noon after the worst of it was dead

Chaos is free but the overtime’ll cost ya,  
Best paid shit show in the Southeast — welcome, I’ll host ya

(darker, slower, almost amused)  
Now Greg — Lord Greg — rolled up with the strangest energy,  
Lawn chair in the shade like the job site’s his amenity,  
BlueChew in his pocket like it’s doing him a favor,  
Useless as the man, pill ain’t finding no savior,  
Looked at the driller’s legs, said it slow like it was normal —  
“Them legs gave me a hard on” — nothing about it formal,  
Every man on the crew just froze, stared, carried on,  
Couldn’t unhear it, couldn’t process, just moved along,  
Barkin’ out instructions he ain’t qualified to give,  
Soft-dick bastard telling hardworking men how to live,  
More excuses than the pill got listed on the label —  
Greg, sit your ass down and get up from the table

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
(drops to almost a whisper, deliberate)  
Then there’s Ethan —  
Only reason this whole circus ain’t burned to the ground,  
Fixin’ everybody’s disasters without makin’ a sound,  
You can see it in his eyes if you look long enough —  
Tired, worn, runnin’ thin, done with all of this stuff,  
Cleanin’ up behind Rob, cleanin’ up behind Greg,  
Jacob drillin’ crooked with his phone up to his head,  
Ethan’s the only sumbitch here who genuinely knows the trade,  
While the rest of us are circus clowns that somebody got paid,  
Somebody give that man a raise, a drink, a week of sleep —  
He’s carryin’ this whole damn show and it’s gettin’ way too deep

Cable construction circus, everybody losin’ they mind,  
Clowns runnin’ the trencher, monkey one step behind,  
Boss breathin’ fire, dirt flyin’ every direction,  
This whole job site’s a shit show with a fiber optic connection,  
Roll up — big top sunk deep in the mud,  
Cable construction circus, runnin’ on coffee and blood

passages.heading: Cable Construction Circus
passages.text:
(half spoken, fading slow like the beat’s dying)  
Step right up…  
Tickets free but your sanity’s gonna cost ya…  
Somebody pull Rob outta that hole…  
Tell limp dick Greg to sit his ass down…  
Jacob… put the goddamn phone away…  
And somebody get Ethan a drink…  
He earned it…  
We all did…  
…circus don’t close till the fiber’s lit

works.title: How i feel
works.blurb: a confessional song lyric on isolation, creative burnout, and disillusionment with time and fame.

passages.heading: How i feel
passages.text:
How i feel

I see your face in shadows so sweet  
Times replaced, emotion heaps  
Maybe I'm better left unseen  
Playing aloud within my own scene  
Feels like friends have left me all alone  
Walking corpses, not a word just a groan

Everyones hungry for new ideas  
Forgetting we're just kids  
selling us off like they got dibs  
Burning us out before we first sprout  
Never touched a pen till i got tinged  
from fake friends with minds unhinged  
Walking alone in silent dreams  
 just wondering what I might be

Trying to survive, never gonna fade inside  
in a world full of jump scares  
nightmares got me pulling out my hair  
Lost without a place to call found  
people be saying “is that all now”  
don’t worry i get your in a hurry  
ill make it quick fast forward to the hit

passages.heading: How i feel
passages.text:
Maybe my dreams are only my own  
Maybe I'm just trying to find my soul  
When did it become overrated to be outrageous  
am I outdated?

Before my time, before its line  
In a time that ain't even mine  
Yes, I'm tired of talk about time  
Because it only wastes what's mine

Every day I sit and rest  
Is another day I can't invest  
Every hour is a deadlines call  
because one day ill lose it all

When we all head to heaven  
Sit around eating bread unleaven  
we’ll see we were just living free  
Now we're living life's greatest luxury

works.title: Ballad of the Iron Beast
works.blurb: a HollowMere platform hand's work ballad for the Daily Train — the crew, the freight, the black wax, the back car — turning on the brother who stayed for him.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
*(no music; boots on frozen planks)*
Ten past five in the mornin', November, ninety-three,
Frost on the spur and the platform lantern still burnin' for me,
HOLLOWMERE — EST. BY THE RAILROAD EXPANSE, sign swingin' on its chain,
Town don't wake till the Beast clears its throat — then the whole town's waitin' on the train

——

Step on up, frost on the boards, keep your hat in your hand,
Barons own the mill and the bank and the dirt where you stand,
You want bread, you want news, you want somewhere to go —
Seven days' walk to a soul and the walk's mostly snow,
Here she comes round the black pines, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
HollowMere, end of the line, wash the mud off your name,
Whatever you do, boys — don't miss the train

——
(storytelling cadence, laid back, heavy)
Now Len's on the spikes singin' time to the maul,
Swears the rails go walkin' when nobody's watchin' at all,
Stan Pike on the switch with a cough like a saw,
Calls it a cold — been a cold since the thaw,
Jack Rudd liftin' whiskey, one bottle a load,
Calls it a tariff, says the Company owes,
Clem reads the manifests out loud, every word,
Only man on the platform who reads, so the loudest one heard,
And Ernie, twelve, with the bucket, askin' every train
Where she goes after us — and nobody's ever explained

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
Six o'clock, flour for Crumb's, sacks white as the frost,
Seven, the whiskey for the Lantern, I count what got lost,
Eight, tonics for the morgue — morgue orders ahead,
Nine, the gunpowder, the railyard, sign here for the lead,
I unload the flour. I unload the lead.
I unload whatever the Barons said.

——

Step on up, frost on the boards, keep your scrip in your hand,
Clerk comes at noon for the rent on the dirt where you stand,
Banks fallin' back east like the pines in a blow,
Seven days' walk to a soul and the walk's mostly snow,
Here she sits on the spur, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
Ticket out costs a year, and the year's in the Company's name —
Can't afford the train, boys — so don't miss the train

——
(sacks hit the boards)
Ten o'clock, mailbags, heavy as a man,
Gazette on the top, tossed down like contraband,
Prints yesterday's secrets, every sin that got proved,
Names nobody it can't — so the rest of us move,
Clem reads the headline, nobody looks at each other,
Every man on the platform real interested in his brother,
And down in the bag there's a letter sealed black,
Somebody's name on it, and nobody's lookin' back,
I sort around it slow like a snake in the flour,
Don't touch it, don't turn it, don't ask it the hour.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
Then I slip in my three, outbound, Ma's name in my hand,
Jack Rudd grins, "Arthur too rich now to write her? Too grand?"
"Arthur's busy gettin' rich," I say, and the whole crew roars,
And I laugh along, tie off the bag, and I heave it aboard.

What's a platform hand worth on a Panic year?
A dollar in scrip and a back that don't quit?
And who's countin' — the Clerk, or the man in the mirror?

——

(beat drops out)
WHO SIGNED FOR THE LEAD.

WHO SIGNED FOR THE LEAD.

CLEM. CLEM, PUT THE GAZETTE DOWN.

THAT CRATE IS BREATHING.

NOBODY OPENS THAT CRATE.

NOBODY TOUCHES THE BLACK WAX. NOBODY.

COFFINS TO THE BACK CAR.

THE BACK CAR.

EVERY DAY.

EVERY GODDAMN DAY.

(beat rolls back in slow and heavy)
Crate went quiet by one, and nobody asked why,
Freight is freight, and the Company don't ask, so don't I.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
——
(darker, slower)
Afternoon car, and the new Vicar steps down,
Father Bray died or ran, depends who's drinkin' in town,
Collar so white it hurts in the fog,
Shakes every hand like he's countin' a flock,
And they say every soul here confesses to him, sooner or later —
I carry his trunk up the hill, and I keep mine for later.

Town rioted Tuesday. Wednesday, the Baron,
Cornelius Thorne in a coat worth more than I'm earnin',
Pinkertons, dogs, and a rifle apiece,
Steps on the boards like the boards owe him peace,
Took off my hat. Took his bags. Took his scrip.
Hated myself, and I bowed at the hip.

And Stan Pike's switch is quiet — cough stopped Monday night,
Stan caught the Dusk train, back car, lid on tight,
Len sang him spike-time, Ernie held his cap,
I signed for Stan Pike like a sack, and I set him in back.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
And who loads the back car, if not the hand that's here?
Who's left to sign for a man?
Who'd carry them out, if I went?

——

Step on up, light's goin' down, take your hat off your head,
She brings the bread and the whiskey, the priest and the lead,
She brings the Baron and the dogs and the letter sealed black,
She takes the ones we can't keep, in a box, in the back,
Here she sits on the spur, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast on the Thorne and Expanse, she don't wait, don't explain,
Owns the clock, owns the town, owns the mud and the rain —
Don't miss the train, boys — she don't miss you, all the same

——
(drops to almost a whisper, deliberate)
But Arthur didn't miss the train.

Two springs back — two tickets, one for him, one for me,
Punched for a Tuesday, Dusk, out past the trees,
Arthur on the step with his hat in his hand,
Me on the boards like I'm bolted to the land,
Scrip debt for an excuse. Fear for a reason.
Clerk's rent for a story I could tell every season.
He looked at me once. He stepped back down.
He stayed for me. He stayed in this town.

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
Called her the Iron Beast, like he did when we were boys,
To make me laugh — and it did — just a word, just a noise,
Whistled the Dusk whistle a half-step flat,
Every night on the platform, and I'd tell him quit that,
Then winter. The mere-rot. The same cough as Stan.
Then the back car.
I loaded the flour. I loaded the lead.
I loaded my brother.

And every week since, Ma, I write you in his hand —
*Doin' fine, Ma. Good wages. The West agrees with me, Ma* —
I sign it Arthur. I post it outbound.
I load the bag myself.
His ticket's in the hatband, never punched past Tuesday.
I wear the hat. I whistle flat.

So which of us missed it?
The one who never boarded —
or the one who boarded in a box?

——

Step on up, frost on the boards, keep your hat in your hand,
Barons own the mill and the bank and the dirt where you stand,
You want bread, you want news, you want somewhere to go —
Seven days' walk to a soul and the walk's mostly snow,
There she goes round the black pines, smoke hangin' like chain,
Iron Beast — that was Arthur's word — she don't wait, don't explain,
HollowMere, end of the line, wash the mud off your name,
Town says don't miss the train, boys — I never missed the train

passages.heading: Ballad of the Iron Beast
passages.text:
——
(half-spoken, fading slow like the beat's dying)
Dusk whistle…
Somebody tell Ernie to get off the tracks…
Back car's full…
See you at five…

Don't miss the train, they tell you. I never missed it once —
I just let it carry everyone I couldn't follow.

works.title: Trips Are Like Exes
works.blurb: Prose-poem on self-discovery and impermanence via a travel/relationship duality.

passages.heading: Trips Are Like Exes
passages.text:
Trips are like exes— We’d like to think it’s all their fault when it goes wrong, Love the memories, but wouldn’t ever go back. Yet we take another trip, another chance, Finding ourselves while we are out looking for others. Turns out maybe every trip has a story, And every story has two sides.  
Like Jekyll and Hyde, we run and we hide from the truth. Life’s ugly, love’s got a metallic aftertaste, But in the end, we’d drink poison to feel more alive. We flirt with death at every chance for celebration— Birth, betrothal, or betrayal, we always celebrate. That’s what life’s about: To plan the party, crash it, and clean up after it. Because for fuck's sake, we’ve only got today.  
But the most beautiful part Is finding yourself after a trip. You were broken and lost, Your ego dissolved, your inner self bare. The moment that you thought would bring the ultimate peace Was actually just the moment you lost what you loved.  
When you are freed from your ego, you yearn for your life. Not that you are in any peril, But for a moment, your mind is forced outside itself. Then comes that moment when your self collects back to you, Like a pool of identity in the shards of the after-party. That cleaning up is you coming back, Choosing to be you, And watching as every sliver that is you comes back.

passages.heading: Trips Are Like Exes
passages.text: “In the end we’d love to think it’s all beautiful or ugly but instead the ugly is fucking beauty and every beauties got an ugly side” PART 1

works.title: Growing Up
works.blurb: Mortality and memory through a grandfather relationship.

passages.heading: Growing Up
passages.text:
Growing up is realizing that no one dies of old age.  
Just another fairytale; they don’t mention their pain.  
But why? Youth clings to illusion and fades faster than it,  
and with its passing you see those who died are no different than you and me.  
It is sad, but it is true; that is why we give the passing their due—  
we lay them in boxes their lives’ worth can barely afford.  
Bountiful blessings fall upon deaf ears, past curses forgotten from the years,  
loved ones who never knew them look teary-eyed down at a stranger.  
Go on, pray to some God born from a manger; no plea will bring them back.  
Once the light is extinguished, there’s no coming back.  
Death is neither sad nor happy; like life, it is the tool by which we measure.  
Every point has an end, or else it defies its premise; every life has a death that makes you live.  
So I learned to measure life by its textures: peanuts in bobbing in a cold Coke, baseball on the weekends, the faint smell of dirt under his nails.  
Saturdays were baseball on the tv, the crack of a bat, him calling out names like  he knew the players.  
He built raised beds the way some men pray—measured, squared, patient—  
each seed tucked in like a promise he could keep; soil under his nails smelled of time.  
His office was a pile of paper and tiny things, a life in clutter;  
when I was small I called him an archivist, later I called it what it was: hoarding.  
Still, those piles were his language—how he said he mattered.  
He loved in small rituals: peanuts in Coke, a game on the radio, a row of tomatoes.  
For it is simple to see that life is full of what you look for—  
not why for or who for, but the looking you do when you don’t see.  
Through each breath you are living life, and through each thought of the future you are closing in on death.  
No sermon will bring back the ordinary; only the echo of habit remains.  
So plant your beds, keep your odd comforts, learn the geometry of a double play,  
notice the textures—the fizz, the crack, the dirt, the shuffle of paper—and hold them close.  
Only you can decide what your last breath will look like.  
Make it beautiful, make it memorable, make it a… CRESCENDO!!!

works.title: Am I Me Enough
works.blurb: Self-worth and love, moving toward self-acceptance.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
“Am I Me Enough?”

I remember it like it was yesterday — being young.  
I would’ve said young, dumb, and in love,  
but the truth is youth was the only thing I ever lost  
while trying to prove I was enough.

For to be so in love  
that it drives you toward something foolish —  
well, that must’ve been good love.  
The kind pirates plunder,  
kings cling to,  
and paupers pity from afar.  
A treasure so bright it blinds you  
into believing you’re worthy of it.

And wasn’t that always the question?  
Not is this love real,  
but am I real enough for this love.  
Every heartbeat felt like a test,  
every promise like a wager,  
every kiss like a crown  
I wasn’t sure I deserved to wear.

And so I spent whole seasons  
trying to polish myself into something worthy—  
sanding down my softness,  
sharpening my silence,  
learning how to love like a man  
who never asked for anything in return.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
I mistook endurance for virtue,  
mistook sacrifice for proof,  
mistook my own breaking  
for a sign I was finally doing love right.  
I kept offering pieces of myself  
like coins into a wishing well,  
hoping the splash meant something,  
hoping someone would hear the echo  
and call it devotion.

But the truth is,  
I wasn’t chasing people—  
I was chasing permission.  
Permission to be held,  
to be chosen,  
to be seen without earning it.  
Every goodbye felt like a verdict,  
every silence like a sentence,  
every almost‑love like a mirror  
asking the same old question  
in a new, cruel light:  
Was I ever enough for anyone  
if I was never enough for myself.

But time has a way of softening the blade,  
of turning questions into quiet companions.  
I learned that worth was never something  
I could win by bleeding for it,  
never something another person  
could stamp onto my chest like a medal.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
I spent years trying to be chosen,  
never realizing I was the one  
doing the choosing all along.  
And maybe that’s the cruelest trick of youth—  
believing love is a door someone else must open,  
when all along the hinges were in my hands.

So was I good enough?  
Maybe that was the wrong question.  
Maybe the truth is simpler,  
gentler,  
truer:

I was growing.  
I was learning.  
I was becoming.

And in the becoming,  
I found a version of myself  
who no longer begs for permission,  
who no longer trades pieces of his heart  
for a glimpse of belonging,  
who no longer mistakes being chosen  
for being worthy.

Now, when I look back,  
I don’t ask if I was good enough.  
I ask if I was honest,  
if I was trying,  
if I was becoming someone  
I could stand beside without flinching.

And maybe that’s the quiet miracle of it all—  
that after everything,  
after the longing and the losing,  
after the crowns I didn’t feel fit my head,  
I finally learned to wear my own name  
without apology.

passages.heading: Am I Me Enough
passages.text:
I finally learned  
I was enough  
because I was mine.

works.title: When You Know to Much
works.blurb: Creative ambition and defiance in the face of mortality.

passages.heading: When You Know to Much
passages.text:
When You Know to Much

It pains me to know so many beautiful words have leapt from my mind without me even catching hold.  
It pains me to know I could have written something beautiful, something that could have lasted.  
Maybe I’m foolish to believe the words bumbling around in my head like a beehive would mean anything on paper.  
I want to be great, I say. But I don’t know what to call greatness. I want to be happy, I think. But still I never know joy.  
For who am I to be great—like Shakespeare or King Arthur? One was a drunk and a womanizer. The other was a fairy tale told long ago.  
Are we to keep telling our kids of fae or troll, to let their imaginations run wild with things that go bump in the night? Only for them to grow old as I do now and find it was never true.  
Or should we slay the beautiful creatures that dance in our dreams, call forth misery from adulthood’s fate, and let myth vanish from our lives?  
I cry out one last time to whoever could be listening. Still no change comes that would matter. Because time is the end of all, and it never stops. Maybe that’s why joy fades and light diminishes. Why we wish to be something more is because we know we are slowly becoming less.  
The child in us weeps every day. Will you dry his tears, or tell him never to cry again?

passages.heading: When You Know to Much
passages.text:
Some may think I’m crying over a child, over childhood at its loss. But no—know that I weep for someone else. Myself.  
The world grew around me. I did not grow for the world. They made me into a jest. They made me small so they could stand tall. They defiled what was sacred and called it comedy.  
But here’s what they didn’t know while they laughed:  
I was watching.  
I may not be great. But I can be vain. And vanity—oh, vanity is the one thing the destroyed understand perfectly. We who have nothing left to lose see the game without the mercy of blindness. We speak past you, through you, into the void where those who come after might hear.  
You built your idols on facts you ignored. You called it destiny. You called it talent. You called it greatness.  
But I know the secret now: there is no difference between a god and a joke until someone decides there is. And I have decided.  
So let me laugh—joyful, bitter, knowing. Let me spit gold that tastes like ash. Let me build mountains from the wreckage you left me. Let me push the great ones from the heights not because I’m stronger, but because I’m already falling, and I’ve learned how to fly on the way down.  
This is the power of the defiled: we move without fear. We speak without hope. We climb without asking permission from those who never owned the mountain anyway.  
My words aren’t great. They’re mine.  
And that’s more than enough to shake what was never real.

works.title: Inherited
works.blurb: Generational cycles and becoming your parents.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
Inherited

I remember the nights I tried to stay awake to see my father’s headlights touch my window.  
The way you would sleep in on the weekends because you were tired.  
My heartaches when you weren’t there to play catch.  
But now I know the noose money became as it trickled out like water, pushing you further out to sea.

My mother yelled not out of anger but fear.  
I felt like we were at odds but the truth is I fought while you protected.  
I believed you were my greatest enemy only to find you were the only one defending me.  
I thought you meant to break me but you were the one who made me.

You cared for me longer than I have memory.  
You cried for me before I had fears of my own to cry about.  
Yet you still bore them. Even when I added to them.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
I’m not sorry for being young.  
I’m sorry for doubting your love when you never showed us contempt.

Now I see you.  
You were no older than I am now when you became a mother—  
just 19 facing the world with such courage.  
A caretaker. A protector. A dream builder in the dark.

I thank you for all the times you weren’t there dad because I needed you to be somewhere else.  
I thank you for the nights you slept because exhaustion was all you could muster.

You felt the pain deeper than I ever could as just a child.  
You bore it with honor.  
And now I grieve that suffering—the kind you never let me see,  
the kind I can only know now that it’s too late to unknow  
and the suffering ill never know because you spared me.

But here is what keeps me awake now:  
I see exactly why you had to leave.  
I see exactly why you had to yell.  
I understand the aftermath of survival.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
And I am standing at the threshold of becoming what you were,  
I know will make the same choices.  
I know will not be there when they need me.  
I will seem angry to gain obedience because sometimes cruelty is mercy.  
I will stretch myself thin in ways they cannot comprehend  
until they stand where I’m standing now,  
understanding everything,  
unable to change anything.

My children will feel what I felt.  
They will doubt me.  
They will grow into the terrible knowledge that I did the best 
but it was never enough.

And they will stand at their own threshold,  
terrified they’ll do the same.

The cycle doesn’t break.  
It just gets inherited with fuller sight.  
We see it coming and we cannot stop it.  
We only bear it with whatever honor we can find.

The bridge between childhood anger and adulthood understanding  
is learning that both things are true at once:  
You saved me.  
You hurt me.  
And I will do both to them.

passages.heading: Inherited
passages.text:
This is what clarity costs.  
This is what it means to grow up and become your parents,  
not despite understanding their pain,  
but because of it.

works.title: Was I Good Enough
works.blurb: Self-worth, loneliness, and family, a companion piece to "Am I Me Enough".

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
“Was I Good Enough”

I remember being young, sprawled across the couch,  
no fear in my body except the quiet tremor of my thoughts.  
I watched anime until the sky bruised purple,  
dodging deadlines, dodging myself,  
dodging the question humming under my ribs:  
Was I good enough?

I worried about my friends—  
if they liked me, if I mattered,  
if the girl on the playground  
ever saw me the way I rehearsed in my head.  
Funny how early doubt learns your name,  
how it follows you like a shadow  
that grows longer than your legs ever did.

I guess that’s the curse of a soft heart—  
to sit among friends  
and still feel set apart.  
Nights I begged for a call, any call,  
just to drown out the echo in my chest.  
A phone ringing in another room  
felt like someone else’s life calling me  
while mine stayed pressed  
beneath the weight of the question.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
I grew up measuring my worth  
by the noise I could pull from other people—  
a laugh, a text, a name spoken like a vow.  
I stayed awake for signs I wasn’t drifting  
too far to be found somehow.  
But most nights, it was only me, myself, and I—  
three shadows sharing one body,  
three voices asking why  
I still wasn’t enough for myself.

Some mornings we get along.  
I’ll make breakfast without rushing,  
choose fruit instead of skipping the meal,  
and for a moment we sit at the same table  
like three people learning how to feel  
without fear of failing.

Other days we argue in the mirror.  
Me wanting to slow down,  
myself replaying something someone said last week,  
I caught in the middle,  
trying to keep the peace  
between two versions of me  
who both believe they’re the one  
who wasn’t good enough.

Some nights we surprise each other—  
I’ll let a thought pass without chasing it,  
myself won’t turn a small mistake into a prophecy,  
and I will breathe like I’ve been practicing for years.  
Those are the nights we feel almost whole,  
almost clear,  
almost worthy.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
But there are still moments  
when one of us storms off inside my chest,  
slamming a door only I can hear.  
Moments when I fall back into old habits,  
Looking for someone else to fill the silence  
instead of sitting with the three of us  
and learning how to steer  
my own life.

Some days the sun hits my hands just right,  
warm enough to feel like someone holding me  
without asking for anything in return.  
It’s strange how a little light  
can feel like a memory of love  
I never fully got to earn—  
or thought I didn’t.

I think about the past more than I admit—  
the way my mom yelled when I was too young  
to understand she was drowning too,  
how my dad’s absence filled the cabinets  
but emptied the room,  
how my brother’s anger cracked the walls  
long before I learned it was pain  
trying to bloom  
in a house that didn’t know how.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
And I carried all of it,  
quietly,  
like a child holding a box too heavy  
but too proud to set down—  
as if endurance could answer the question  
no one ever asked me out loud.

But lately, something’s shifting.  
I feel it in the small things—  
the way the morning air forgives me,  
the way a soft breeze brushes my cheek  
like an apology I never asked for.  
I catch myself smiling at nothing,  
letting the sun warm my hands  
without comparing it to anyone else’s touch,  
as if warmth itself is proof  
I might be enough.

We don’t talk enough about the way  
a stupid coincidence can make you laugh  
harder than it deserves,  
how that tiny burst of joy  
can soften the sharpest nerves  
and remind you you’re still alive.

We forget to honor the moments  
when a sunrise catches us off guard,  
or a sunset paints the sky  
like it’s trying to mend what’s scarred.  
Those times we smile for no reason  
and feel our own heart warm in return—  
those are the moments that teach us  
what we once had to learn  
from someone else.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
Sure, I miss the warmth of a kiss,  
the safety of a hug,  
the feeling of someone choosing me  
without hesitation.  
But I found something quieter,  
something steadier than infatuation—  
a love that doesn’t leave  
when the room goes silent.

I found myself.  
Not in a self‑help,  
“love your flaws” kind of way,  
not in the watered‑down guru garbage  
that tries to sell healing like a trend.  
I mean the real thing—  
the kind of love that grows  
when you sit with yourself long enough  
to call yourself a friend  
and believe it.

I like my own company now.  
I trust it.  
Me and myself don’t leave  
when it gets heavy.  
We stay,  
we breathe,  
we laugh at nothing,  
we watch the sun rise and fall  
like it’s a show made just for us—  
steady, ready,  
finally enough.

I realized, in a life we may tell one or countless others  
that they are our whole world,  
that we’d choose them in every lifetime,  
that we’d die for them—  
and don’t get me wrong, I love that.  
But maybe we forget to ask  
if we’d do the same for ourselves.

passages.heading: Was I Good Enough
passages.text:
Would I choose me  
in every version of my life  
or only when I’m easy to love?  
Would I stand by myself  
when the room goes quiet,  
when the thoughts get loud,  
when the world feels too heavy  
for one pair of hands?

Maybe the real promise—  
the one no one teaches you to make—  
is learning to choose yourself  
with the same tenderness  
you once saved for everyone else.

And maybe that’s what love looks like now:  
not grand declarations,  
not dying for someone,  
but living with myself  
in a way that feels like choosing me  
every single time.

works.title: In Search Of Truth
works.blurb: Existentialist prose-poem on truth and self-deception.

passages.heading: In Search Of Truth
passages.text:
In Search Of Truth:  
Elijah W. Skinner

The lengths we go to chase our perceived truths often stretch beyond the reach of our own comprehension.  
We build scaffolds of belief— not to ascend toward reality, but to shield ourselves from its raw, unfiltered glare.  
In our hunger for clarity, we craft versions of truth that feel digestible, symmetrical, safe.  
Not because they are real, but because they are bearable.  
Factual reality: cold, indifferent, unyielding— demands surrender. 
But the mind, ever defiant, prefers a substitute: a truth softened by narrative, shaped by bias, stitched together with the thread of familiarity.  
We do not always seek what is true.  
We seek what can be held without burning our hands.  
There is a moment, quiet, unannounced— when the false truth begins to rot.  
Its symmetry cracks.  
Its safety suffocates.  
Its sweetness turns sour in the mouth.  
And reality begins to press in— not with force, but with the quiet weight of something that has been put off.  
To face it is not to conquer it.  
It is to kneel.  
To let it burn.  
To let it strip away the scaffolds until only the raw truth remains.  
This is not clarity.  
This is nakedness.  
When we lay ourselves barren we are able to be seen, and to see. 
This is the only place truth can be witnessed without illusion.  
This is not the end of seeking.  
It is the end of hiding.  
You no longer chase truth.  
You must live it.

works.title: The Unfamiliar
works.blurb: Growth and courage, written in second person.

passages.heading: The Unfamiliar
passages.text:
The Unfamiliar

To rise from the dust of the ordinary  
into the rare air of the extraordinary,  
one must step beyond the borders of the known,  
To know what can not be known.

The familiar is a warm cage-  
its bars invisible,  
its floor worn smooth by the pacing of your own feet.  
It will not harm you,  
but it’s fate is a hollow death.

The unfamiliar waits outside,  
its shape shifting in the half-light,  
its voice a language you have not yet learned.  
It will not promise safety,  
but it will promise change.

To ascend,  
you must open your arms to what unsettles you,  
let it press its strange weight into your skin,  
let it teach you the names of things  
you once feared to touch.

For only in the company of the unknown  
does the self shed its husk,  
and in that agonizing act of shedding the old 
the beginning of something new unfolds.

passages.heading: The Unfamiliar
passages.text:
And as you move into the heart of the unfamiliar,  
you will feel the ground tilt,  
the air sharpen,  
the horizon pull at your ribs.

This is how ascent begins—  
not with triumph,  
but with a single step taken  
before you feel ready.

Followed by the toil of beginning 
again and again 
with that experience forever more 
As it presses itself into you deeper

The extraordinary is built  
from moments like these.

And when you cross that trembling threshold,  
the world will not applaud.  
It will simply rearrange itself around you,  
as if it had been waiting  
for your arrival all along.

The sky will feel wider.  
Your breath will feel truer.  
And the person you once were  
will watch from a distance,  
grateful you did not stay with them.

works.title: The Knife I Chose
works.blurb: Betrayal and cyclical harm, written in third person.

passages.heading: The Knife I Chose
passages.text:
The Knife I Chose

The night swallows her footsteps,  
each one a drumbeat of fear against the hollow streets.  
Shadows stretch long and hungry,  
the evils of the world at her back,  
their breath cold on her neck.

She runs toward the only light she knows—  
a figure waiting in the dark,  
familiar, steady,  
a harbor she has clung to in storms before.  
Her chest heaves, her pulse a frantic hymn,  
and when she reaches him,  
she falls into his arms  
as though the world might finally loosen its grip.

But the embrace is not salvation.  
It is the moment the blade finds her—  
cold, precise,  
sliding between ribs with the intimacy of a whispered secret.  
Her heart clenches,  
not only from the steel,  
but from the truth that blooms with it:  
trust has teeth,  
and wolf’s don’t only hide beneath sheep’s skin

passages.heading: The Knife I Chose
passages.text:
Warmth spreads across her skin,  
thick and clinging,  
the metallic scent of betrayal rising with the steam of her breath.  
The night does not pause.  
The shadows do not retreat.  
And in that final clarity,  
she understands—  
the knife was always there,  
waiting in the arms she thought would save her.

The blade is still there,  
buried deep,  
its cold edge pulsing with her heartbeat.  
Each breath is a ragged thread,  
but she clings to it—  
not because she cannot pull away,  
but because the thought of facing the night alone  
is a greater terror than the steel in her chest.

The world’s evils still prowl beyond these arms,  
and here, at least,  
she knows the shape of the monster holding her.

Her hands rise, trembling,  
fingers brushing the jaw of her betrayer  
as though memorizing the lines of a face  
she has always known would end her.  
She draws him closer,  
their foreheads almost touching,  
and with the last breath she owns,  
she presses her lips to his—  
a kiss not of love,  
but of surrender to the only warmth left to her.

passages.heading: The Knife I Chose
passages.text:
Her body slackens,  
the weight of her falling into his grasp.  
Blood hums against her skin,  
sticky and slow,  
and yet a faint smile curves her lips—  
not joy,  
but the quiet relief  
of someone who has chosen  
the pain they understand  
over the darkness they do not.

And yet—  
she does not die.  
Not in body, at least.  
For this is not an ending,  
but an inheritance:  
a story older than memory,  
repeated like a sacred curse,  
etched into the laws of this world  
where love and ruin  
so often share the same embrace.

works.title: The Stripes Remain
works.blurb: Resilience and redemption, reads as a rebuttal to "The Knife I Chose".

passages.heading: The Stripes Remain
passages.text:
The Stripes Remain

She said, “A tiger can’t change its stripes.”  
She spoke it like a sentence passed,  
as if my flaws were carved into the marrow,  
as if my shadow was born of nothing but my own rot.  
And in that moment, I believed her.  
That was my first defeat.

I fell.  
Not once, but again and again,  
each failure a stone dragging me deeper.  
I learned the taste of ash,  
the weight of silence,  
the slow suffocation of being seen only as the sum of my sins.

But the trial did not end in the pit.  
It began there.  
I walked through fires that stripped the flesh from my pride.  
I descended into depths where the air itself conspired to crush me.  
And in those depths, I did not die.  
I endured.  
I endured until endurance became my crown.

passages.heading: The Stripes Remain
passages.text:
When I rose, it was not as the man she left behind.  
The stripes remained,  
but they were no longer her prophecy.  
They were my regalia —  
marks of survival,  
sigils of the battles I had bled through.

Now I stand above the ruins,  
not cleansed,  
but sovereign.  
Not forgiven,  
but unbroken.  
The throne I claim is carved from the bones of my trials,  
and the crown I wear was forged in the heat of my own damnation.

She will never see the man I became.  
And that is my final triumph —  
for the one who swore I could never change  
will never know how high I have risen.

works.title: For My Papa
works.blurb: Grief and legacy, a companion piece to "Growing Up".

passages.heading: For My Papa
passages.text:
For My Papa

I would be dishonest if I said my heart wasn’t heavy.  
The pain of his passing is a burden—  
but it’s a burden I will gladly carry,  
because it is the weight of love,  
and the blessings of his memory.

My papa, more than anyone else,  
taught me that when you love someone,  
you accept that there will be pain.  
For better and for worse—  
those words should never be confined to wedding vows.  
They are a way of living,  
a testament to the choice to love,  
to care,  
to stand beside someone no matter the season.

No one embodied that more than my grandparents.  
Their love overflowed into the branches of the family tree they built.  
Many of us here today would not be here  
if not for the commitment they showed.  
They are the roots of a great oak,  
digging deep into the mantle of the earth,  
holding us steady in a world of shifting ground.  
Even now, with his passing,  
he holds us strong.  
His memory will live forever in all of us.

passages.heading: For My Papa
passages.text:
People say not to judge a book by its cover—  
and the same is true of life.  
My grandfather was born in 1949,  
and today, as we close his casket,  
the story of his life does not end.  
The chapters remain with us—  
in the way we speak,  
in the way we love,  
in the way we carry ourselves through this world.

Though we have lost his presence,  
we have not lost him.  
He is woven into us,  
a golden thread running through the fabric of our lives.  
And as long as we live,  
his story will never close.

works.title: Darkness
works.blurb: Cycles of violence and retaliation resolving toward forgiveness.

passages.heading: Darkness
passages.text:
Darkness

To answer shadow with shadow  
is to feed the very night you wish to end.  
Strike for strike, wound for wound—  
the cycle closes in,  
a serpent devouring its own tail.

Darkness does not starve  
when given more of itself.  
It swells,  
it thickens,  
it learns your name.

Only those who have walked its corridors  
and felt its cold breath on their skin  
can choose to turn,  
to lift a lantern instead of a blade.

Light is not the absence of shadow—  
it is the defiance of it.  
It is the hand that refuses to strike,  
the voice that refuses to echo hate.

And when light is offered  
where darkness once reigned,  
the night does not vanish—  
but it begins to retreat,  
step by reluctant step,  
until the horizon remembers the sun.

works.title: Past, Present, and Future
works.blurb: Self-transformation and groundedness.

passages.heading: Past, Present, and Future
passages.text:
Past, Present, and Future

I am but a vessel —  
neither shackled to the ruins of my past  
nor tethered to the mirage of my future.  
Behold the fragments of who I was,  
woven with the tender threads of what I am becoming.  
Like all living things,  
I am caught in the endless turning of metamorphosis —  
never still, never finished,  
forever shedding, forever forming.

The path beneath your feet  
is the loom upon which your destiny is woven.  
Stand tall, with the poise of one who knows their own weight,  
and let no misstep cloud the horizon of your sight.  
Sink your roots deep into the soil of your being,  
for without knowing yourself,  
you risk becoming a ghost  
wandering through the corridors of your own life.

A flower, though radiant, cannot still the hunger in our bellies.  
If all the world’s flora were only petals,  
our bodies would starve.  
Yet if every plant were only sustenance,  
stripped of beauty,  
our spirits would wither.  
So it is with humanity:  
if all were teachers,  
wisdom would smother joy;  
if all sought only comfort,  
our minds would dull,  
and our days would pass like smoke.

passages.heading: Past, Present, and Future
passages.text:
Every taking demands its recompense.  
Nothing in this world comes without a price.  
The natural order knows this well —  
even the plants, breathing in the air,  
return it as oxygen,  
a quiet covenant with all who live.

What some call flaws,  
others name beauty —  
like a weed in a garden  
that refuses to bow to the gardener’s design.  
So too with us:  
if our worth is unseen,  
perhaps it is not we who are lacking,  
but the garden itself  
that fails to recognize  
the rare bloom in its midst.

works.title: Love
works.blurb: Childhood trauma and distrust within family.

passages.heading: Love
passages.text:
Love

I never pray for love.  
Why would I?  
I grew up in a house where love was sharpened,  
where it glinted in the light like something beautiful  
until you felt it slide between your ribs.

In that place, love was not a gift—  
it was a lesson,  
a rulebook written in invisible ink  
that only appeared when you broke it.  
I learned early that love was never unconditional,  
only conditioned—  
a currency you earned by obedience,  
by silence,  
by swallowing the truth whole and smiling as it burned.

I was conditioned to love my mother  
because that was the role assigned to me,  
because the world said  
a child must love the woman who bore them.  
But her hugs were snares,  
closing around me with the soft weight of a trap.  
Even as her arms wrapped tight,  
my body remembered  
what her hands had done before,  
and I felt myself recoil,  
a shadow pulling back from the flame.

passages.heading: Love
passages.text:
I was conditioned to love my father  
because his wallet was always open,  
but his heart stayed locked.  
He gave in bills and coins,  
in gifts that glittered but never warmed.  
Even his embraces came with a price tag,  
the paper rasping against my soul,  
reminding me that nothing he gave  
was ever truly free.

So I learned to keep love at a distance.  
To build a moat around my heart  
and salt the earth between myself and anyone  
who might try to cross.  
Because no one I love can wound me  
if I wound myself first—  
if I lay the blade to my own skin  
before they ever get the chance.

And maybe that is the truest thing I know about love:  
that for me,  
it has always been a shadow  
I watch from across the room,  
never daring to step close enough  
to see if it might be warm.

works.title: From Ashes to Ascendancy
works.blurb: Childhood abuse recast as resilience and reclamation.

passages.heading: From Ashes to Ascendancy
passages.text:
### I. The Seeds of Burden  
At eight, a weight of sorrow pressed on tender frame,  
The world dismissed my worth and cloaked me in its shame.  
A teacher’s scorn declared that I was trouble in a guise,  
Yet lonely halls became my strength, where silent hope would rise.

They threatened, “Stop your tears or face a harsher fate,”    
But every sequestered tear forged courage over hate.  
With honors bright as beacons and diplomas to defy  
The twisted words they threw at me, I soared from every lie.

---

### II. The Tower of Silence  
Before me loomed the giants—monsters cloaked in human guise,  
Whose vile, forbidden acts stole trust and dimmed the skies.  
In that crushing, fateful moment, innocence was torn apart,  
Transforming dreams of gentle grace into chains upon my heart.

passages.heading: From Ashes to Ascendancy
passages.text:
Their breach of sacred boundaries etched a scar I can’t ignore,  
Yet even in that darkest hour, from pain I learned to soar.  
Though shadows linger long in echoes of the acts they wove,  
I lit a flame of inner strength no terror can remove.

---

### III. The Stolen Narrative  
They penned a tale in twisted ink, a story not my own,  
Distorting truth with crafted lies until my voice was overthrown.  
Voices rose to mute my plea, to cage the truth inside,  
Yet from the silence of that theft, a rebel soul replied.

I reclaimed each stolen line and reshaped every wounded part,  
Transforming manufactured history into a testament of heart.  
No puppet strings of false accounts can bind what is set free—  
I own my truth, my scars, and now I write my destiny.

---

### IV. The Shield of the Moment  
In storms of doubt and bitter trials, I stand a fortress strong,  
Holding back the ghosts of past, rejecting every wrong.  
With every steady heartbeat, I summon fierce and steady power,  
Defying threats and bitter voices with a spirit that won’t cower.

passages.heading: From Ashes to Ascendancy
passages.text:
I arm myself with memories turned into badges of my fight,  
Each step a rhythmic anthem carved in defiant, pulsing light.  
The silence after all their venom bursts with victories untold—  
In reclaiming all I once had lost, I transmute the dark to gold.

---

### V. Epilogue – Rising in Resilience  
Those hollow words that bound with “I love you, but” like chains,  
Could never root in a resolve that triumphs over pains.  
The blaze of hate and anguish that scorched my tender days  
Now fuels a vibrant courage, igniting ever-brighter rays.

Today, my eyes hold embers that no threat can disbelieve,  
For I rise each day unbroken—a phoenix born to weave  
A life of raw resistance, a story fiercely self-made.  
A survivor’s truth affirmed in every step and every shade.

works.title: A Crown Without a Kingdom
works.blurb: Mortality and the impermanence of ambition, argued in a generalized voice rather than confessional first-person.

passages.heading: A Crown Without a Kingdom
passages.text:
A crown without a kingdom

We are not the architects of our fate. 
We are the sculptors of a stone we did not choose. 
Its grain was set before our first breath— its flaws, its fractures, its hidden veins of weakness.

Every strike of the chisel is not creation… it is revelation.

Whether born in the filth of the gutter or the halls of kings, all men are bound to the same laws: Time is finite, but the map stretches on without end, and yet the hunger for completion is never sated.

The pauper who climbs finds the summit barren; the noble who inherits finds the air thin.

Both learn the same truth— the game was never meant to be won.  
There is no finish line… only death.

Contrast gives this world its form. Sweetness is born of bitterness.  
Light is crowned by shadow.  
Value exists only in the presence of its opposite. 
And a blank canvas is not void—its value emerges from your actions.

passages.heading: A Crown Without a Kingdom
passages.text:
Time is the salt that makes the feast worth tasting. 
Without it, there is no urgency. No weight. No worth.

This design is deliberate; no final quest, No ultimate reward. 
Only the eternal cycle—acquire, decay, replace.

Every man dies, but few will learn to live.

When he departs this world, his followers will gather. 
His work will remain—unfinished, unresolved. 
But this… this is not tragedy. 
It is inevitability.

What greater ending than this: To know that those who loved you will carry forward your final chapters.  
When your quill slows… and falls…  
theirs will rise, and the writing will begin anew.

So I say this: do not seek to conquer the world, do not dream of the crown, for all of this is vain. 
Carve your stone knowing it will never be complete, revel in every moment, breathe, and result of your actions.

March knowing the road has no end. For the game is not meant to be won… it was meant to live, to love, and do it again all before Time runs out.

works.title: How It Is
works.blurb: Poverty, inequality, and indifference.

passages.heading: How It Is
passages.text:
How It Is

The first homeless man I ever saw  
His clothes, brittle as the wind, clung to him like a second skin  
My parents whispered he didn’t work hard enough—that he had earned his place beneath the overpass  
I nodded, believing I’d never be like that  
I saw the world exactly as I was told it was

Most of what I saw pressed against my ribs, heavy

Poverty—sprawled in quiet corners, invisible until you learned to see it  
Hardship—etched into the backs of hands, into the cracks of worn soles  
Hunger—lean and hollow, curling around ribs like a slow, patient fire  
Overdose—bodies turned to stillness, faces emptied of time  
Pain—woven into the fabric of existence, stitched into shadows

I asked why people would choose this  
Why they would drift instead of stand, break instead of build

passages.heading: How It Is
passages.text:
Years passed, and I learned:  
“How it is” isn’t how it has to be

No one had to starve  
No one had to suffer  
No one had to taste the bitterness of being forgotten

So why?

passages.heading: Because that’s just the way it is
passages.text:
I watched the world forget,  
watched people step over suffering like cracks in the sidewalk,  
like it wasn’t worth bending down to acknowledge.

They whispered reasons under their breath—  
*They should have tried harder.*  
*They must have done something wrong.*  
*You can’t save everyone.*

Their voices curled into silence,  
settling into the empty spaces between convenience and indifference.

I saw them turn their heads at hunger,  
walk faster past the hollow-eyed ghosts of the system’s failure,  
tighten their grips on purses and convictions,  
because sympathy costs too much.

I asked why—  
why the world carries wealth in its pockets but lets children starve,  
why comfort is built on the backs of the broken,  
why suffering is the price of stability.

Years passed, and I learned:  
It isn’t just “how it is.”  
It’s how we allow it to be.

No one had to turn away.  
No one had to forget.  
No one had to accept pain as collateral for progress.

passages.heading: Because that’s just the way it is
passages.text:
So why?

Because it’s easier than change.

I watched them feast,  
watched their tables bend beneath the weight of their indulgence,  
watched them drink until their laughter slurred,  
until hunger became a rumor,  
until excess rotted inside them, turning their stomachs sick with privilege.

They carved the world into portions,  
sold the sky in parcels,  
hoarded the sun in bank vaults,  
turned land into numbers, lives into assets,  
until nothing was untouched by price.

Their children never hungered, never reached, never wondered.  
They lived on money they never earned,  
slept in beds they never built,  
walked streets where no footstep before them was truly their own.

With nothing to strive for, they found misery in luxury,  
crafted suffering from silk sheets and golden halls,  
called it *ennui*, called it *emptiness*,  
never once tasted the bitterness of having nothing.

I asked why—  
why wealth could grow but never fill,  
why abundance could rot but never nourish,  
why they ate the world only to leave it hollow.

passages.heading: Because that’s just the way it is
passages.text:
Years passed, and I learned:  
It isn’t just “how it is.”  
It’s how it was bought to be.

works.title: My Wish
works.blurb: Authenticity, self-acceptance, and autonomy.

passages.heading: My Wish
passages.text:
My wish

My wish is not for material worries.  
I do not beg for gold.  
I do not wish to never grow old.  
My wish is not wealth like winter flurries.

My wish is not for love never-ending.  
I do not groan for fable.  
I do not grovel for a seat at the table.  
My wish is not for a will unbending.

No my wish is to be me.  
Not better or worse.  
Not to live with remorse.  
My wish is to be.

My wish is to be me.  
No matter who it angers.  
No matter the strangers.  
My wish is to be, who ever the fuck that my be.

works.title: The Sun's Bright Light
works.blurb: Gratitude and vitality through nature imagery.

passages.heading: The Sun's Bright Light
passages.text:
The sun's bright light, a golden hue,  
Forever young, yet ancient too.  
Its beams stretch wide from corner to ledge,  
With my eye I see the sky, where azure sings and pledges.  
As it draws near, its glow is clear,  
A gentle warmth that I hold dear.  
I recall what I've always known—  
Like a tree in December, its light has shone.  
For it is life, and it gives us breath,  
A radiant gift that conquers death.

works.title: Taking All From the Rich
works.blurb: Satirical critique of wealth inequality, argued rather than confessed.

passages.heading: Taking All From the Rich
passages.text:
Taking all from the rich, to give to the poor  
Is the same as taking from the poor, to give the rich more.  
The world doesn’t need another Robin Hood,  
Just someone who’s willing to do something good.

For though King John wore the villain's crown,  
Two wrongs can’t make a right; they just drag us down.  
In the end, it’s a dirge we all must face,  
A cycle of heartache in an endless race.

works.title: Today's Wine
works.blurb: Impermanence and present-moment mindfulness.

passages.heading: Todays Wine
passages.text:
Todays Wine

Today's wine is particularly fine,  
Exquisitely crafted, a true divine.

For yesterday's wine has slipped from our grasp,  
Its taste lingers sweet, but it doth not last

And tomorrow's wine has yet to delight,  
For it’s future’s promise, not here in our sight.

Today’s wine is ours, to savor and share,  
Though it may not be perfect, it’s still worth a care.  
Remember, not all things are destined to last,  
For memories linger, but they are the past.

Embrace the present, let your spirit flow,  
For today is a gift; in this moment, we grow.

works.title: The Daybook of Crumb's Ovens
works.blurb: Tamsin Crumb's daybook for Saturday 21 October 1893, room by room through the four back rooms of Crumb's Ovens, with one sack and the sweepings, three dead, the island's arithmetic of loaves and the unsigned papers she folds into the bread.

passages.heading: I. The cold room. The island's hour.
passages.text:
Up before anyone.

The cold room has a door to the shop, a shelf for the crock, a gap behind the crock where a hand can go, and a place where I am found out. This morning that place is the flour bin. One sack and the sweepings. No flour came Friday. None will come today.

Recipe: one spoon of yesterday, one cup of flour, water to the second knuckle. Stir on the island's hour, not the mainland's. The clock on the wall is the Company's. The crock keeps the other one.

I feed the crock. I feed the town. I feed the dead.

Three nights now, they say, since Aldous Vane. The wire said it, or the square did. I could not tell you which, and nobody in this town would think to ask me. I did not cry. I fed the crock at the hour, and the crock rose, and I took that for an answer, because it was the only one I was given.

passages.heading: I. The cold room. The island's hour.
passages.text:
People used to ask whether I came inland for him or for the cup. I still do not know. I know the spoon. I know the hour. I know that what rises in this crock is the cup's life and not the cup, and that the cup went where he went.

Who feeds the cup now?

passages.heading: II. The mixing room. Four.
passages.text:
I don't know. That is the first thing I knead into the dough every morning: I don't know.

Recipe for a Rumour Loaf: flour, water, salt, a fist of the daughter, and one folded paper. Fold the paper twice. Lay it flat under the fold of the dough. Shape it tight so nothing shows at the seam.

The papers come to me unsigned. Under a coin on the counter. Under the door before light. Once, inside a glove someone handed back across the counter. I have never written one. I have folded every one.

I do not read them. I read them. I bake them anyway.

This week the slips go to the Tribunal, and a day is all it takes to harden a rumour into an indictment, and the gallows stands at the Bell. I cannot tell you whether any paper that passed through my hands ever reached the trapdoor. I can tell you I did not ask.

passages.heading: II. The mixing room. Four.
passages.text:
This morning I cut into a loaf I shaped last night, to test the crumb, and there was a paper in it already. Folded twice. Laid flat. Not mine. It could have been a customer's hand reaching over the bench while my back was turned. It could have been the boy who carries the baskets. It could have been my own hands, tired past remembering. I write all three down and I choose none.

If I do not know what I carry, am I innocent of it?

passages.heading: III. The oven room. Five.
passages.text:
The oven answers that, the way it answers everything: no.

The oven is clay. Vane's men built it behind the tents before there was a town to put it in, and the town grew up around it like a crust. Recipe: fire it till the walls go white. Rake it. Swab it. Bake out yesterday's proof. Do not open the door to look.

On Thursday night, or Wednesday (the week runs together now), someone emptied the till. They left a gold coin on the hearth-lip, the way you tip for good bread. They left a boot in the flour dust, long in the stride, the toe toward the back door.

I swept it.

I sweep every night. That is my alibi, and it is theirs. The Detective came with his case file the next noon and asked whether anything was out of place. I said the floor was clean, and that was true.

passages.heading: III. The oven room. Five.
passages.text:
I cannot spend the coin. Gold asks where it came from. So it sits behind the crock, in the place a hand can go.

Up before anyone, and still somebody was here first.

What is a gold coin worth in a town where flour comes by train, and the train brought none?

passages.heading: IV. The proofing room. Before the train.
passages.text:
Less than a sack of flour. Exactly what I did next.

The proofing room is the only room in this house that belongs to tomorrow. Recipe: shape, cover, set in the cold, and leave it alone to become what it is going to be.

Three dead. Dora Finch. Wilf. Percy. One loaf to every mourner and three to each of the dead. That is the island's arithmetic, four hundred years old, and I have one sack and the sweepings.

The Company recognises no custom of mourning, the Articles say, and then they tolerate my table and write: "No rent shall be assessed on the three loaves set for the dead". The bread of the dead is the only bread in HollowMere the Company takes no cut of.

But who is the bread for?

This part is mine, and nobody else's. I cut the mourners' loaves to halves. Every living mouth at that table will get half, so that every dead one keeps three. Nobody ordered it. Nobody will thank me for it. I did it with the scraper in one stroke, the way you do a thing you have already decided.

passages.heading: IV. The proofing room. Before the train.
passages.text:
And there is more. On my way in, before the crock, I went to the stone with tomorrow's date, as I have gone every morning this week, and read the new name on it. I have not written that name in this book. I will not write it here.

But three more loaves are proving under the cloth at the end of the bench, made from the living's flour, and they are not for Dora, or Wilf, or Percy.

Did I bake for a death, or does a death come to be baked for? Nobody has seen the name cut. Nobody has seen me shape these.

Is it grief, done early, or an order filled?

passages.heading: V. The wake table. Station Rush.
passages.text:
I do not answer. I set the table.

Ten plates. Three for the dead, three loaves to each. Six for the halves, heaped. The tenth I set for whoever remains, and leave.

I know who bought which loaf. That is the whole of my office.

Dora Finch bought the end of the rye and held the seal up close to read it, through spectacles mended with thread, as if a crumb could have writing on it. Wilf paid for a heel once in the key of G, on my step, because he had no scrip and I had no mind to refuse a tune. Percy came in with three marbles and his bootlace undone and asked every time whether the dead ones were for eating, and every time I said, not by you.

I press a crumb into each loaf and seal it in candle wax, white on the dark crust. Every mouth that eats carries off a small hard piece of who is gone.

passages.heading: V. The wake table. Station Rush.
passages.text:
At the rush the Undertaker's boy comes in with his cap in his hands. Four, he says. Make it four. I ask him four for whom. He looks at his paper and says the paper says four. I count the dead I know of and get three, and the numbers will not lie down together. I do not bake it. I do not refuse it. I look at the tenth plate, already set.

The mourners sit. They eat the halves. Nobody says the loaves are small. Nobody has to.

Up before anyone, flour to the elbows, and the dead fed first.

The island taught me to feed the dead. HollowMere taught me who goes hungry for it.

works.title: Hopscotch
works.blurb: the counting rhyme chalked under the lantern on the square: ten squares, ten children with grown-up names, a stanza each for a landmark of HollowMere, and a refrain about hopping the stone and not looking down.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
One for the bell, and the bell brings the town.
Alfie counted the gallows stairs: thirteen up, and none come down.
Alfie climbed in a crate on the morning train.
The crate went east. It never wrote.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Two for the pump, two hands on the iron.
Nell pumped first and Nell drank first.
Fever by Friday. Ribbons, blue.
Nell rode the back car east.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Three for the lantern we chalk it under.
It keeps the wolves off. It keeps us in.
Sid chased his shadow to where the light stops.
Where does the light stop?
Sid knew. His cap's on the fence.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Four for the Lantern, sign and all.
The barman carried it into the mere.
Flo swept the floor for a penny a night
and finished the cups when Mrs Grieves wasn't looking.
Something in a cup was not sugar.
Flo's broom is still by the door.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Five for the oven, up before light,
ten plates on the wake table, laid out right.
Peg stole the heel off every loaf.
One for each mourner and three for the dead:
three on Peg's plate,
and nobody took the heel.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Six for the manor, where the clock stopped
at eleven forty-seven and stayed.
Ted wound his gran's clock every night
and told the time by the train.
Rent comes due when the sun's straight up.
Ted went to the mill to pay it with his hands.
He's at the loft window. He doesn't wave.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Seven for the well, and the ladder down.
Winnie dropped pebbles and counted the splash.
Winnie threw her stone and the stone went in.
Winnie went down the ladder to fetch it.
We counted for her.
We are counting still.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Eight for the chapel and the Company bell.
Lil sang loudest, always a beat ahead.
Lil went up to the rope to ring it in.
The hymn came out one voice short.
There's a glove in the rope.
Nobody says whose.

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Nine for the pines, and the pines aren't empty.
May was scared of the dark,
so May walked toward every light.
There was a light in the fen. May walked.
Who's holding the lantern out there in the fen?

*Ten chalk squares and ten of us.*
  *Hop the stone and don't look down.*

Who chalks it fresh when we're all in bed?

But the tenth square isn't chalk.

Ten for the stone with tomorrow's name.
I hopped every one of them. That's the rule:
you never land where the stone is lying.
Alfie. Nell. Sid. Flo. Peg.
Ted. Winnie. Lil. May.
I hid. I watched. I remember.
I can read. I read it.
I won't read it out.

passages.heading: chalked under the lantern on the square
passages.text:
*Ten chalk squares and one of me.*
  *Throw your stone. It's your turn now.*

Nobody's out in HollowMere.
Everybody's next.

works.title: Dear Katie
works.blurb: an amends letter reckoning with a past relationship's harm and the author's own role in it.

passages.heading: Dear Katie
passages.text:
Dear Katie,

I don’t think I’m writing this for you. In truth, I’m writing to get something off my chest.

I loved you even when it wasn’t good for both of us. I was so consumed by your love that I lost sight of my own. I craved your approval so much that I ignored my own feelings. I ran through every stop sign in what I called love, but it was just a hormonal cry for help because I was alone in this scary world, navigating changes I couldn’t comprehend. I was filled with hate that came from twisted feelings of love.

I pushed you away because losing you meant not being able to be with you. But truthfully, I didn’t even know what that meant. Love isn’t just sex. I knew that, but then again, maybe I thought the only way you’d love me like I loved you was if I was good at sex. I wanted something for you that I didn’t even want. In my hurry to please some idealistic version of our love, I crossed both our boundaries and created so much shame in our friendship that I left.

passages.heading: Dear Katie
passages.text:
I didn’t just leave physically; I left emotionally, mentally, and with all my presents. I went from a force of love in your life to just another example of the shitty men who leave. I fear I might have failed to keep my promises to you and to my younger self. I meant to be there for you, but I put myself first and became selfish, twisted, and alone. I used my time to cause harm when I could have sought to heal myself sooner and helped those around me find their way to healing as well.

That’s why I’ve come to the conclusion that in order to heal myself, I must first accept and apologize for doing harm to others when I was in pain. My actions were not my best, and I seek to amend them in the present.

I can’t predict the future or change the past. Instead, I’ll focus on the present moment and appreciate the experiences that come my way. I’ll see people for who they are and understand that no one is a mere object of my desires.

works.title: Dream Journal
works.blurb: six dream entries tracing artistic self-mythology, romantic reckoning, and anima integration.

passages.heading: Dream Journal
passages.text: Dream Journal

passages.heading: The Night I Became the Artist
passages.text:
I went to sleep expecting nothing more than rest, but instead I slipped into a world that felt like revelation. I woke inside the dream with a brush already in my hand, sweat gathering at my temples, my brow tight with focus. Before me stretched a blank expanse—an abyss waiting to be transformed. And from that nothingness, color erupted. It didn’t flow gently; it detonated, volcanic and alive, as if creation itself had been compressed inside me and was finally breaking free.

I watched myself paint with a precision I’ve never known in waking life. Every stroke had depth, width, intention. I measured instinctively, like a scientist calibrating an experiment that could alter the world. Yet I wasn’t just the painter. I was also the witness—hovering just outside my own body, astonished by the confidence and mastery I saw. It felt holy, as if some divine hand had reached down to guide mine. I didn’t feel like myself, and yet I felt more myself than ever.

passages.heading: The Night I Became the Artist
passages.text:
The strangest part was how the real world seeped into the dream. Each time my eyes flickered open, the window beside my bed poured its light into the vision. Tree limbs cast silhouettes across the room, and those shapes bent themselves into the dream’s canvas. The shimmer of morning light became brushstrokes. The organic structures outside fused with the inner studio of my mind. Even when I woke, the dream didn’t stop. It waited for me, held its shape, and pulled me back in.

There was another version of me inside that dream—an older, steadier, impossibly confident self. He moved like a producer, a creator, an elder who had already lived the life I’m still reaching for. He never hesitated. He never doubted. He painted as if he had been doing it for centuries. And I realized I wasn’t just dreaming; I was being taught. I was the student, absorbing lessons from a future self who knew exactly what I needed to see.

passages.heading: The Night I Became the Artist
passages.text:
The dream carried the same magic I knew as a child—the forests and glades where I once danced alone, imagining spirits in the trees and castles on the horizon. Back then, I bent reality with my thoughts. In this dream, that power returned, but refined, matured, sharpened. It felt like the child I used to be and the artist I hope to become finally met in the same room.

When I finally woke for good, the dream clung to me—vivid, emotional, impossibly alive. I felt gratitude, fulfillment, and a strange sense of being chosen. It was a gift, a reminder, a covenant. A message from the deepest part of myself saying: You are becoming. Don’t give up. The best version of you is already waiting.

V. 2  
There are dreams that feel like static—loose, dissolving, forgettable.  
And then there are the other ones.  
The ones that arrive like detonations.
